stem: Use the diagram. Give another name for plane K.
title: Another name for a plane
steps: Plane K contains D, E, F, G, and H.
A plane can be named with one capital letter, like plane K, or with three points that are in it. Plane K contains points D, E, F, G, and H.
J is on line c, above the plane: not in plane K.
Point J is on line c, but it sits above the plane, so we can't use J.
The three points can't all be on one line.
The three points also can't all lie on one line. D, E, and F are all on line k, so don't use those three together.
plane FHG
F, H, and G are in the plane and are not on one line. So another name is plane F H G. Other answers like plane D H G work too.

stem: Use the diagram. Name a point that is not coplanar with E, G, and H.
title: A point that is not coplanar
steps: E, G, and H are in plane L.
Coplanar points lie in the same plane. E, G, and H are all in plane L.
Which point is not in plane L?
So look for a point that is not in plane L.
K is on line j, above the plane.
Point K is on line j, but it is above the plane, not in it. Every other point is in plane L.
K
So the answer is K.

stem: Use the diagram. Give another name for line DH.
title: Another name for a line
steps: Line DH goes through D, E, and H: it is line m.
A line can be named by any two of its points, or by its lowercase letter. D, E, and H are all on line m.
line m, line DE, line EH, line HD, …
So line D H is also line m, line D E, line E H, or line H D. The order of the two points doesn't matter.
line HD
One answer is line H D.

stem: Use the diagram. Name three collinear points.
title: Three collinear points
steps: collinear: on the same line
Collinear points lie on the same line.
K, L, and M are all on line d.
Points K, L, and M are all on line d.
K, L, and M
So K, L, and M are collinear. Watch out: Q is on line w, not line d, so it can't be used with K and M.

stem: Use the diagram. Name the intersection of line k and plane X.
title: The intersection of a line and a plane
steps: Line k crosses plane X.
Line k is not in plane X. It passes through it.
It crosses at point S.
A line that crosses a plane meets it at one point. Line k goes through plane X at point S.
point S
So the intersection is point S.

stem: Use the diagram. What is another name for ray PQ?
title: Another name for a ray
steps: Ray PQ starts at P and goes through Q.
A ray is named by its endpoint first, then any other point on it. Ray P Q starts at P and goes through Q.
It keeps going through R.
It keeps going in the same direction, through R.
ray PR
So ray P Q is also ray P R. The endpoint P always comes first.

stem: Use the diagram. What is another name for Q̅P̅?
title: Another name for a segment
steps: Q̅P̅: the segment with endpoints Q and P
Q P with a bar over it is a segment. Its endpoints are Q and P.
P̅Q̅
A segment can be named with its endpoints in either order. So Q P is also P Q.

stem: Use the diagram. Name a pair of opposite rays.
title: A pair of opposite rays
steps: opposite rays: same endpoint, opposite directions, one line
Opposite rays share an endpoint and point in opposite directions along the same line.
On line u, P is between H and Q.
On line u, point P is between H and Q.
ray PH and ray PQ
So ray P H and ray P Q are opposite rays. Ray P T and ray P S, on line m, are another pair.

stem: Use the diagram. Name all rays with endpoint G.
title: All rays with a given endpoint
steps: G is where lines j and a cross.
Point G is where the two lines cross.
From G, a ray goes toward each other point.
From G, there is one ray toward each point on the lines: F, K, H, and J.
ray GF, ray GK, ray GH, ray GJ
So the rays are G F, G K, G H, and G J. Each name starts with G, the endpoint.

stem: Use the diagram. Name a pair of rays that are not opposite rays.
title: Rays that are not opposite
steps: opposite rays: same endpoint, opposite directions, one line
Opposite rays share an endpoint and point in opposite directions along one line.
Pick two rays from L on different lines.
To get rays that are not opposite, pick two rays from L that are on different lines.
ray LH and ray LU
Ray L H is on line m, and ray L U is on line p. They are not opposite rays.

stem: Use the diagram. Name all the points that are not coplanar with points J, H, and L.
title: Points that are not coplanar (box)
steps: J, H, and L are on the bottom face HJKL.
In the box, J, H, and L are corners of the bottom face, H J K L.
K is the fourth corner of that face.
K is the fourth corner of that face, so K is coplanar with them.
The top corners are not in that plane.
The top corners, D, E, F, and G, are not in the plane of the bottom face.
D, E, F, G
So the points that are not coplanar with J, H, and L are D, E, F, and G.

stem: Use the diagram. Name the intersection of plane DHE and plane LQD.
title: The intersection of two planes (box)
steps: Plane DHE is the top face DEHL.
Find the face that holds each plane. D, H, and E are on the top face, D E H L.
Plane LQD is the left face DLXQ.
L, Q, and D are on the left face, D L X Q.
They share edge DL.
Two planes meet in a line. These two faces share the edge D L.
line DL
So the intersection is line D L.

stem: Use the diagram. Name a point that is coplanar with points S, K, and P.
title: A point coplanar with three points (box)
steps: S, K, and P are corners of the face KNSP.
S, K, and P are corners of the left face, K N S P.
The fourth corner is N.
The fourth corner of that face is N.
N
So N is coplanar with S, K, and P.

stem: Name the geometric term modeled by the edge of a ruler.
title: Geometric terms in real life
steps: Point: one location
A point is a single location, like a star in the sky or the tip of a pencil.
Segment: straight, two endpoints
A segment is straight with two endpoints, like the edge of a ruler.
Ray: one endpoint, goes on in one direction
A ray starts at one point and goes on forever in one direction, like a flashlight beam.
Line: goes on in both directions
A line goes on forever in both directions, like a straight track that never ends.
Plane: a flat surface that goes on forever
A plane is a flat surface, like a floor or a wall that goes on and on.
the edge of a ruler: straight, with two ends → segment
The edge of a ruler is straight and has two ends, so it models a segment.

stem: What is the intersection of a line and a plane, when the line crosses the plane but does not lie in it?
title: What is the intersection?
steps: two lines that cross → a point
Two different lines that cross meet at one point.
two planes that cross → a line
Two different planes that cross meet in a line, like two walls meeting in a corner.
a line crossing a plane → a point
A line that passes through a plane meets it at one point.
a line in a plane → the whole line
If the line lies in the plane, every point of the line is in the plane, so the intersection is the whole line.
parallel planes → no intersection
Parallel planes never meet.
crosses the plane, not in it → a point
In this question, the line crosses the plane but is not in it, so the answer is a point.

stem: 11 points are marked on a line. How many different segments have two of these points as endpoints? How many different rays have one of these points as their endpoint?
title: Challenge: counting segments and rays
steps: 11 points on one line
There are 11 points on a line. Count segments first, then rays.
each point pairs with 10 others: 11 · 10
Every segment uses two of the points. Each point pairs with the 10 others: 11 times 10 is 110.
110 ÷ 2 = 55 segments
That counts every segment twice, once from each end. So divide by 2: 55 segments.
each point: 2 opposite rays → 2 · 11 = 22 rays
Each point is the endpoint of two rays, one going each way. 2 times 11 is 22 rays.
55 segments; 22 rays
So there are 55 segments and 22 rays.

stem: Use the ruler to find the length of L̅Q̅ to the nearest tenth of a centimeter.
title: Measuring with a ruler
steps: L is at 0.4 cm.
Read where each endpoint lines up on the ruler. L lines up with 0.4 centimeters.
Q is at 2.6 cm.
Q lines up with 2.6 centimeters.
The length is the distance between the two readings: the absolute value of their difference.
2.6 minus 0.4 is 2.2. So L Q is 2.2 centimeters.

stem: Plot the points A(5, 3), B(5, 7), C(6, 0), and D(8, 0) on the grid (use Draw). Then determine whether A̅B̅ and C̅D̅ are congruent.
title: Are the segments congruent?
steps: Plot the four points. Congruent segments have the same length, so find both lengths.
A and B have the same x → vertical: AB = |7 − 3| = 4
A and B have the same x coordinate, so A B is vertical. Its length is the difference of the y values: 7 minus 3 is 4.
C and D have the same y → horizontal: CD = |8 − 6| = 2
C and D have the same y coordinate, so C D is horizontal. Its length is 8 minus 6, which is 2.
4 ≠ 2 → not congruent
The lengths are different, so the segments are not congruent.

stem: Find HQ.
title: Segment Addition: find the whole segment
steps: HQ = HL + LQ
Segment Addition Postulate: when L is between H and Q, the two parts add up to the whole. H Q equals H L plus L Q.
H L is 8 and L Q is 25.
So H Q is 33.

stem: MP = 35. Find MN.
title: Segment Addition: find a part
steps: MP = MN + NP
The whole segment M P is made of the parts M N and N P.
M P is 35 and N P is 19.
Subtract 19 from both sides: M N is 16.

stem: EG = 45. Find the value of x. Then find EF and FG.
title: Segment Addition with x
steps: EF + FG = EG
The two parts add up to the whole: E F plus F G equals E G.
Put in the expressions and the total, 45.
Combine like terms: 6 x plus 5 x is 11 x, and negative 12 plus 2 is negative 10.
Add 10: 11 x is 55. Divide by 11: x is 5.
Put 5 back in: E F is 30 minus 12, which is 18. F G is 25 plus 2, which is 27.
Check: 18 plus 27 is 45.

stem: Point B lies on segment AC. AB = 3x + 9, BC = 6x + 2, and AC = 6x + 26. Find x and the length of AC.
title: Challenge: Segment Addition with three expressions
steps: AB + BC = AC
B is on segment A C, so A B plus B C equals A C.
Put in all three expressions.
Combine like terms on the left.
Subtract 6 x and 11 from both sides: 3 x is 15, so x is 5.
The question also asks for A C: 30 plus 26 is 56.

stem: Line e bisects D̅T̅ at L. Find DL.
title: Segment bisector: find half the segment
steps: bisects → L is the midpoint: DL = LT
A bisector cuts a segment at its midpoint. So D L equals L T.
Set the two halves equal.
Subtract 4 x and 13 from both sides: 4 x is 20, so x is 5.
Put 5 into D L: 40 plus 13 is 53.

stem: Line u bisects A̅C̅ at B. Find AC.
title: Segment bisector: find the whole segment
steps: bisects → B is the midpoint: AB = BC
The bisector cuts A C at its midpoint B, so A B equals B C.
Set the halves equal.
Subtract 2 x and 4 from both sides: 12 equals 2 x, so x is 6.
Each half: 12 plus 16 is 28.
The question asks for the whole segment, A C. That's two halves: 56.

stem: The endpoints of C̅D̅ are C(6, 7) and D(4, 8). Find the coordinates of the midpoint M.
title: The Midpoint Formula
steps: The midpoint averages the x coordinates and averages the y coordinates.
The x values are 6 and 4: their average is 5.
The y values are 7 and 8: their average is 7.5.
So the midpoint is 5, 7.5.

stem: The midpoint M and one endpoint G of G̅H̅ are given. Find the coordinates of the other endpoint H.   G(6, 7) and M(4, −9)
title: Find the other endpoint
steps: From G to M, find how far each coordinate moves.
x goes from 6 to 4: that's 2 to the left. y goes from 7 to negative 9: that's 16 down.
M is halfway, so H is the same distance past M. 4 minus 2 is 2, and negative 9 minus 16 is negative 25.
Check with the Midpoint Formula: the averages are 4 and negative 9. That's M.

stem: Find the distance between K(9, 7) and L(6, 8). Round to the nearest tenth if necessary.
title: The Distance Formula
steps: d = √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²)
The Distance Formula: the square root of the change in x squared plus the change in y squared.
From K to L, x changes by negative 3 and y changes by 1.
Square them: 9 and 1. Add: 10.
The square root of 10 is about 3.2.

stem: M(−3, −7) is the midpoint of segment AB, and A is at (−9, −1). Find the coordinates of B and the length of AB. Give an exact answer.
title: Challenge: the other endpoint, then the length
steps: Example: from A to M, x goes up 6 and y goes down 6.
M is halfway, so B is 6 more in x and 6 less in y: 3, negative 13.
From A to B, x changes by 12 and y changes by negative 12.
144 plus 144 is 288, which is 144 times 2. The square root is 12 root 2.

stem: Classify the polygon by the number of sides. Tell whether it is convex or concave, and whether it is regular or irregular.
title: Classify a polygon
steps: count the sides: 7 → heptagon
First count the sides. This polygon has 7 sides, so it is a heptagon. 3 is a triangle, 4 a quadrilateral, 5 a pentagon, 6 a hexagon, 7 a heptagon, and 8 an octagon.
convex or concave? Does any side's line go through the inside?
Next, convex or concave. Imagine extending each side into a line. If one of those lines goes through the inside of the polygon, it is concave. A concave polygon has a dent, a corner pointing in.
no dents → convex
This polygon has no dents. None of those lines go through the inside, so it is convex.
regular: all sides and all angles congruent
Last, regular or irregular. A regular polygon has all sides congruent and all angles congruent.
sides are different lengths → irregular
These sides are not all the same length, so it is irregular.
heptagon; convex; irregular
So the answer is heptagon, convex, irregular.

stem: Find the perimeter of the polygon. Round to the nearest tenth if necessary.
title: Perimeter in the coordinate plane
steps: Perimeter is the distance around. Find each side length, then add.
GK = 4 (horizontal: count)
G K is horizontal: from x equals negative 2 to 2 is 4 units.
WG = 4 (vertical: count)
W G is vertical: from y equals negative 3 to 1 is 4 units.
K W is slanted, so use the Distance Formula: x changes by 4 and y changes by 4. The square root of 16 plus 16 is root 32, about 5.7.
Add the three sides: about 13.7 units.

stem: Find the area of the polygon.
title: Area in the coordinate plane: a triangle
steps: This polygon is a triangle.
base GK = 4
Pick a horizontal side as the base. G K goes from x equals negative 2 to 2, so the base is 4.
height = vertical distance to W = 4
The height is the vertical distance from the base up to W: from y equals negative 3 to 1 is 4.
The area of a triangle is one half base times height: one half times 4 times 4 is 8 square units.

stem: Find the area of the polygon with the given vertices.   G(−4, −6), R(0, −6), S(0, −1), U(−4, −1)
title: Area in the coordinate plane: a rectangle
steps: These four points make a rectangle. Its sides are horizontal and vertical.
length GR = 0 − (−4) = 4
G R is horizontal: from x equals negative 4 to 0 is 4.
width RS = −1 − (−6) = 5
R S is vertical: from y equals negative 6 to negative 1 is 5.
Area of a rectangle is length times width: 20 square units.

stem: Rectangle ABCD has vertices A(1, −6), B(3, −9), C(12, −3), and D(10, 0). Find its perimeter (exact) and its area.
title: Challenge: a tilted rectangle
steps: The sides are slanted, so you can't count the width and height on the grid. Use the Distance Formula.
From A to B, x changes by 2 and y by 3. A B is root 13.
From B to C, x changes by 9 and y by 6. 81 plus 36 is 117, which is 9 times 13. So B C is 3 root 13.
A rectangle has two of each side: 2 times 4 root 13 is 8 root 13.
Area is length times width: root 13 times 3 root 13 is 3 times 13, which is 39.

stem: Which list gives three correct names for the angle?
title: Naming angles
steps: vertex: L
An angle can be named three ways. First, find the vertex, where the two rays start. Here it's L.
∠L
You can name it by its vertex alone: angle L. That works when only one angle is at that vertex.
You can name it by the number inside it: angle 2.
∠HLQ or ∠QLH
Or by three points: one on each ray, with the vertex in the middle. Angle H L Q, or angle Q L H.
∠HLQ, ∠QLH, ∠L
So a correct list is angle H L Q, angle Q L H, angle L. A name like angle L H Q is wrong, because the vertex isn't in the middle.

stem: Use the protractor. Find m∠PQM. Then classify the angle.
title: Measure and classify with a protractor
steps: QP crosses the scale at 40°
Read both rays on the same scale. Use the scale that starts at 0 on one of the sides. Ray Q P crosses that scale at 40.
QM crosses the same scale at 135°
Ray Q M crosses the same scale at 135.
The angle is the difference: 135 minus 40 is 95 degrees.
acute < 90°, right = 90°, obtuse 90°–180°, straight = 180°
Acute is less than 90, right is exactly 90, obtuse is between 90 and 180, and straight is 180.
95° → obtuse
95 degrees is obtuse.

stem: Find m∠FGJ.
title: Angle Addition: find the whole angle
steps: m∠FGJ = m∠FGH + m∠HGJ
Angle Addition Postulate: ray G H splits angle F G J into two parts, and the parts add up to the whole.
39 plus 49 is 88 degrees.

stem: ∠HLU is a straight angle. Find m∠QLU.
title: Angle Addition: a straight angle
steps: ∠HLU is straight: 180°
A straight angle is a straight line, and it measures 180 degrees.
m∠HLQ + m∠QLU = 180°
Ray L Q splits it into two parts that add to 180.
One part is 136, so the other is 180 minus 136: 44 degrees.

stem: m∠MNQ = 71°. Find m∠MNP.
title: Angle Addition: find a part
steps: m∠MNP + m∠PNQ = m∠MNQ
The two parts add up to the whole angle M N Q.
Angle P N Q is 35 and the whole is 71.
Subtract: 36 degrees.

stem: ∠EFH is a right angle. Find m∠EFG and m∠GFH.
title: Angle Addition with x: a right angle
steps: A right angle is 90 degrees, so the two parts add to 90.
Combine like terms.
Add 53: 13 x is 143. Divide by 13: x is 11.
Put 11 back in: 57 degrees and 33 degrees. Check: they add to 90.

stem: m∠EFH = 143°. Find m∠EFG and m∠GFH.
title: Angle Addition with x: a given total
steps: The two parts add to the whole angle, 143 degrees.
Combine like terms.
Subtract 26: 13 x is 117. Divide by 13: x is 9.
Put 9 back in: 127 and 16 degrees. Check: they add to 143.

stem: ∠JMX is a straight angle. Find m∠JMP and m∠PMX.
title: Angle Addition with x: a straight angle
steps: A straight angle is 180 degrees, so the parts add to 180.
Combine like terms.
Subtract 92: 11 x is 88, so x is 8.
Put 8 back in: 120 and 60 degrees. They add to 180.

stem: Ray LQ bisects ∠HLU. m∠HLQ = 21°. Find m∠ULQ and m∠HLU.
title: Angle bisector: given one half
steps: bisector → two congruent halves
A bisector splits an angle into two congruent angles.
m∠ULQ = m∠HLQ = 21°
So the other half, angle U L Q, is also 21 degrees.
The whole angle is two halves: 42 degrees.

stem: Ray JN bisects ∠AJP. Find m∠AJN, m∠PJN, and m∠AJP.
title: Angle bisector with x
steps: m∠AJN = m∠PJN
The bisector makes the two halves equal.
Set the expressions equal.
Subtract 4 x and add 50: 55 equals 5 x, so x is 11.
Each half is 44 plus 5: 49 degrees.
The whole angle is 98 degrees.

stem: Ray BD bisects ∠ABC. m∠ABD = (2x + 14)° and m∠ABC = (7x + 1)°. Find x and m∠ABC.
title: Challenge: angle bisector with expressions
steps: m∠ABC = 2 · m∠ABD
A bisector splits the angle into two equal halves, so the whole angle is twice one half.
Put in the expressions and distribute the 2.
Subtract 4 x and 1: 3 x is 27, so x is 9.
The whole angle is 63 plus 1: 64 degrees.

title: Find an angle: vertical angles
steps: two lines cross → 4 angles
Two lines cross and make four angles.
∠4 and ∠2 are across from each other
Angles 4 and 2 are across from each other, so they are vertical angles.
vertical angles are congruent: m∠2 = 148°
Vertical angles are congruent, so angle 2 is also 148 degrees.

title: Find an angle: a linear pair
steps: ∠1 and ∠2 are side by side on a line
Angles 1 and 2 are next to each other, and together they make a straight line. They form a linear pair.
linear pair → supplementary: they add to 180°
A linear pair is supplementary: the two angles add to 180 degrees.
So angle 2 is 180 minus 73: 107 degrees.

stem: Identify all the linear pairs that include ∠1.
title: Linear pairs
steps: linear pair: adjacent angles whose outer sides make a line
A linear pair is two angles that are side by side, with their outside rays making a straight line.
∠1 is next to ∠2 and ∠4
Angle 1 sits next to angle 2 and next to angle 4.
∠1 and ∠2;  ∠1 and ∠4
So the linear pairs with angle 1 are angles 1 and 2, and angles 1 and 4. Angle 3 is across from angle 1, so it's a vertical angle, not a linear pair.

stem: Which angle forms a pair of vertical angles with ∠3?
title: Vertical angles
steps: vertical angles: across from each other where two lines cross
Vertical angles are the angles across from each other where two lines cross.
∠3 is across from ∠1
Angle 3 is directly across from angle 1.
So angle 1 and angle 3 are vertical angles. The angles beside angle 3 are linear pairs, not vertical angles.

stem: ∠5 is a complement of ∠4, and m∠5 = 70°. Find m∠4.
title: Find a complement
steps: complementary: add to 90°
Complementary angles add to 90 degrees.
So angle 4 is 90 minus 70: 20 degrees.

stem: ∠8 is a supplement of ∠2, and m∠8 = 55°. Find m∠2.
title: Find a supplement
steps: supplementary: add to 180°
Supplementary angles add to 180 degrees.
So angle 2 is 180 minus 55: 125 degrees.

stem: Find m∠EFG and m∠GFH.
title: Angles with x in a diagram: complementary
steps: the angles make a right angle → add to 90
In the diagram, the two angles together make a right angle, so they are complementary: they add to 90 degrees.
Add the expressions and set the sum equal to 90.
Combine like terms: 18 x plus 18 equals 90. Subtract 18, then divide by 18: x is 4.
Put 4 back in: 49 and 41 degrees. Check: they add to 90.

stem: Find m∠FGH and m∠HGJ.
title: Angles with x in a diagram: a linear pair
steps: the angles make a straight line → add to 180
In the diagram, the two angles make a straight line. They form a linear pair, so they add to 180 degrees.
Add the expressions and set the sum equal to 180.
Combine like terms, subtract 26, then divide by 14: x is 11.
Put 11 back in: 120 and 60 degrees. They add to 180.

stem: ∠JPT and ∠TPU are complementary angles, m∠JPT = (7x + 8)°, and m∠TPU = (9x − 30)°. Find the measure of each angle.
title: Complementary angles with x
steps: complementary → add to 90
The angles are complementary, so they add to 90 degrees.
Add the expressions and set the sum equal to 90.
Combine like terms, add 22, then divide by 16: x is 7.
Put 7 back in: 57 and 33 degrees.

stem: ∠KLM and ∠MLN are supplementary angles, m∠KLM = (4x + 52)°, and m∠MLN = (9x − 2)°. Find the measure of each angle.
title: Supplementary angles with x
steps: supplementary → add to 180
The angles are supplementary, so they add to 180 degrees.
Add the expressions and set the sum equal to 180.
Combine like terms, subtract 50, then divide by 13: x is 10.
Put 10 back in: 92 and 88 degrees. They add to 180.

stem: The measure of an angle is 1/5 the measure of its complement. Find the measure of the angle and its complement.
title: Angle word problem: complements
steps: complements add to 90°
Complementary angles add to 90 degrees.
let the larger angle be x; the smaller is x/5
The angle is one fifth of its complement. Let the complement, the larger angle, be x. Then the angle is x over 5.
The two add to 90.
x plus one fifth x is six fifths x. Multiply both sides by 5 over 6: x is 75.
The angle is 75 divided by 5, which is 15. So the angles are 15 and 75 degrees.

stem: Two angles form a linear pair. The measure of one angle is 4 times the measure of the other angle. Find the measure of each angle.
title: Angle word problem: a linear pair
steps: linear pair → add to 180°
A linear pair is supplementary, so the two angles add to 180 degrees.
smaller = x, larger = 4x
One angle is 4 times the other. Let the smaller be x and the larger be 4 x.
x plus 4 x is 5 x, which equals 180. So x is 36.
The larger is 4 times 36, which is 144. The angles are 36 and 144 degrees.

stem: The ratio of the measure of an angle to the measure of its complement is 4:6. Find the measure of the angle and its complement.
title: Angle word problem: a ratio
steps: ratio 4:6 → the angles are 4x and 6x
A ratio of 4 to 6 means the angles are 4 x and 6 x for some number x.
complement → add to 90: 4x + 6x = 90
An angle and its complement add to 90. For a supplement, use 180 instead.
10 x is 90, so x is 9.
The angles are 4 times 9, which is 36, and 6 times 9, which is 54 degrees.

stem: The supplement of an angle is 35° more than twice its complement. Find the measure of the angle and the measure of its complement.
title: Challenge: supplement in terms of the complement
steps: angle x: complement 90 − x, supplement 180 − x
Let x be the angle. Its complement is 90 minus x, and its supplement is 180 minus x.
The supplement is 35 more than twice the complement. Translate that into an equation.
Distribute: 2 times 90 minus x is 180 minus 2 x. Add 35: 215 minus 2 x.
Add 2 x and subtract 180 from both sides: x is 35.
complement: 90 − 35 = 55°
The angle is 35 degrees, and its complement is 55 degrees.

stem:
If it is Valentine’s Day, then it is February.
What is the conclusion?
title: Hypothesis and conclusion
steps: If it is Valentine’s Day, then it is February.
A conditional statement has the form if p, then q.
hypothesis p: the part after “if”
The hypothesis is the part right after the word if: it is Valentine's Day.
conclusion q: the part after “then”
The conclusion is the part right after the word then: it is February.
Conclusion: it is February
So the conclusion is: it is February. Don't include the words if or then in your answer.

stem:
Rewrite the conditional statement in if-then form.
When it rains, the game is canceled.
title: Rewrite in if-then form
steps: When it rains, the game is canceled.
To rewrite in if-then form, find the condition and what happens because of it.
hypothesis: it rains
The condition is: it rains. That's the hypothesis.
conclusion: the game is canceled
What follows is: the game is canceled. That's the conclusion.
If it rains, then the game is canceled.
Put them together: If it rains, then the game is canceled.

stem:
Write the negation of the statement.
The triangle is isosceles.
title: Negation
steps: The triangle is isosceles.
The negation of a statement says the opposite. If the statement is true, its negation is false, and the other way around.
The triangle is not isosceles.
Usually you just add the word not: The triangle is not isosceles.
not “The triangle is scalene.”
Be careful: “The triangle is scalene” is not the negation. A triangle could be neither one, so that isn't the exact opposite.

stem: Let p be “you are in math class” and let q be “you are in Geometry.” Which statement is the contrapositive?
title: Converse, inverse, and contrapositive
steps: p → q: If you are in math class, then you are in Geometry.
Start with the conditional, if p then q: If you are in math class, then you are in Geometry.
converse q → p: switch
The converse switches the hypothesis and the conclusion: If you are in Geometry, then you are in math class.
inverse ∼p → ∼q: negate both
The inverse negates both parts, adding not: If you are not in math class, then you are not in Geometry.
contrapositive ∼q → ∼p: switch and negate
The contrapositive switches and negates: If you are not in Geometry, then you are not in math class.
contrapositive: If you are not in Geometry, then you are not in math class.
The question asks for the contrapositive, so that's the answer.

stem: Let p be “you are not an only child” and let q be “you have a sibling.” Think about the conditional p → q, its converse, its inverse, and its contrapositive. Which are true?
title: Which related conditionals are true?
steps: p → q: If you are not an only child, then you have a sibling. (true)
First decide whether the conditional is true. If you are not an only child, then you have a sibling. That is true.
contrapositive: same truth value as the conditional → true
The contrapositive always has the same truth value as the original conditional, so it is true too.
converse: If you have a sibling, then you are not an only child. (true)
Now check the converse on its own: If you have a sibling, then you are not an only child. That's also true.
inverse: same truth value as the converse → true
The inverse always matches the converse, so it is true.
All four are true.
So all four are true. If the converse had been false, the inverse would have been false too.

stem:
Decide whether the statement about the diagram is true. Explain using definitions.
A is the midpoint of B̅M̅.
title: Is the statement about the diagram true?
steps: A is the midpoint of B̅M̅.
Read the statement, then check the diagram for the marks that prove it. Don't trust how the picture looks.
The tick marks show B̅A̅ ≅ A̅M̅.
The tick marks show that B A is congruent to A M.
midpoint: divides a segment into two congruent segments
A midpoint is a point that divides a segment into two congruent segments.
True
So the statement is true. Without those tick marks, you couldn't say A is the midpoint, even if it looked like it.

stem:
Rewrite the definition as a biconditional statement.
Two angles are adjacent angles when they share a common vertex and side but have no common interior points.
title: Write a definition as a biconditional
steps: Two angles are adjacent angles when they share a common vertex and side but have no common interior points.
Every definition works in both directions, so it can be written as a biconditional, using if and only if.
replace “when” with “if and only if”
Keep the term being defined first, and replace the word when with if and only if.
Two angles are adjacent angles if and only if they share a common vertex and side but have no common interior points.
So: Two angles are adjacent angles if and only if they share a common vertex and side but have no common interior points.

stem:
Rewrite the statements as a biconditional statement.
If two angles are complementary, then the sum of their measures is 90°.
If the sum of the measures of two angles is 90°, then the angles are complementary.
title: Combine two statements into a biconditional
steps: If two angles are complementary, then the sum of their measures is 90°.
Here is a conditional,
If the sum of the measures of two angles is 90°, then the angles are complementary.
and here is its converse. Both are true.
p if and only if q
When a conditional and its converse are both true, combine them with if and only if.
Two angles are complementary if and only if the sum of their measures is 90°.
So: Two angles are complementary if and only if the sum of their measures is 90 degrees.

stem: Complete the truth table for ∼(q → p). Which list gives the last column, from top to bottom?
title: Truth tables
steps: p → q is false only when p is T and q is F.
A conditional is false only when its hypothesis is true and its conclusion is false. Every other row is true.
∼(q → p): find q → p first, then switch
Here we need not, q then p. First find q then p, then switch every value.
row 1: q T, p T → T → ∼: F
Row 1: q is true and p is true, so q then p is true. Its negation is false.
row 2: q F, p T → T → ∼: F
Row 2: q is false, so q then p is true. Negation: false.
row 3: q T, p F → F → ∼: T
Row 3: q is true and p is false. That's the one false case, so q then p is false. Negation: true.
row 4: q F, p F → T → ∼: F
Row 4: q is false, so it's true. Negation: false.
F, F, T, F
So the last column is F, F, T, F.

stem: Statement: “If two angles are supplementary, then they form a linear pair.” Decide whether the converse, the inverse, and the contrapositive are true or false.
title: Challenge: truth of the converse, inverse, and contrapositive
steps: If two angles are supplementary, then they form a linear pair.
First decide whether the statement itself is true.
false: two 90° angles apart are supplementary but not a linear pair
It's false. Two 90 degree angles in different places add to 180, but they don't form a linear pair.
contrapositive: same as the statement → false
The contrapositive always has the same truth value as the statement, so it is false.
converse: If two angles form a linear pair, then they are supplementary. → true
Now the converse: if two angles form a linear pair, then they are supplementary. That's true.
inverse: same as the converse → true
The inverse always matches the converse, so it is true.
converse true, inverse true, contrapositive false
So the converse and inverse are true, and the contrapositive is false.

stem:
Describe the pattern. Then write the next two terms.
B, F, J, N, R, …
title: Describe a pattern: letters
steps: B, F, J, N, R
Look at how you get from each term to the next.
B → F: forward 4 letters (C, D, E, F)
From B, count forward: C, D, E, F. That's 4 letters.
F → J, J → N, N → R: also 4
F to J, J to N, and N to R are each 4 letters too.
R → V → Z
Keep going: 4 letters after R is V, and 4 after V is Z.
Go forward 4 letters each time. Next: V, Z
So the pattern is: go forward 4 letters each time. The next two terms are V and Z.

stem:
Describe the pattern. Then write the next two terms.
−4, −11, −18, −25, −32, …
title: Describe a pattern: adding the same number
steps: Find the change from each term to the next.
−11 − (−4) = −7 each time
Negative 4 to negative 11 is a change of negative 7, and every step is the same.
Keep adding negative 7: negative 39, then negative 46.
Add −7 each time. Next: −39, −46
So: add negative 7 each time. The next two terms are negative 39 and negative 46.

stem:
Describe the pattern. Then write the next two terms.
3, 9, 27, 81, 243, …
title: Describe a pattern: multiplying
steps: The differences are 6, 18, 54: not the same. So try dividing.
Each term divided by the one before is 3. So each term is 3 times the last.
243 times 3 is 729, and 729 times 3 is 2187.
Multiply by 3 each time. Next: 729, 2187
So: multiply by 3 each time. The next two terms are 729 and 2187.

stem:
Describe the pattern. Then write the next two terms.
1, 5, 12, 22, 35, …
title: Describe a pattern: growing differences
steps: Find the differences: 4, 7, 10, 13.
differences: 4, 7, 10, 13 → each is 3 more
The differences aren't the same, but they go up by 3 each time.
next differences: 16, 19
So the next differences are 16 and 19.
35 plus 16 is 51, and 51 plus 19 is 70.
Next: 51, 70
The next two terms are 51 and 70.

stem:
Describe the pattern. Then write the next two terms.
2, −3, 4, −5, 6, …
title: Describe a pattern: alternating signs
steps: Look at the size of each number and its sign separately.
sizes: 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 → count up by 1
Ignoring signs, the numbers count up by 1.
signs: +, −, +, −, + → alternate
The signs switch every time: positive, negative, positive, negative.
Next: −7, 8
So the next size is 7 with a negative sign, then 8 with a positive sign.

stem: Describe the pattern. Then name the next two figures.
title: Describe a pattern of figures
steps: triangle, square, pentagon: 3, 4, 5 sides
Count the sides of each figure: 3, 4, then 5. Each figure has one more side than the one before.
next: 6 sides, then 7 sides
The next two figures have 6 sides and 7 sides.
hexagon, then heptagon
A 6-sided polygon is a hexagon, and a 7-sided polygon is a heptagon.

stem:
Which is a counterexample that shows the conjecture is false?
All prime numbers are odd.
title: Counterexamples
steps: All prime numbers are odd.
A counterexample is one example that fits the first part but makes the statement false.
look for a prime number that is even
Here, look for a number that is prime but not odd.
2 is prime, and 2 is even
2 is prime: its only factors are 1 and 2. And 2 is even.
So 2 is a counterexample. One counterexample is enough to show a conjecture is false.

stem:
Use the Law of Detachment to determine what you can conclude from the given information, if possible.
If your cousin lets you borrow a car, then you will go to the mountains with your friend.
Your cousin lets you borrow a car.
title: Law of Detachment: a conclusion follows
steps: If your cousin lets you borrow a car, then you will go to the mountains with your friend.
Law of Detachment: if a conditional is true and its hypothesis is true, then its conclusion is true.
Fact: Your cousin lets you borrow a car. → matches the hypothesis
The fact matches the hypothesis, the part after if.
You will go to the mountains with your friend.
So the conclusion is true: You will go to the mountains with your friend.

stem:
Use the Law of Detachment to determine what you can conclude from the given information, if possible.
If you score 90% or higher on the test, then you earn an A.
You earn an A.
title: Law of Detachment: no conclusion
steps: If you score 90% or higher on the test, then you earn an A.
Here's the conditional.
Fact: You earn an A. → matches the conclusion, not the hypothesis
The fact matches the conclusion, not the hypothesis.
You might have earned an A another way.
The Law of Detachment only works when the hypothesis is true. Knowing you earned an A doesn't tell you your test score.
No conclusion is possible.
So no conclusion is possible.

stem:
Use the Law of Syllogism to write a new conditional statement that follows from the pair of true statements, if possible.
If an angle measures 120°, then it is obtuse.
If an angle is obtuse, then it is not acute.
title: Law of Syllogism: the statements link
steps: If an angle measures 120°, then it is obtuse.
Law of Syllogism: if p then q, and if q then r, give if p then r.
If an angle is obtuse, then it is not acute.
The conclusion of the first statement, it is obtuse, is the hypothesis of the second.
If an angle measures 120°, then it is not acute.
So they link: take the first hypothesis and the last conclusion. If an angle measures 120 degrees, then it is not acute.

stem:
Use the Law of Syllogism to write a new conditional statement that follows from the pair of true statements, if possible.
If a figure is a square, then the figure has four right angles.
If a figure is a square, then the figure has four congruent sides.
title: Law of Syllogism: the statements don't link
steps: If a figure is a square, then the figure has four right angles.
Check whether the conclusion of one statement is the hypothesis of the other.
If a figure is a square, then the figure has four congruent sides.
These two share a hypothesis, a figure is a square. But neither conclusion is the other's hypothesis.
Not possible: no new statement follows.
So the Law of Syllogism doesn't apply. No new statement follows.

stem:
Which law of logic is illustrated?
If a quadrilateral is a square, then it has four right angles.
Quadrilateral QRST is a square.
Quadrilateral QRST has four right angles.
title: Which law? Detachment
steps: If a quadrilateral is a square, then it has four right angles.
There is one conditional,
Quadrilateral QRST is a square. → the hypothesis is true
then a fact that matches its hypothesis,
QRST has four right angles. → the conclusion
then its conclusion.
Law of Detachment
A conditional plus its true hypothesis gives the conclusion. That's the Law of Detachment.

stem:
Which law of logic is illustrated?
If x = 4, then 3x = 12.
If 3x = 12, then 3x + 2 = 14.
If x = 4, then 3x + 2 = 14.
title: Which law? Syllogism
steps: If x = 4, then 3x = 12.  If 3x = 12, then 3x + 2 = 14.
There are two conditionals. The conclusion of the first, 3 x equals 12, is the hypothesis of the second.
If x = 4, then 3x + 2 = 14.
The result is a new conditional joining the first hypothesis to the last conclusion.
Law of Syllogism
Linking two conditionals into a new one is the Law of Syllogism.

stem:
Which law of logic is illustrated?
If you score 90% or higher on the test, then you earn an A.
You earn an A.
You score 94% on the test.
title: Which law? Neither
steps: If you score 90% or higher on the test, then you earn an A.
There is one conditional.
You earn an A. → matches the conclusion
The fact matches the conclusion, not the hypothesis.
You score 94% on the test.
So we can't know the test score. This conclusion does not follow.
Neither law: the conclusion does not follow
Neither law applies. The conclusion doesn't follow.

stem:
Which law of logic is illustrated?
2 + 4 = 6, 6 + 8 = 14, and 10 + 12 = 22. So the sum of any two even numbers is even.
title: Which law? Inductive reasoning
steps: This argument checks a few examples,
So the sum of any two even numbers is even.
then makes a general rule from the pattern.
Inductive reasoning (not a law of logic)
That's inductive reasoning, not a law of logic. The laws of logic start from conditional statements.

stem:
Decide whether inductive reasoning or deductive reasoning is used to reach the conclusion.
You measured the angles of 20 triangles, and they always added to 180°. So, the angles of every triangle add to 180°.
title: Inductive or deductive? Inductive
steps: measured 20 triangles → angles always added to 180°
The conclusion comes from looking at many examples.
So, the angles of every triangle add to 180°.
Then it makes a general rule from the pattern.
Inductive: based on a pattern of observations
Reasoning from a pattern of examples is inductive.

stem:
Decide whether inductive reasoning or deductive reasoning is used to reach the conclusion.
Even numbers are divisible by 2. Odd numbers are not divisible by 2. So, 4 is an even number.
title: Inductive or deductive? Deductive
steps: Even numbers are divisible by 2. Odd numbers are not.
This argument starts from definitions and facts,
So, 4 is an even number.
and applies them to a specific case.
Deductive: uses facts, definitions, and laws of logic
Using facts, definitions, and laws of logic to reach a conclusion is deductive reasoning.

stem: Use the table to make a conjecture about the relationship between x and y. Write an equation for y in terms of x. Then find y when x = 13.
title: A conjecture from a table
steps: Look at how y changes when x goes up by 1.
y goes up 4 each time → slope 4
Each time x goes up 1, y goes up 4.
x = 0 → y = 6 → y-intercept 6
When x is 0, y is 6.
So the conjecture is y equals 4 x plus 6.
When x is 13: 52 plus 6 is 58.

stem: A pattern of dot figures has 3, 4, 7, and 12 dots in figures 1 through 4. How many dots are in figure 10? Which figure has 403 dots? (Look at how the differences change.)
title: Challenge: extend a dot pattern
steps: 3, 4, 7, 12 → differences 1, 3, 5
Find the differences: 1, 3, 5. They go up by 2 each time.
next differences: 7, 9, 11, 13, 15, 17
Keep the differences going: 7, 9, 11, 13, 15, 17.
Add them on: figures 5 through 10 have 19, 28, 39, 52, 67, and 84 dots.
rule: n² − 2n + 4
A rule that fits is n squared minus 2 n plus 4. Check: n equals 1 gives 3.
Try n equals 21: 441 minus 42 plus 4 is 403. So figure 21 has 403 dots.

stem:
Which postulate does the statement illustrate?
Lines ℓ and m intersect at exactly one point, point E.
title: Name the postulate
steps: Lines ℓ and m intersect at exactly one point, point E.
Read what the statement is about: here, two lines and where they meet.
Two Point: through 2 points, exactly one line
Here are the postulates. Two Point: through any two points there is exactly one line.
Line-Point: a line has at least 2 points;  Plane-Point: a plane has at least 3 noncollinear points
Line-Point: a line contains at least two points. Plane-Point: a plane contains at least three noncollinear points.
Three Point: through 3 noncollinear points, exactly one plane;  Plane-Line: 2 points in a plane → their line is in it
Three Point: through any three noncollinear points there is exactly one plane. Plane-Line: if two points are in a plane, the line through them is in the plane.
Line Intersection: 2 lines meet in exactly one point;  Plane Intersection: 2 planes meet in a line
Line Intersection: two lines that intersect meet in exactly one point. Plane Intersection: two planes that intersect meet in a line.
two lines meeting at one point → Line Intersection Postulate
This statement is about two lines meeting at exactly one point. That's the Line Intersection Postulate.

stem: Which statement can you conclude from the diagram?
title: What you can conclude from a diagram
steps: You CAN assume: collinear points, intersecting lines, vertical angles, linear pairs

From a diagram you can assume things that come from how lines and points are connected: points on a line are collinear, lines that cross do intersect, and angles that look like vertical angles or a linear pair are.
You CAN'T assume: lengths, congruence, midpoints, right angles (unless marked)
You can't assume anything about size: lengths, congruent segments or angles, midpoints, or right angles. Those need marks in the diagram.
H, J, F are on one line → ∠HJE and ∠EJF are a linear pair
Here H, J, and F lie on one line, so angles H J E and E J F form a linear pair.
m∠HJE + m∠EJF = 180°
A linear pair adds to 180 degrees, so this statement can be concluded.

stem: Which statement can you NOT conclude from the diagram?
title: What you can NOT conclude from a diagram
steps: You CAN'T assume sizes unless the diagram marks them.
You can't assume lengths, congruence, midpoints, or right angles unless the diagram marks them.
single ticks: T̅U̅ ≅ U̅L̅;  double ticks: H̅U̅ ≅ U̅Q̅
The single tick marks show T U is congruent to U L. The double tick marks show H U is congruent to U Q.
right angle is marked → the lines are perpendicular
The little square marks a right angle, so the lines are perpendicular.
H̅U̅ and T̅U̅ have different marks → can't conclude H̅U̅ ≅ T̅U̅
But H U and T U have different tick marks. Nothing shows they're congruent.
H̅U̅ ≅ T̅U̅
So the statement you can NOT conclude is H U congruent to T U.

stem:
Describe and correct the error in the statement made about the diagram.
“U is the midpoint of H̅Q̅ and T̅L̅.”
title: Error analysis: diagrams
steps: “U is the midpoint of H̅Q̅ and T̅L̅.”
To be a midpoint, the diagram has to show the two halves are congruent.
T̅U̅ ≅ U̅L̅ is marked → U is the midpoint of T̅L̅ ✓
T U and U L have matching tick marks, so U is the midpoint of T L.
nothing marks H̅U̅ ≅ U̅Q̅
H U and U Q have no tick marks. They might look equal, but you can't assume it.
U is the midpoint of T̅L̅ only.
The correction: U is the midpoint of T L. Nothing shows it's the midpoint of H Q.

stem: There are 9 points in space. No three of them lie on the same line, and no four lie in the same plane. How many different lines contain two of the points? How many different planes contain three of the points?
title: Challenge: lines and planes through points
steps: through any 2 points: exactly one line
Through any two points there is exactly one line, so count the pairs of points.
Each of the 9 points pairs with 8 others. That counts every pair twice, so divide by 2: 36 lines.
through any 3 noncollinear points: exactly one plane
Through any three noncollinear points there is exactly one plane, so count the groups of three.
9 times 8 times 7 is 504. Each group of three is counted 6 times, once for each order, so divide by 6: 84 planes.

stem: Write the property that justifies the marked step.
title: The property that justifies a step
steps: Compare the marked step with the line before it. What changed?
6x was added to both sides
The negative 6 x on the right is gone, and the left went from 9 x to 15 x. So 6 x was added to both sides.
Adding the same thing to both sides → Addition Property of Equality
Adding the same amount to both sides is the Addition Property of Equality.
Subtract both sides → Subtraction;  multiply → Multiplication;  divide → Division;  remove parentheses → Distributive

The others work the same way: subtracting from both sides is the Subtraction Property, multiplying is Multiplication, dividing is Division, and getting rid of parentheses is the Distributive Property.

stem:
Solve the equation. Justify each step.
4(4x − 8) = 3(2x + 16)
title: Solve and justify each step
steps: Write the equation and the reason Given.
16x − 32 = 6x + 48   Distributive Property
Distribute on both sides: 16 x minus 32 equals 6 x plus 48. Reason: Distributive Property.
10x − 32 = 48   Subtraction Property of Equality
Subtract 6 x from both sides. Reason: Subtraction Property of Equality.
10x = 80   Addition Property of Equality
Add 32 to both sides. Reason: Addition Property of Equality.
x = 8   Division Property of Equality
Divide both sides by 10. Reason: Division Property of Equality.

stem:
Solve the formula for h.
S = 2πr² + 2πrh
title: Solve a formula for a variable
steps: S = 2πr² + 2πrh
Treat every letter except h like a number. Undo what's being done to h, one step at a time.
S − 2πr² = 2πrh
The 2 pi r squared term is added, so subtract it from both sides.
(S − 2πr²)/(2πr) = h
h is multiplied by 2 pi r, so divide both sides by 2 pi r.
h = (S − 2πr²)/(2πr)
So h equals S minus 2 pi r squared, all over 2 pi r.

stem: The formula for the perimeter P of a rectangle is P = 2ℓ + 2w. Solve the formula for ℓ. Then find the length of a rectangular lawn with a perimeter of 30 meters and a width of 6 meters.
title: Rewrite a formula, then use it
steps: P = 2ℓ + 2w
Solve the formula for length first.
P − 2w = 2ℓ
Subtract 2 w from both sides.
Divide both sides by 2.
Now put in the perimeter, 30, and the width, 6: 30 minus 12 is 18, and half of 18 is 9.
9 meters
The lawn is 9 meters long.

stem:
Name the property of equality that the statement illustrates.
If HL = QU and QU = 21, then HL = 21.
title: Name the property of equality
steps: Reflexive: a = a
Reflexive: anything equals itself.
Symmetric: if a = b, then b = a
Symmetric: you can switch the two sides.
Transitive: if a = b and b = c, then a = c
Transitive: if a equals b and b equals c, then a equals c. It links two equations through a shared middle.
Substitution: if a = b, replace a with b
Substitution: if two things are equal, you can replace one with the other.
Addition, Subtraction, Multiplication, Division: do it to both sides
And the Addition, Subtraction, Multiplication, and Division Properties: doing the same thing to both sides.
If HL = QU and QU = 21, then HL = 21. → Transitive
Here, H L equals Q U, and Q U equals 21, so H L equals 21. That's the Transitive Property of Equality.

stem:
Use the Symmetric Property of Equality to complete the statement.
If m∠2 = m∠1, then ___
title: Complete a statement: Symmetric Property
steps: Symmetric: if a = b, then b = a
The Symmetric Property switches the two sides of an equation.
If m∠2 = m∠1, then m∠1 = m∠2
So if angle 2 equals angle 1, then angle 1 equals angle 2.

stem:
Use the Substitution Property of Equality to complete the statement.
If MN = 30, then MN + PQ = ___
title: Complete a statement: Substitution Property
steps: Substitution: if a = b, a can be replaced by b
The Substitution Property lets you replace something with what it equals.
MN = 30 → replace MN with 30
M N equals 30, so wherever you see M N, you can write 30.
MN + PQ = 30 + PQ
So M N plus P Q equals 30 plus P Q.

stem:
Use the Transitive Property of Equality to complete the statement.
If m∠4 = m∠2 and m∠2 = m∠3, then ___
title: Complete a statement: Transitive Property
steps: Transitive: if a = b and b = c, then a = c
The Transitive Property links two equations that share a middle term.
m∠4 = m∠2 and m∠2 = m∠3
Angle 2 is in both equations.
So angle 4 equals angle 3.

stem:
Use the Reflexive Property of Equality to complete the statement.
m∠FGH = ___
title: Complete a statement: Reflexive Property
steps: Reflexive: a = a
The Reflexive Property says anything equals itself.
m∠FGH = m∠FGH
So angle F G H equals angle F G H.

stem: Solve 5(x − 2) = 2x − 16. Then name the property that justifies the step where you remove 2x from the right side.
title: Challenge: solve and name the property
steps: Solve step by step, naming the property for each step.
5x − 10 = 2x − 16   (Distributive Property)
Distribute the 5: 5 x minus 10.
3x − 10 = −16   (Subtraction Property: subtract 2x)
Remove 2 x from the right side by subtracting it from both sides. That's the step the question asks about: the Subtraction Property of Equality.
3x = −6   (Addition Property: add 10)
Add 10 to both sides.
x = −2   (Division Property: divide by 3)
Divide by 3: x is negative 2.
x = −2; Subtraction Property of Equality
So x is negative 2, and the step is justified by the Subtraction Property of Equality.

stem:
Name the property that the statement illustrates.
E̅H̅ ≅ E̅H̅
title: Properties of congruence
steps: Reflexive: E̅H̅ ≅ E̅H̅
The congruence properties match the equality properties. Reflexive: a segment or angle is congruent to itself.
Symmetric: if A̅B̅ ≅ C̅D̅, then C̅D̅ ≅ A̅B̅
Symmetric: you can switch the order.
Transitive: if A̅B̅ ≅ C̅D̅ and C̅D̅ ≅ E̅F̅, then A̅B̅ ≅ E̅F̅
Transitive: two congruence statements that share a middle piece link together.
E̅H̅ ≅ E̅H̅ → Reflexive Property of Segment Congruence
Here, segment E H is congruent to itself. It's a segment, so the answer is the Reflexive Property of Segment Congruence.

stem: Complete the proof. Which reason belongs in step 4?
title: Complete a proof: the missing reason
steps: Look at the step: 4. RS = VW
Find the step with the question mark. Step 4 says R S equals V W.
Look at the steps before it: RS = TU and TU = VW
Look at what came right before. Step 2 says R S equals T U, and step 3 says T U equals V W.
If a = b and b = c, then a = c
Those two equations share T U, and step 4 links them together. If a equals b and b equals c, then a equals c.

stem: The rotation (x, y) → (−y, x) maps C to C′. Find the measure of the acute or right angle formed by intersecting lines so that C can be mapped to C′ using two reflections.
title: Angle between lines of reflection: given a rule
steps: (x, y) → (−y, x) is a 90° rotation
First, recognize the rule. Switch and make the new x negative: that's a 90 degree rotation.
two reflections at x° = a rotation of 2x°
Two reflections in lines meeting at x degrees make a rotation of 2 x degrees.
So 2 x is 90, and the lines meet at 45 degrees.

stem: △ABC is reflected in line k, and the image is reflected in line m, where k ∥ m. Which lines are perpendicular to the segment from A to A″?
title: Reflections in parallel lines: perpendicular segments
steps: each reflection moves a point along a perpendicular
When you reflect a point, it moves along a segment perpendicular to the line of reflection.
A → A′ ⊥ k;  A′ → A″ ⊥ m
A moves to A prime straight across line k, then to A double prime straight across line m.
k ∥ m → A, A′, A″ are on one line ⊥ to both
Because k and m are parallel, both moves go in the same direction. The segment from A to A double prime is perpendicular to both lines.
Lines k and m
So the answer is lines k and m.

stem: △ABC is reflected in line k, and △A′B′C′ is reflected in line m. Lines k and m are parallel. If the distance between k and m is 1.5 inches, what is the length of C̅C̅″?
title: Reflections in parallel lines: how far it moves
steps: two reflections in parallel lines = a translation
Reflecting in two parallel lines is the same as one translation.
translation distance = 2 × the distance between the lines
The translation moves points twice the distance between the lines.
So C C double prime is 2 times 1.5: 3 inches.

stem:
Tell whether the statement is always, sometimes, or never true.
A reflection changes the orientation of a figure.
title: Always, sometimes, or never (transformations)
steps: A reflection changes the orientation of a figure.
Think about what each transformation does.
a reflection flips the figure: the vertex order reverses
A reflection flips the figure over, like a mirror. If the vertices went clockwise, they now go counterclockwise. That's a change in orientation.
Always
That happens for every reflection, so the answer is always.
rigid motions keep size and shape; translations and rotations keep orientation
Other facts that help: translations, reflections, and rotations never change size or shape. Translations and rotations never change orientation.

stem: Reflect P(6, −7) in the line y = 4, then reflect the image in the line y = 2. Find the final image P″. The two reflections together are the same as a single translation. How far does it move points, and in which direction?
title: Challenge: two reflections make a translation
steps: reflect in y = 4: y → 2(4) − y
Reflecting in the line y equals 4 sends y to 2 times 4 minus y.
Negative 7 becomes 8 plus 7: 15. So P prime is 6, 15.
Now reflect in y equals 2: 15 becomes 4 minus 15, which is negative 11.
So P double prime is 6, negative 11.
lines are 2 apart → translation of 4, from y = 4 toward y = 2: down 4
The lines are 2 units apart, and the translation is twice that: 4 units, in the direction from the first line to the second. That's 4 units down.

stem: △ABC is reflected in line k, and the image is reflected in line m, where k ∥ m. Which single transformation maps △ABC to △A″B″C″?
title: Reflections in parallel lines: which transformation?
steps: reflect in k, then in m, with k ∥ m
Each reflection flips the figure across a line. Flipping twice brings it back to facing the same way.
both flips move points the same direction
Because the lines are parallel, every point moves the same distance in the same direction.
A translation
So the two reflections together are a translation. That's the Reflections in Parallel Lines Theorem. With intersecting lines, it would be a rotation instead.

stem:
Find the scale factor of the dilation with center C that maps P to P′. Then tell whether the dilation is a reduction or an enlargement.
CP = 15, CP′ = 27
title: Scale factor: reduction or enlargement
steps: k = CP′/CP
The scale factor is the image distance divided by the original distance: C P prime over C P.
27 over 15 simplifies to 9 fifths.
k > 1 → enlargement;  0 < k < 1 → reduction
If k is greater than 1, the image is bigger: an enlargement. If k is between 0 and 1, it's a reduction.
9/5 > 1 → an enlargement
9 fifths is more than 1, so this is an enlargement.

stem:
Find the vertices of the image after a dilation with center at the origin and scale factor k = 3/2.
D(0, 4), E(0, 0), F(−4, 0), G(−6, 4)
title: Dilate a figure: positive scale factor
steps: (x, y) → (kx, ky) with k = 3/2
With the center at the origin, multiply each coordinate by the scale factor, 3 halves.
D goes to 0, 6. E is the origin, so it stays put.
F goes to negative 6, 0. G goes to negative 9, 6.

stem:
Find the vertices of the image after a dilation with center at the origin and scale factor k = −1/3.
A(0, −3), B(−3, −6), C(0, 0)
title: Dilate a figure: negative scale factor
steps: (x, y) → (kx, ky) with k = −1/3
Multiply each coordinate by negative one third.
A goes to 0, 1.
B goes to 1, 2. C is the origin, so it stays.
negative k: smaller AND rotated 180°
A negative scale factor resizes the figure and also turns it 180 degrees, to the other side of the center.

stem: A dilation maps a figure to its image. A side of length 4 in the original figure has length 16 in the image. Another side has length 19 in the original. Find the length of that side in the image.
title: A missing length after a dilation
steps: Use the pair of matching sides to find the scale factor: 16 over 4 is 4.
Every length is multiplied by 4, so the other side becomes 4 times 19: 76.

stem: A dilation with center C maps P to P′, where CP = 25 and CP′ = 5. A student writes k = 25/5 = 5. Describe and correct the error.
title: Error analysis: scale factor
steps: k = image ÷ original = CP′/CP
The scale factor is the image distance over the original distance.
the student divided the other way: 25/5
The student divided original over image.
k = 5/25 = 1/5: a reduction
The correct scale factor is 5 over 25, which is one fifth. It's less than 1, so it's a reduction.

stem:
Determine whether the dilated figure or the original figure is closer to the center of dilation.
Center of dilation: outside the figure; k = 4
title: Which figure is closer to the center?
steps: each image point is k times as far from the center
In a dilation, each image point is k times as far from the center as the original point.
k = 4 > 1 → the image is farther away
The scale factor is 4, which is more than 1, so the image points are farther from the center.
The original figure
So the original figure is closer to the center. If k were less than 1, the image would be closer.

stem: A photo is 3 inches by 5 inches. It is dilated so the 3-inch side becomes 6 inches. What is the scale factor, and how long is the other side of the new photo?
title: Dilations in real life: a photo
steps: The 3 inch side becomes 6 inches, so the scale factor is 6 over 3, which is 2.
other side: 5 × 2 = 10 in.
The other side gets multiplied by 2 as well: 5 times 2 is 10 inches.

stem: Your notes cover 5 inches by 8 inches. On the enlarged copy, the smaller side is 7.5 inches. What is the scale factor of this dilation?
title: Dilations in real life: find the scale factor
steps: smaller side: 5 in. → 7.5 in.
Match the sides. The smaller side of the notes, 5 inches, becomes 7.5 inches.
The scale factor is new over original: 7.5 divided by 5 is 1.5.

stem: You use a magnifying glass with a magnification of 5×. A ladybug is 4.5 millimeters long. How long does it look through the magnifying glass?
title: Dilations in real life: a magnifying glass
steps: magnification 5× → k = 5
A magnification of 5 times is a scale factor of 5.
Multiply the real length by 5: the ladybug looks 22.5 millimeters long. If you're given how big it looks, divide by 5 instead.

stem: Triangle PQR has area 9 square units. It is dilated with center C(3, 2) and scale factor 1/3. Find the image of vertex P(12, −7) and the area of the image triangle.
title: Challenge: dilation about a point, and the new area
steps: Find how far P is from the center C: 9 right and 9 down.
Multiply that by the scale factor, one third: 3 right and 3 down.
Add that to C: P prime is 6, negative 1.
Lengths are multiplied by one third, so areas are multiplied by one third squared, one ninth. The new area is 1 square unit.

stem:
Find the vertices of the image of △FGH after the similarity transformation.
Dilation: (x, y) → (2x, 2y)
Reflection: in the x-axis
F(3, 0), G(1, −3), H(2, 2)
title: Image after a similarity transformation
steps: first dilate: (x, y) → (2x, 2y)
Do the transformations in order. First the dilation: multiply each coordinate by 2.
then reflect in the x-axis: (x, y) → (x, −y)
Then reflect in the x-axis: change the sign of y.
F goes to 6, 0, and the reflection doesn't change it.
G goes to 2, negative 6, then to 2, 6.
H goes to 4, 4, then to 4, negative 4.

stem: Describe a similarity transformation that maps the blue preimage to the green image.
title: Describe a similarity transformation
steps: compare sizes: the image is twice as big → dilation, k = 2
First compare sizes. The green image's sides are twice as long, so start with a dilation with scale factor 2, centered at the origin.
The dilation sends L at 2, 2 to 4, 4. But L prime is at 6, 5.
From 4, 4 to 6, 5 is 2 right and 1 up. That's a translation.
Check M: dilate to negative 6, negative 2, then 2 right and 1 up: negative 4, negative 1. That's M prime.
dilation k = 2, then a translation 2 right and 1 up
So: a dilation with scale factor 2, followed by a translation 2 units right and 1 unit up.

stem:
Determine whether the polygons with the given vertices are similar. Use transformations to explain your reasoning.
P(−1, 3), Q(3, −2), R(−2, −3), S(−2, 1) and
T(2, −6), U(−6, 4), V(4, 6), W(4, −2)
title: Similar or not? Yes
steps: P(−1, 3) → T(2, −6): ×2 and both signs flipped
Compare matching vertices. P at negative 1, 3 goes to T at 2, negative 6. The numbers doubled and both signs changed.
dilate by 2, then rotate 180°: (x, y) → (−2x, −2y)
Doubling is a dilation with scale factor 2. Changing both signs is a 180 degree rotation.
Check Q: 3, negative 2 becomes negative 6, 4. That's U.
dilation + rigid motion → similar
A dilation followed by a rigid motion is a similarity transformation, so the figures are similar.

stem:
Determine whether the polygons with the given vertices are similar. Use transformations to explain your reasoning.
D(4, 1), E(−2, −4), F(−2, 1) and
P(7, −1), Q(−5, −11), R(−3, −1)
title: Similar or not? No
steps: Compare matching sides. From D to E is 6 left and 5 down. From P to Q is 12 left and 10 down. That's twice as long.
But E F is 5 units long, and Q R is root 104, about 10.2. That's not exactly 2 times 5.
not all ×2 → not similar
The sides are not all multiplied by the same scale factor, so the figures are not similar.

stem: A dilation centered at the origin followed by a translation maps A(4, 2) to A′(5, 0) and B(6, −6) to B′(8, −12). Find the scale factor and the translation (x, y) → (x + h, y + k).
title: Challenge: find the dilation and translation
steps: A translation doesn't change lengths or directions, so compare the step from A to B before and after.
scale factor = 3 ÷ 2 = 3/2
The step got multiplied by 3 halves, so the scale factor is 3 halves.
The dilation sends A at 4, 2 to 6, 3.
The translation must move 6, 3 to 5, 0: 1 left and 3 down.
So the translation is x minus 1, y minus 3.

stem: A triangle has side lengths of 13 inches, 13 inches, and 18 inches. Which of the following best describes the triangle?
title: Classify a triangle by its sides
steps: longest side: 18
To classify by angles, compare the squares of the sides. Start with the longest side, 18.
Square the two shorter sides and add them: 338.
Square the longest side: 324.
If the sum is bigger, the triangle is acute. If it's equal, it's right. If it's smaller, it's obtuse. 338 is bigger, so it's acute.
two equal sides → isosceles
For the sides: two sides are 13, so it's isosceles. All three equal would be equilateral, and none equal would be scalene.
acute and isosceles
So the triangle is acute and isosceles.

stem: In △HJY, what is the value of x?
title: Triangle Sum Theorem: find x
steps: The three angles of a triangle add to 180 degrees. Add the expressions and set the sum equal to 180.
Combine like terms: x plus 4 x plus 4 x is 9 x, and 15 plus 19 plus 47 is 81.
Subtract 81: 9 x is 99. Divide by 9: x is 11.

stem: In △EFG, what is m∠F?
title: Triangle Sum Theorem: find an angle
steps: The three angles add to 180 degrees.
Combine like terms, subtract 63, and divide by 9: x is 13.
The question asks for angle F, not x. Put 13 into angle F's expression: 39 plus 34 is 73 degrees.

stem: In △ABC, side BC is extended through C to point D, as shown. The measure of ∠A is (3x + 26)°, the measure of ∠B is (3x − 10)°, and the measure of ∠ACD is (8x − 18)°. What is the measure of ∠ACB?
title: Exterior angle with algebra
steps: exterior angle = sum of the two remote interior angles
The Exterior Angle Theorem: an exterior angle equals the sum of the two interior angles that are not next to it.
Angle A C D is the exterior angle, and angles A and B are the remote interior angles.
Combine like terms, then solve: x is 17.
The exterior angle is 136 minus 18: 118 degrees.
Angle A C B forms a linear pair with the exterior angle, so it's 180 minus 118: 62 degrees.

stem: In the figure shown, points Q, R, and S are collinear. What is the measure of the largest interior angle of △PQR?
title: Exterior angle with a ratio
steps: The 110 degree angle is an exterior angle. It equals the sum of the two remote interior angles, 3 x and 8 x.
11 x is 110, so x is 10.
remote angles: 30° and 80°
The two remote angles are 3 times 10, which is 30, and 8 times 10, which is 80.
The interior angle at R makes a linear pair with 110, so it's 70.
largest: 80°
The three angles are 30, 80, and 70, so the largest is 80 degrees.

stem: In △EFG, m∠E = (3x + 10)° and m∠F = (2x + 14)°. The exterior angle at G measures (6x + 11)°. Find x and m∠EGF.
title: Challenge: Exterior Angle Theorem with algebra
steps: The exterior angle at G equals the sum of the remote interior angles, E and F.
Combine like terms, then subtract 5 x and 11: x is 13.
exterior angle: 6(13) + 11 = 89°
The exterior angle is 78 plus 11: 89 degrees.
Angle E G F forms a linear pair with it: 180 minus 89 is 91 degrees.

stem: The two quadrilaterals shown are congruent. Which of the following is a pair of congruent corresponding parts?
title: Congruent corresponding parts from the marks
steps: match angles with the same marks
In congruent figures, matching angles have the same arc marks. Pair them up.
The marks pair C with F, H with Y, J with W, and X with S.
CHJX ≅ FYWS
So C H J X is congruent to F Y W S, with the letters in matching order.
J̅X̅ ↔ W̅S̅
Sides match by their endpoints. Side J X matches side W S, because J goes with W and X goes with S.
W̅S̅
So W S is congruent to J X. Check each answer choice by matching its endpoints this way.

stem: In the figure, △PRX ≅ △EZT. What is m∠P?
title: Corresponding parts: find an angle
steps: △PRX ≅ △EZT → P ↔ E, R ↔ Z, X ↔ T
The congruence statement lists matching vertices in the same order: P with E, R with Z, and X with T.
Angle R is 50 degrees. Angle X matches angle T, which is 90 degrees.
The angles of triangle P R X add to 180, so angle P is 180 minus 50 minus 90: 40 degrees.

stem: In the figure, △GKW ≅ △STU. What is WG?
title: Corresponding parts: find a length
steps: △GKW ≅ △STU → G ↔ S, K ↔ T, W ↔ U
Match the vertices in order: G with S, K with T, W with U.
W̅G̅ ↔ U̅S̅
Side W G matches side U S.
WG = US = 5
U S is 5 in the figure, so W G is 5.

stem: In the figure, △JLQ ≅ △KMR. What are the values of x and y?
title: Congruent triangles: find x and y
steps: third angle of △JLQ: 180° − 64° − 85° = 31°
First use the triangle with the numbers. Its third angle is 180 minus 64 minus 85: 31 degrees.
Angle K matches angle J, so 4 x minus 53 equals 31. Add 53 and divide by 4: x is 21.
Side K M matches side J L, which is 7. So 3 y minus 17 equals 7. Add 17 and divide by 3: y is 8.

stem: Use the markings in the figure. The two triangles are congruent. Which of the following is a correct congruence statement?
title: Write a congruence statement from the marks
steps: one arc: J ↔ S;  two arcs: S ↔ J
Match vertices by their marks. The angles with one arc match, and the angles with two arcs match.
A ↔ L (the third angles)
The remaining angles, A and L, must match too.
△JAS ≅ △SLJ
Write the vertices in matching order: J A S is congruent to S L J. Check that each pair of letters lines up.

stem: Use the markings in the figure. Which reason explains why ∠A ≅ ∠G?
title: Which reason? The Third Angles Theorem
steps: ∠ADM ≅ ∠GMD and ∠AMD ≅ ∠GDM
The marks show two pairs of congruent angles in the two triangles.
2 pairs of angles congruent → the third pair is congruent
If two angles of one triangle are congruent to two angles of another, the third angles are congruent too. The angles of each triangle add to 180.
Third Angles Theorem
So angle A is congruent to angle G by the Third Angles Theorem.

stem: In the figure, angles with the same marks are congruent. What is m∠1?
title: Third Angles Theorem
steps: two pairs of angles match → the third pair matches
Two pairs of angles have matching marks, so by the Third Angles Theorem the third pair is congruent too.
∠1 matches ∠J
Angle 1 matches the third angle of the other triangle, angle J.
Angle J is 180 minus 54 minus 100: 26 degrees. So angle 1 is 26 degrees.

stem: DEFG ≅ UTVW. Name the side that corresponds to G̅D̅.
title: Name a corresponding side
steps: DEFG ≅ UTVW: D ↔ U, E ↔ T, F ↔ V, G ↔ W
In a congruence statement, matching vertices are in the same position. Pair them up.
G̅D̅: G ↔ W, D ↔ U
Side G D uses G and D. G matches W, and D matches U.
W̅U̅
So the corresponding side is W U, in that order.

stem: DEFG ≅ QNMP. Name the angle that corresponds to ∠MPQ.
title: Name a corresponding angle
steps: DEFG ≅ QNMP: D ↔ Q, E ↔ N, F ↔ M, G ↔ P
Pair up the vertices by position.
∠MPQ: M ↔ F, P ↔ G, Q ↔ D
Angle M P Q uses M, P, and Q. They match F, G, and D.
∠FGD
So the corresponding angle is F G D. The middle letter, the vertex, matches the middle letter.

stem: △BCD ≅ △TVU. Identify all pairs of congruent corresponding parts.
title: All pairs of corresponding parts
steps: △BCD ≅ △TVU: B ↔ T, C ↔ V, D ↔ U
Pair up the vertices in order.
angles: ∠B ≅ ∠T, ∠C ≅ ∠V, ∠D ≅ ∠U
Each pair of matching vertices gives a pair of congruent angles.
sides: B̅C̅ ≅ T̅V̅, C̅D̅ ≅ V̅U̅, D̅B̅ ≅ U̅T̅
For sides, take the letters two at a time in order: B C with T V, C D with V U, and D B with U T.

stem: △BCD ≅ △TVU. Is the statement true or false?   ∠D ≅ ∠V
title: Corresponding parts: true or false
steps: △BCD ≅ △TVU: B ↔ T, C ↔ V, D ↔ U
Pair up the vertices in order.
∠D ≅ ∠V? D matches U, not V
The statement says angle D is congruent to angle V. But D is third in the first triangle, and U is third in the second. D matches U.
False
So the statement is false. Angle D is congruent to angle U.

stem: △BCD ≅ △TVU. Which is another correct way to write the congruence statement?
title: Rewrite a congruence statement
steps: B ↔ T, C ↔ V, D ↔ U
The pairs must stay together: B with T, C with V, D with U.
reorder both the same way: D B C → U T V
You can list the vertices in a different order, as long as you change both sides the same way.
△DBC ≅ △UTV
So triangle D B C is congruent to triangle U T V. For polygons, the letters also have to stay in order around the shape.

stem: △XYZ ≅ △JKM. XY = 4x − y, JK = 16, m∠Y = (3x + y)°, and m∠K = 19°. Find x and y.
title: Challenge: corresponding parts give a system
steps: XY = JK: 4x − y = 16
Corresponding parts are congruent. Side X Y matches side J K: 4 x minus y equals 16.
m∠Y = m∠K: 3x + y = 19
Angle Y matches angle K: 3 x plus y equals 19.
Add the equations to eliminate y: 7 x is 35, so x is 5.
Put 5 into the second equation: 15 plus y is 19, so y is 4.

stem: Use the markings in the figure. Part A: Which postulate or theorem proves the triangles congruent? If they cannot be proven congruent, choose “Not possible.” Part B: If they are congruent, write a congruence statement.
title: Prove triangles congruent: SSS
steps: F̅G̅ ≅ V̅E̅ and E̅F̅ ≅ G̅V̅
List what you know. Two pairs of sides are congruent: F G with V E, and E F with G V.
shared side: G̅E̅ ≅ E̅G̅ (Reflexive Property)
Look for anything the figure gives for free. Both triangles share side G E, and a segment is congruent to itself.
three pairs of sides → SSS
That makes three pairs of congruent sides, so the triangles are congruent by S S S.
△GFE ≅ △EVG
For the statement, match the vertices: G with E, F with V, E with G. Triangle G F E is congruent to triangle E V G.

stem: Use the markings in the figure. Part A: Which postulate or theorem proves the triangles congruent? If they cannot be proven congruent, choose “Not possible.” Part B: If they are congruent, write a congruence statement.
title: Prove triangles congruent: SAS
steps: ∠YKM ≅ ∠KYH and K̅M̅ ≅ Y̅H̅
List what you know: one pair of angles, at K and Y, and one pair of sides, K M and Y H.
shared side: Y̅K̅ ≅ K̅Y̅ (Reflexive Property)
The triangles share side Y K, which is congruent to itself.
the angle is between the two sides → SAS
Now we have two sides and an angle. The angle at K is between sides K M and K Y, so it is the included angle. That is S A S.
△YMK ≅ △KHY
Match the vertices: Y with K, M with H, K with Y. Triangle Y M K is congruent to triangle K H Y.

stem: Use the markings in the figure. Part A: Which postulate or theorem proves the triangles congruent? If they cannot be proven congruent, choose “Not possible.” Part B: If they are congruent, write a congruence statement.
title: Prove triangles congruent: ASA
steps: Q̅N̅ ≅ Q̅C̅ and ∠QNP ≅ ∠QCS
List what you know: sides Q N and Q C, and the angles at N and C.
vertical angles: ∠PQN ≅ ∠SQC
The figure gives one more pair: the angles at Q are vertical angles, so they are congruent.
the side is between the two angles → ASA
That is two angles and a side. The side Q N is between the angles at Q and N, so it is the included side. That is A S A.
△PQN ≅ △SQC
Match the vertices: P with S, Q with Q, N with C. Triangle P Q N is congruent to triangle S Q C.

stem: Use the markings in the figure. Part A: Which postulate or theorem proves the triangles congruent? If they cannot be proven congruent, choose “Not possible.” Part B: If they are congruent, write a congruence statement.
title: Prove triangles congruent: AAS
steps: ∠MQJ ≅ ∠MQB and ∠QJM ≅ ∠QBM
List what you know: two pairs of angles, at Q and at J and B.
shared side: M̅Q̅ ≅ M̅Q̅
The triangles share side M Q.
the side is not between the two angles → AAS
Two angles and a side, but the side M Q is not between the angles at Q and J. It is a non-included side, so this is A A S.
△MQJ ≅ △MQB
Match the vertices: triangle M Q J is congruent to triangle M Q B.

stem: Use the markings in the figure. Part A: Which postulate or theorem proves the triangles congruent? If they cannot be proven congruent, choose “Not possible.” Part B: If they are congruent, write a congruence statement.
title: Prove triangles congruent: HL
steps: H̅N̅ ≅ U̅D̅;  ∠NUH and ∠DHU are right angles
List what you know: sides H N and U D are congruent, and both triangles have a right angle.
H̅N̅ and U̅D̅ are across from the right angles → hypotenuses
H N and U D are across from the right angles, so they are the hypotenuses.
shared leg: U̅H̅ ≅ H̅U̅
The triangles share side U H, a leg of each right triangle.
hypotenuse and leg of right triangles → HL
A hypotenuse and a leg of right triangles: that is H L.
△HNU ≅ △UDH
Match the vertices: triangle H N U is congruent to triangle U D H.

stem: Use the markings in the figure. Part A: Which postulate or theorem proves the triangles congruent? If they cannot be proven congruent, choose “Not possible.” Part B: If they are congruent, write a congruence statement.
title: Prove triangles congruent: Not possible
steps: U̅V̅ ≅ B̅C̅ and V̅W̅ ≅ C̅W̅
List what you know: two pairs of sides.
vertical angles: ∠VWU ≅ ∠CWB
The angles at W are vertical angles, so they are congruent.
is the angle between the two sides? No → SSA
Check where the angle is. Angle V W U is between sides V W and W U. But W U is not one of our congruent sides. So the angle is not between the two congruent sides. That is S S A.
SSA does not prove congruence → Not possible
S S A does not prove triangles congruent, and so does A A A. So it is not possible.

stem: Given: F̅G̅ ≅ V̅E̅; E̅F̅ ≅ G̅V̅. Use the figure. Part A: Which postulate or theorem proves the triangles congruent? If they cannot be proven congruent, choose “Not possible.” Part B: If they are congruent, write a congruence statement.
title: Prove triangles congruent: SSS
steps: F̅G̅ ≅ V̅E̅ and E̅F̅ ≅ G̅V̅
List what you know. Two pairs of sides are congruent: F G with V E, and E F with G V.
shared side: G̅E̅ ≅ E̅G̅ (Reflexive Property)
Look for anything the figure gives for free. Both triangles share side G E, and a segment is congruent to itself.
three pairs of sides → SSS
That makes three pairs of congruent sides, so the triangles are congruent by S S S.
△GFE ≅ △EVG
For the statement, match the vertices: G with E, F with V, E with G. Triangle G F E is congruent to triangle E V G.

stem: Given: U̅V̅ ≅ B̅C̅; V̅W̅ ≅ C̅W̅. Use the figure. Part A: Which postulate or theorem proves the triangles congruent? If they cannot be proven congruent, choose “Not possible.” Part B: If they are congruent, write a congruence statement.
