stem: △CQX and △BFZ are right triangles with right angles at Q and F. CX = 3x − 10, BZ = x, and CQ = BF = 4. Find the value of x that makes the triangles congruent by the HL Congruence Theorem, and then find FZ.
title: Challenge: HL with algebra, then the Pythagorean Theorem
steps: HL needs: hypotenuses congruent and one pair of legs congruent
The legs C Q and B F are both 4. For H L, the hypotenuses must also be congruent.
CX = BZ: 3x − 10 = x
Set the hypotenuses equal.
Subtract x and add 10: 2 x is 10, so x is 5. Each hypotenuse is 5.
Use the Pythagorean Theorem: the other leg is the square root of 25 minus 16, which is 3.

stem: Complete the statement. State which theorem you used.   If G̅T̅ ≅ I̅T̅, then ∠___ ≅ ∠___.
title: Base Angles Theorem: complete the statement
steps: G̅T̅ ≅ I̅T̅ → look at △GIT
The two congruent sides, G T and I T, are both in triangle G I T.
G̅T̅ is opposite ∠GIT;  I̅T̅ is opposite ∠IGT
Find the angle across from each side. Side G T is across from the angle at I, angle G I T. Side I T is across from the angle at G, angle I G T.
congruent sides → congruent opposite angles
If two sides of a triangle are congruent, the angles opposite them are congruent. That's the Base Angles Theorem.
∠GIT ≅ ∠IGT  (Base Angles Theorem)
So angle G I T is congruent to angle I G T. If you're given congruent angles instead, use the converse to get congruent sides.

stem: Find the value of x.
title: Isosceles triangle: find x
steps: the legs are congruent → the base angles are congruent
The tick marks show two congruent sides, so the angles opposite them, the base angles, are congruent.
each base angle: (180° − 100°)/2 = 40°
The vertex angle is 100 degrees. The other two angles share what's left: 80 degrees, so 40 each.
The base angle is 5 x plus 30, so 5 x plus 30 equals 40. Subtract 30 and divide by 5: x is 2.

stem: Find the values of x and y.
title: Equilateral triangle: find x and y
steps: all three sides congruent → equilateral → equiangular
All three sides are marked congruent, so the triangle is equilateral. An equilateral triangle is also equiangular.
each angle = 180° ÷ 3 = 60° → x = 60
Three equal angles that add to 180 are each 60 degrees. So x is 60.
The sides are all equal, so 2 y minus 4 equals 16. Add 4 and divide by 2: y is 10.

stem: Find the perimeter of the triangle.
title: Perimeter of an isosceles triangle
steps: the two marked sides are congruent: 4x + 7 = 2x + 25
The tick marks show which two sides are congruent. Set those two expressions equal.
Subtract 2 x and 7: 2 x is 18, so x is 9.
Find all three sides: 43, 43, and 36.
perimeter = 43 + 43 + 36 = 122
Add them: the perimeter is 122.

stem: Each base angle of an isosceles triangle measures 62°. Find the measure of the vertex angle.
title: Isosceles triangle: find the vertex angle
steps: two base angles: 62° each
The two base angles are congruent, so both are 62 degrees.
The angles add to 180, so the vertex angle is 180 minus 124: 56 degrees.

stem: The vertex angle of an isosceles triangle measures 40°. Find the measure of each base angle.
title: Isosceles triangle: find the base angles
steps: base angles: x and x;  vertex 40°
Call each base angle x. They're congruent.
The angles add to 180: 2 x plus 40 equals 180. So x is 70 degrees.

stem: In an isosceles triangle, the exterior angle at the vertex measures 140°. Find the measure of each base angle.
title: Isosceles triangle: from an exterior angle
steps: vertex angle = 180° − 140° = 40°
The exterior angle at the vertex forms a linear pair with the vertex angle, so the vertex angle is 40 degrees.
each base angle = (180° − 40°)/2 = 70°
The base angles share the remaining 140 degrees: 70 each.
Check: the exterior angle equals the sum of the two remote angles, 70 plus 70.

stem: The lengths of the sides of a triangle are 4t + 11, 3t + 18, 2t + 21. Find all values of t that make the triangle isosceles.
title: Values that make a triangle isosceles
steps: isosceles: at least two sides equal → try each pair
A triangle is isosceles when at least two sides are equal. There are three pairs of sides to try.
First pair: t is 7. The sides are 39, 39, and 35. All positive, and the two short sides add to more than the long side, so it's a real triangle.
Second pair: t is 5. Sides 31, 33, 31. That works.
Third pair: t is 3. Sides 23, 27, 27. That works too.
So t can be 3, 5, or 7. If a value gave a negative side or failed the Triangle Inequality, you'd throw it out.

stem: The base of isosceles △JKL is K̅L̅. What can you prove?
title: Parts of an isosceles triangle
steps: base K̅L̅ → legs J̅K̅ and J̅L̅
The legs are the two sides that are not the base: J K and J L.
legs are congruent: J̅K̅ ≅ J̅L̅
In an isosceles triangle the legs are congruent.
base angles at K and L: ∠K ≅ ∠L
The base angles are at the ends of the base, at K and L. By the Base Angles Theorem they're congruent.

stem: A hiker walking along a straight trail travels along a straight line from point R toward point T. At R, the angle between the path and the line of sight to the radio tower L is 32°. After traveling 3 kilometers to point S, the angle between the path and the line of sight to L is 64°. How far is the radio tower from point S (find SL)?
title: Isosceles triangles in real life
steps: △RSL: ∠R = 32°, exterior ∠LST = 64°
Look at triangle R S L. The angle at R is 32 degrees, and the 64 degree angle at S is an exterior angle of the triangle.
An exterior angle equals the sum of the two remote angles, so 64 equals 32 plus angle L. Angle L is 32 degrees.
∠R ≅ ∠L → SL = RS
Angles R and L are congruent, so the sides opposite them are congruent. That's the Converse of the Base Angles Theorem.
SL = 3 km
So the tower is 3 kilometers from S, the same as the distance traveled.

stem: △MPX is isosceles with legs M̅P̅ and M̅X̅. MP = 2x + 18, MX = 4x + 8, and PX = 3x − 3. Find x and the perimeter of △MPX.
title: Challenge: isosceles legs give x; find the perimeter
steps: legs congruent: 2x + 18 = 4x + 8
The legs are M P and M X, and they're congruent. Set them equal.
Subtract 2 x and 8: 10 equals 2 x, so x is 5.
legs: 28 and 28;  base: 3(5) − 3 = 12
Each leg is 28. The base is 15 minus 3: 12.
perimeter = 28 + 28 + 12 = 68
The perimeter is 68.

stem: G(4, −7) and H(−3, −7). Find the midpoint, the distance, and the slope of G̅H̅.
title: Midpoint, distance, and slope
steps: Midpoint: average the x values and the y values. 4 plus negative 3 is 1, halved is 0.5. Both y values are negative 7.
both y = −7 → horizontal: d = |4 − (−3)| = 7
The y values match, so the segment is horizontal. The distance is just the difference in x: 7.
slope = rise/run = 0/(−7) = 0
Slope is rise over run. The rise is 0, so the slope is 0. A horizontal segment always has slope 0.

stem: The endpoints of C̅D̅ are C(6, 7) and D(4, 8). Find the coordinates of the midpoint M.
title: The Midpoint Formula
steps: The midpoint averages the x coordinates and averages the y coordinates.
6 plus 4 is 10, halved is 5. 7 plus 8 is 15, halved is 7.5. The midpoint is 5, 7.5.

stem: Find the distance between G(5, −8) and H(−2, −8).
title: Distance: a horizontal segment
steps: G(5, −8), H(−2, −8): same y → horizontal
The y values are the same, so the segment is horizontal.
The distance is the difference in x: the absolute value of negative 2 minus 5 is 7. For a vertical segment, subtract the y values instead.

stem: Find the distance between F(−3, −1) and U(−11, 14).
title: Distance: the Distance Formula
steps: d = √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²)
For a slanted segment, use the Distance Formula.
x changes by negative 8 and y changes by 15.
Square them: 64 and 225. Add: 289. The square root is 17.

stem: Find the slope of the line that passes through the given points.   (−1, −1), (2, 1)
title: Slope from two points
steps: m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁)
Slope is the change in y over the change in x.
1 minus negative 1 is 2. 2 minus negative 1 is 3. The slope is 2 thirds.

stem: Find the slope of the line that passes through the given points.   (2, 2), (8, 2)
title: Slope: a horizontal line
steps: The y values are the same.
The rise is 0, so the slope is 0. Horizontal lines have slope 0.

stem: Find the slope of the line that passes through the given points.   (−5, −5), (−5, −12)
title: Slope: a vertical line
steps: The x values are the same.
run = 0 → can't divide by 0 → undefined
The run is 0, and you can't divide by 0. Vertical lines have undefined slope.

stem: The midpoint M and one endpoint G of G̅H̅ are given. Find the coordinates of the other endpoint H.   G(6, 7) and M(4, −9)
title: Find the other endpoint
steps: From G to M, x goes down 2 and y goes down 16.
M is halfway, so H is the same distance past M: 2, negative 25.

stem: Segment 1 goes through (4, 0) and (6, −4). Segment 2 goes through (3, 1) and (7, −7). Are they parallel, perpendicular, or neither?
title: Parallel, perpendicular, or neither? Parallel
steps: Find each slope: both are negative 2.
same slope → parallel
Equal slopes mean the segments are parallel.

stem: Segment 1 goes through (0, −3) and (3, −4). Segment 2 goes through (−4, 3) and (−3, 6). Are they parallel, perpendicular, or neither?
title: Parallel, perpendicular, or neither? Perpendicular
steps: slope 1 = −1/3;  slope 2 = 3/1 = 3
The slopes are negative one third and 3.
(−1/3)(3) = −1 → perpendicular
They multiply to negative 1, so the segments are perpendicular.

stem: Segment 1 goes through (−6, −2) and (−2, 2). Segment 2 goes through (−3, −5) and (2, −9). Are they parallel, perpendicular, or neither?
title: Parallel, perpendicular, or neither? Neither
steps: slope 1 = 4/4 = 1;  slope 2 = −4/5
The slopes are 1 and negative 4 fifths.
not equal, product ≠ −1 → neither
They aren't equal, and their product is negative 4 fifths, not negative 1. So neither.

stem: The distance between A(2, 5) and B(9, k) is 25. Find every possible value of k.
title: Challenge: an unknown coordinate from a distance
steps: Write the Distance Formula with the unknown k.
Square both sides. 7 squared is 49.
Subtract 49: 576. Take the square root, both positive and negative: 24 or negative 24.
So k is 29 or negative 19. One point is above A and one is below.

stem: Find the indicated measure. Find UL.
title: Perpendicular Bisector Theorem
steps: U̅Q̅ ⊥ H̅L̅ and bisects it → the perpendicular bisector
The marks show U Q is perpendicular to H L and cuts it in half, so U Q is the perpendicular bisector of H L.
a point on the ⊥ bisector is equidistant from the endpoints
Any point on the perpendicular bisector is the same distance from both endpoints. That's the Perpendicular Bisector Theorem.
UL = UH = 4.7
So U L equals U H, which is 4.7.

stem: Find the indicated measure. Find EF.
title: Converse of the Perpendicular Bisector Theorem
steps: HE = HF (marked) → H is on the ⊥ bisector of E̅F̅
The marks show H is the same distance from E and F. By the converse, H is on the perpendicular bisector of E F, so G is the midpoint.
The two halves are equal.
Subtract 5 x and add 25: 27 equals 3 x, so x is 9.
each half: 5(9) + 2 = 47 → EF = 94
Each half is 47, and the whole segment E F is 94.

stem: Find the indicated measure. Find YV.
title: Perpendicular bisector with x
steps: Y is on the ⊥ bisector of V̅W̅ → YV = YW
Y is on the perpendicular bisector of V W, so Y is the same distance from V and W.
Set the distances equal. Subtract 6 x and 1: x is 8.
So Y V is 48 plus 9: 57.

stem: Tell whether the information in the figure allows you to conclude that point U lies on the perpendicular bisector of H̅L̅.
title: On the perpendicular bisector? Yes
steps: U̅Q̅ ⊥ H̅L̅ (right angle) and HQ = QL (ticks)
The figure marks a right angle and congruent halves. So U Q is perpendicular to H L and bisects it.
U̅Q̅ is the perpendicular bisector → U is on it
That makes U Q the perpendicular bisector, and U is on that line.
Yes
So yes.

stem: Tell whether the information in the figure allows you to conclude that point H lies on the perpendicular bisector of E̅F̅.
title: On the perpendicular bisector? Yes (equidistant)
steps: HE = HF (marked)
The marks show H is the same distance from E and F.
equidistant from the endpoints → on the ⊥ bisector
By the Converse of the Perpendicular Bisector Theorem, a point equidistant from the endpoints is on the perpendicular bisector.
Yes
So yes.

stem: Tell whether the information in the figure allows you to conclude that point T lies on the perpendicular bisector of Q̅R̅.
title: On the perpendicular bisector? No (no right angle)
steps: S is the midpoint of Q̅R̅ (ticks)
The tick marks show S is the midpoint of Q R.
no right angle mark
But nothing shows T S is perpendicular to Q R.
No
A perpendicular bisector needs both: it must be perpendicular and go through the midpoint. So you can't conclude it.

stem: Tell whether the information in the figure allows you to conclude that point Q lies on the perpendicular bisector of M̅N̅.
title: On the perpendicular bisector? No (no midpoint)
steps: Q̅P̅ ⊥ M̅N̅ (right angle)
The right angle mark shows Q P is perpendicular to M N.
no tick marks → P not known to be the midpoint
But nothing shows P is the midpoint of M N.
No
Without the midpoint, you can't conclude Q P is the perpendicular bisector.

stem: Find the indicated measure. UQ
title: Angle Bisector Theorem: find a distance
steps: H̅U̅ bisects ∠LHQ (marked congruent angles)
The marks show H U splits angle L H Q into two congruent angles, so it's the angle bisector.
a point on the bisector is equidistant from the sides
A point on an angle bisector is the same distance from both sides of the angle. Those distances are the perpendicular segments.
UQ = UL = 7
So U Q equals U L, which is 7.

stem: Find the indicated measure. m∠FEG
title: Converse of the Angle Bisector Theorem: find the angle
steps: HF = HG, both ⊥ to the sides → H is on the bisector
H is the same distance from both sides, measured along perpendiculars. By the converse, H is on the bisector of angle F E G.
So the two halves are equal. Subtract 2 x and add 27: 20 equals 2 x, so x is 10.
each half: 2(10) − 7 = 13° → m∠FEG = 26°
Each half is 13 degrees, so the whole angle is 26 degrees.

stem: Tell whether the information in the figure allows you to conclude that HU bisects ∠LHQ.
title: Does the ray bisect the angle? Yes
steps: perpendicular distances from U to both sides are marked congruent
The segments from U to the sides are perpendicular, and they are marked congruent. So U is equidistant from the sides.
equidistant from the sides → on the bisector
By the Converse of the Angle Bisector Theorem, U is on the bisector.
Yes
So yes, H U bisects the angle.

stem: Tell whether the information in the figure allows you to conclude that MQ bisects ∠NMP.
title: Does the ray bisect the angle? No (not perpendicular)
steps: Q̅N̅ ≅ Q̅P̅, but no right angles
The segments are congruent, but they are not marked perpendicular to the sides.
distance to a side must be perpendicular
The distance from a point to a side is measured along a perpendicular. These segments might be slanted.
No
So you can't conclude the ray bisects the angle.

stem: Tell whether the information in the figure allows you to conclude that EH bisects ∠FEG.
title: Does the ray bisect the angle? No (not congruent)
steps: the segments are ⊥ to the sides, but not marked congruent
The segments are perpendicular to the sides, but there are no marks showing they are congruent.
can't tell H is equidistant
So you don't know H is the same distance from both sides.
No
You can't conclude the ray bisects the angle.

stem: Write an equation of the perpendicular bisector of the segment with endpoints K(−10, 0) and W(−4, −6).
title: Equation of a perpendicular bisector
steps: The perpendicular bisector goes through the midpoint. Average the coordinates: negative 7, negative 3.
The slope of K W is negative 6 over 6, which is negative 1.
perpendicular slope: 1
The perpendicular slope is the opposite reciprocal: 1.
Point-slope form through negative 7, negative 3, then solve for y: y equals x plus 4.

stem: Point P lies on the y-axis and is the same distance from A(1, 1) and B(5, 7). Find the coordinates of P.
title: Challenge: a point on an axis, equidistant from two points
steps: equidistant from A and B → on the ⊥ bisector of A̅B̅
A point the same distance from A and B lies on the perpendicular bisector of A B.
midpoint (3, 4);  slope AB = 6/4 = 3/2 → perpendicular slope −2/3
The midpoint is 3, 4. The slope of A B is 3 halves, so the perpendicular slope is negative 2 thirds.
The perpendicular bisector is y minus 4 equals negative 2 thirds times x minus 3.
on the y-axis: x = 0 → y − 4 = 2 → y = 6
P is on the y-axis, so x is 0. Then y minus 4 is 2, and y is 6.
P(0, 6);  check PA = PB = √26
So P is 0, 6. Check: P A and P B are both root 26.

stem: Point F is the circumcenter of △CDE. FC = 6x + 7 and FD = 9x − 5. Find FE.
title: Circumcenter: equal distances to the vertices
steps: circumcenter → equidistant from the vertices
The circumcenter is where the perpendicular bisectors meet. It's the same distance from all three vertices.
FC = FD: 6x + 7 = 9x − 5
So F C equals F D. Set them equal.
Subtract 6 x and add 5: 12 equals 3 x, so x is 4.
F E is the same as F C: 24 plus 7 is 31.

stem: Point V is the incenter of △CPT. A, F, and W are the points where the perpendicular segments from V meet the sides. VA = 4x − 1 and VF = 8x − 33. Find VW.
title: Incenter: equal distances to the sides
steps: incenter → equidistant from the sides
The incenter is where the angle bisectors meet. It's the same distance from all three sides, measured along perpendiculars.
So V A equals V F. Set them equal.
Subtract 4 x and add 33: 32 equals 4 x, so x is 8.
V W is the same distance: 32 minus 1 is 31.

stem: The angle bisectors of △DHR meet at point Y. Point U is on D̅H̅ with Y̅U̅ ⊥ D̅H̅. YD = 15 and DU = 12. Find the distance from Y to H̅R̅.
title: Incenter with the Pythagorean Theorem
steps: angle bisectors meet at Y → Y is the incenter
The angle bisectors meet at the incenter, Y.
△YUD: right angle at U, hypotenuse YD = 15, leg DU = 12
Y U is perpendicular to D H, so triangle Y U D is a right triangle. Its hypotenuse is Y D, 15, and one leg is D U, 12.
Pythagorean Theorem: Y U is the square root of 225 minus 144, which is 9.
distance to H̅R̅ = 9
Y is the incenter, so it's the same distance from every side. The distance to H R is also 9.

stem: Find the coordinates of the circumcenter of the triangle with vertices T(0, 6), U(4, 2), and W(0, 2).
title: Circumcenter from coordinates
steps: the circumcenter: where the ⊥ bisectors meet
The circumcenter is where the perpendicular bisectors of the sides meet.
W̅U̅ is horizontal (y = 2): its ⊥ bisector is x = 2
W U goes from 0, 2 to 4, 2, a horizontal segment. Its midpoint is 2, 2, so its perpendicular bisector is the vertical line x equals 2.
W̅T̅ is vertical (x = 0): its ⊥ bisector is y = 4
W T goes from 0, 2 to 0, 6, a vertical segment. Its midpoint is 0, 4, so its perpendicular bisector is the horizontal line y equals 4.
they meet at (2, 4)
The two lines meet at 2, 4.
check: distance to each vertex = 2√2
Check: 2, 4 is root 8, which is 2 root 2, from each vertex.

stem: You want to locate a donation center the same distance from a department store, an electronics store, and a grocery store. Which point of the triangle formed by the three locations should you use?
title: Which point of concurrency?
steps: same distance from three places (points) → circumcenter
Ask what the point should be the same distance from. Three locations are points, the vertices of the triangle. The point equally far from the vertices is the circumcenter.
same distance from three walls or roads (sides) → incenter
If it should be equally far from three sides, like walls or roads, use the incenter.
three stores → points → Circumcenter
Here the stores are three points, so use the circumcenter.

stem: Point I is the incenter of △GHJ. D is on G̅H̅ and E is on G̅J̅, with I̅D̅ ⟂ G̅H̅ and I̅E̅ ⟂ G̅J̅. ID = 6x − 30, IE = x + 5, and IG = 20. Find x and GD.
title: Challenge: incenter algebra, then the Pythagorean Theorem
steps: incenter → ID = IE: 6x − 30 = x + 5
The incenter is the same distance from every side, so I D equals I E.
Solve: x is 7, and I D is 42 minus 30: 12.
△IGD: hypotenuse IG = 20, leg ID = 12
Triangle I G D is a right triangle with hypotenuse I G, 20, and leg I D, 12.
G D is the square root of 400 minus 144, which is 16.

stem: Point P is the centroid of △LMN, and N̅Q̅ is a median. PQ = 8. Find NP and NQ.
title: Centroid on a median: from the short piece
steps: centroid: 2/3 of the way from the vertex to the midpoint
Centroid Theorem: the centroid is two thirds of the way along each median, from the vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side.
so the vertex piece is twice the short piece
That means the piece from the vertex to the centroid is twice as long as the piece from the centroid to the midpoint.
P Q is the short piece, 8. So N P is 16.
The whole median N Q is 16 plus 8: 24.

stem: Point T is the centroid of △HLQ, and Q̅U̅ is a median (U is the midpoint of H̅L̅). QU = 15. Find TU and QT.
title: Centroid on a median: from the whole median
steps: QU = 15 is the whole median
Q U is the whole median, 15.
The centroid T is two thirds of the way from the vertex Q: two thirds of 15 is 10.
The rest, from T to the midpoint U, is one third: 5.

stem: Point G is the centroid of △ABC. B̅F̅, A̅E̅, and C̅D̅ are medians (D, E, and F are midpoints of A̅B̅, B̅C̅, and A̅C̅). BG = 16, AF = 16, and AE = 21. Find G̅F̅.
title: Centroid segment lengths
steps: vertex → centroid = 2/3 of the median;  centroid → midpoint = 1/3
On each median, the vertex to centroid piece is two thirds of the median, and the centroid to midpoint piece is one third. So the long piece is twice the short piece.
GF is the short piece of median BF; BG is the long piece
G F is the short piece of median B F, and B G is the long piece.
So G F is half of B G: 8.
F is a midpoint → AF = FC
Also remember the medians go to midpoints. For example, A F equals F C. Use that if the question asks for half a side.

stem: Find the coordinates of the centroid of the triangle with vertices G(−4, −6), H(−2, 4), and J(−6, 5).
title: Centroid from coordinates
steps: centroid = the average of the vertices
The centroid is the average of the three vertices.
Add the x coordinates and divide by 3: negative 12 over 3 is negative 4.
Add the y coordinates and divide by 3: 3 over 3 is 1.
So the centroid is negative 4, 1.

stem: Tell whether the orthocenter of the triangle with vertices B(7, −2), S(7, 6), and W(−5, 4) is inside, on, or outside the triangle. Then find its coordinates.
title: Orthocenter: an acute triangle
steps: acute → orthocenter inside
The orthocenter is where the altitudes meet. For an acute triangle it's inside, for a right triangle it's at the right angle, and for an obtuse triangle it's outside.
B̅S̅ is vertical (x = 7) → the altitude from W is horizontal: y = 4
Side B S is vertical, so the altitude from W is horizontal, through W: y equals 4.
slope SW = 1/6 → altitude from B: slope −6: y + 2 = −6(x − 7)
Side S W has slope one sixth, so the altitude from B has slope negative 6.
Put y equals 4 into that: 6 equals negative 6 times x minus 7, so x is 6.
inside; (6, 4)
The orthocenter is at 6, 4, inside the triangle.

stem: Tell whether the orthocenter of the triangle with vertices U(0, 4), V(4, −1), and W(0, −1) is inside, on, or outside the triangle. Then find its coordinates.
title: Orthocenter: a right triangle
steps: W(0, −1) to U(0, 4) is vertical; W to V(4, −1) is horizontal → right angle at W
Side W U is vertical and side W V is horizontal, so the triangle has a right angle at W.
in a right triangle, the legs are altitudes
In a right triangle, each leg is an altitude, and the legs meet at the right angle.
on the triangle; (0, −1)
So the orthocenter is on the triangle, at the right-angle vertex: 0, negative 1.

stem: Tell whether the orthocenter of the triangle with vertices B(−4, −4), E(6, 6), and F(4, 0) is inside, on, or outside the triangle. Then find its coordinates.
title: Orthocenter: an obtuse triangle
steps: obtuse → orthocenter outside
This triangle is obtuse, so the orthocenter is outside it.
slope EF = 3 → altitude from B: slope −1/3: y + 4 = −(1/3)(x + 4)
Side E F has slope 3, so the altitude from B has slope negative one third.
slope BF = 1/2 → altitude from E: slope −2: y = −2x + 18
Side B F has slope one half, so the altitude from E has slope negative 2. Through E at 6, 6, that's y equals negative 2 x plus 18.
solve: x = 14, y = −10
Solve the two equations together: x is 14 and y is negative 10.
outside; (14, −10)
So the orthocenter is outside, at 14, negative 10.

stem: The centroid of △CDE is G(3, 3). Two vertices are C(3, 6) and D(−8, −1). Find the coordinates of vertex E.
title: Challenge: find a vertex from the centroid
steps: centroid = average: (3 + (−8) + x)/3 = 3
The centroid is the average of the vertices. For x: 3 plus negative 8 plus the unknown x, divided by 3, equals 3.
Multiply by 3: the sum is 9. So x is 9 minus 3 plus 8: 14.
Same for y: 6 plus negative 1 plus y equals 9, so y is 4.
So E is 14, 4.

stem:
△CDE has vertices C(4, 5), D(3, 6), and E(−7, −1). 
• F is the midpoint of C̅E̅.
• G is the midpoint of E̅D̅.
• H is the midpoint of D̅C̅.
Find the coordinates of F, G, and H.
title: Midpoints on the coordinate plane
steps: F is the midpoint of C E. Average C and E: 4 plus negative 7 is negative 3, halved is negative 3 halves. 5 plus negative 1 is 4, halved is 2.
G averages E and D: negative 2, and 5 halves.
H averages D and C: 7 halves, and 11 halves.
each midsegment is ∥ to the third side and half as long
Joining these midpoints makes midsegments. Each one is parallel to the third side and half as long.

stem: T̅U̅ is a midsegment of △HLQ. Find the value of x.
title: Midsegment: find the shorter segment
steps: midsegment = (1/2)(third side)
Triangle Midsegment Theorem: a midsegment is half as long as the side it's parallel to.
T U is parallel to L Q, which is 8. So T U is 4, and x is 4.

stem: P̅Q̅ is a midsegment of △LMN. Find the value of x.
title: Midsegment: find the longer side
steps: side = 2 × midsegment
The side is twice the midsegment parallel to it.
P Q is 8, so M N is 16, and x is 16.

stem: H̅J̅ is a midsegment of △EFG. Find the value of x.
title: Midsegment with x
steps: FG = 2 · HJ
The side F G is twice the midsegment H J.
Substitute and distribute.
Subtract 4 x and 16: 20 equals 2 x, so x is 10.

stem: In △EHL, Q, T, and U are the midpoints of E̅H̅, H̅L̅, and E̅L̅. Complete the statement.   Q̅T̅ ∥ ___
title: Midsegments: what is it parallel to?
steps: Q̅T̅ joins the midpoints of E̅H̅ and H̅L̅
Q is on E H and T is on H L, so Q T joins the midpoints of those two sides.
→ Q̅T̅ ∥ the third side, E̅L̅
A midsegment is parallel to the third side, the one it doesn't touch: E L.

stem: In △LMN, P, Q, and R are the midpoints of L̅M̅, M̅N̅, and L̅N̅. Complete the statement.   L̅M̅ ∥ ___
title: Midsegments: which midsegment is parallel to a side?
steps: Find the midsegment that doesn't touch side L M.
P is on L̅M̅ → skip midsegments through P
P is the midpoint of L M, so any midsegment through P touches L M.
Q̅R̅
The midsegment Q R joins the midpoints of the other two sides. It's parallel to L M.

stem: In △EFG, H, J, and K are the midpoints of E̅F̅, F̅G̅, and E̅G̅. Complete the statement.   If FG = 20, then HK = ___
title: Midsegments: find a length
steps: H̅K̅ joins the midpoints of E̅F̅ and E̅G̅ → H̅K̅ ∥ F̅G̅
H K joins the midpoints of E F and E G, so it's the midsegment parallel to F G.
It's half as long: 10.

stem: In △PQR, S, T, and U are the midpoints of P̅Q̅, Q̅R̅, and P̅R̅. Complete the statement.   Q̅T̅ ≅ ___ ≅ ___
title: Midsegments: congruent segments
steps: Q̅T̅ ≅ T̅R̅ (T is the midpoint of Q̅R̅)
T is the midpoint of Q R, so the two halves, Q T and T R, are congruent.
S̅U̅ ∥ Q̅R̅ and half as long → S̅U̅ ≅ Q̅T̅
The midsegment S U is parallel to Q R and half as long, so it's the same length as each half.
Q̅T̅ ≅ T̅R̅ ≅ S̅U̅
So Q T is congruent to T R and to S U.

stem: Oak Street joins the midpoints of Walnut Street and Maple Street, which form two sides of a triangle with Spruce Street. Walnut Street is 1.2 miles long, Maple Street is 1.2 miles long, and Spruce Street is 2.6 miles long. A parade float starts where Walnut Street meets Spruce Street, travels up Walnut Street to Oak Street, along Oak Street to Maple Street, and then down Maple Street to Spruce Street. About how far does the float travel?
title: Midsegments in real life: a parade route
steps: half of Walnut: 0.6 mi
The float travels up Walnut Street to the midpoint, which is half of 1.2: 0.6 miles.
Oak St is a midsegment: half of Spruce = 1.3 mi
Oak Street joins the midpoints, so it's a midsegment, half as long as Spruce Street: 1.3 miles.
half of Maple: 0.6 mi
Then down half of Maple Street: 0.6 miles.
In all: 2.5 miles.

stem: The distance between consecutive bases on a baseball field is 60 feet. The pitcher fields a ball halfway between first base and third base, and the shortstop stands halfway between second base and third base. The pitcher, shortstop, and the bases form a triangle with a midsegment. Find the distance between the shortstop and the pitcher.
title: Midsegments in real life: a baseball field
steps: pitcher: midpoint of 1st–3rd;  shortstop: midpoint of 2nd–3rd
Both players are at midpoints of sides of the triangle made by first, second, and third base.
the segment between them is a midsegment, ∥ to 1st–2nd
The segment between them is a midsegment, parallel to the side from first to second base.
So it's half of 60: 30 feet.

stem: The midpoints of the sides of △CDE are F(5, 6) on C̅D̅, G(−2, 2) on D̅E̅, and H(−1, 2) on C̅E̅. Find the coordinates of C.
title: Challenge: work backwards from the midpoints
steps: G̅H̅ ∥ C̅D̅ and F̅G̅ ∥ C̅E̅ → CFGH is a parallelogram
Each midsegment is parallel to the third side, so C F G H is a parallelogram, with C across from G.
C = F + H − G
In a parallelogram, the opposite corner is F plus H minus G.
x: 5 plus negative 1 plus 2 is 6. y: 6 plus 2 minus 2 is 6.
So C is 6, 6.

stem: Write the first step in an indirect proof of the statement.   If 3x + 5 ≠ 17, then x ≠ 4.
title: Indirect proof: the first step
steps: If 3x + 5 ≠ 17, then x ≠ 4.
An indirect proof starts by assuming the conclusion is false.
conclusion: x ≠ 4 → its opposite: x = 4
The conclusion is x is not 4. Its opposite is x equals 4.
Assume temporarily that x = 4.
So the first step is: Assume temporarily that x equals 4. Then you show that leads to a contradiction.

stem: List the angles of △LXY in order from smallest to largest.
title: Order the angles from the sides
steps: smallest angle ↔ shortest side;  largest angle ↔ longest side
In a triangle, the smallest angle is across from the shortest side, and the largest angle is across from the longest side.
22 is opposite ∠Y;  25 opposite ∠L;  26 opposite ∠X
Find the angle across from each side. The side of length 22 is across from angle Y, 25 is across from angle L, and 26 is across from angle X.
So from smallest to largest: angle Y, angle L, angle X.

stem: List the sides of △CDE in order from shortest to longest.
title: Order the sides from the angles

stem: A triangle has sides of length 3x + 1, 2x − 2, and 3x + 4. Describe the possible values of x.

Third pair: x is more than negative one half.
all true (and every side positive): x > 2.5

stem: Two flights leave from the same airport. Flight 1 flies 150 miles due east, then turns 40° toward south and flies 100 miles. Flight 2 flies 150 miles due north, then turns 50° toward east and flies 100 miles. Which flight is farther from the airport?
title: Hinge Theorem in real life: flights
steps: each path: sides 150 and 100 mi
Each flight makes a triangle with sides 150 and 100 miles. The distance from the airport is the third side.
included angle = 180° − the turn
The angle between the two legs of the trip is 180 minus the turn.
Flight 1 turned 40 degrees, so its angle is 140. Flight 2 turned 50, so its angle is 130.
larger angle → farther: Flight 1
The larger included angle gives the longer third side, so Flight 1 is farther. Careful: the bigger turn makes the smaller angle.

stem: In △EFH and △GFH, E̅F̅ ≅ G̅F̅ and the triangles share F̅H̅. m∠EFH = 58°, m∠GFH = 38°, EH = 30, and GH = 6x − 3. Find the possible values of x.

steps: The angle for G H is smaller, so G H is shorter than E H.

a length is positive: 6x − 3 > 0 → x > 1/2

stem: In △LMN and △SWZ, L̅M̅ ≅ S̅W̅ and L̅N̅ ≅ S̅Z̅. m∠L = (3x + 24)°, m∠S = 87°, and MN > WZ. Find the possible values of x.

steps: MN > WZ → m∠L > m∠S (Converse of the Hinge Theorem)
Two pairs of sides are congruent, and M N is longer than W Z. By the converse of the Hinge Theorem, angle L is larger than angle S.
So 3 x plus 24 is more than 87. Subtract 24 and divide by 3: x is more than 21.
an angle is less than 180°: 3x + 24 < 180 → x < 52
Also, an angle in a triangle is less than 180. So 3 x plus 24 is less than 180, and x is less than 52.
So x is between 21 and 52.

stem: In a regular polygon, each interior angle is 150° greater than each exterior angle. How many sides does the polygon have, and what is the sum of its interior angle measures?

The exterior angles add to 360, so there are 360 divided by 15: 24 sides.

stem: Each interior angle of a regular polygon is 2 times as large as each exterior angle. How many sides does the polygon have, and what is the sum of its interior angle measures?

Interior plus exterior is 180: 3 e is 180, so e is 60.
360 divided by 60 is 6 sides.
The interior angle sum is 4 times 180: 720 degrees.

stem: △PQR ~ △EFG. PQ = 19 and EF = 57. The median from R in △PQR has length 12. Find the length of the corresponding median from G in △EFG.

stem: The rectangles are similar. A side of the first has length 10 m, and the corresponding side of the second has length 40 m. The area of the first is 28 m². Find the area of the second.

Rope goes around each site. A's perimeter is 150 meters and B's is 45.
total: 195 m
Both together: 195 meters.

stem: Your family puts a rectangular patio in your backyard, similar to the shape of the backyard. The backyard has a length of 40 feet and a width of 20 feet. The length of the patio is 15 feet. Find the perimeter of the patio.
title: Similar polygons in real life: a patio
steps: scale factor: 15/40 = 3/8
The patio's length over the backyard's length: 15 over 40, which is 3 eighths.
backyard perimeter: 2(40 + 20) = 120 ft
The backyard's perimeter is 120 feet.
Perimeters scale by the same factor: 120 times 3 eighths is 45 feet.

stem: Two similar triangles have areas of 540 square inches and 735 square inches. The smaller one has a perimeter of 42 inches and one side 30 inches long. Find the perimeter of the larger one and the length of the corresponding side.
title: Challenge: areas give the scale factor
steps: area ratio = (scale factor)²: 540/735 = 36/49
The ratio of the areas is the square of the scale factor. 540 over 735 simplifies to 36 over 49.
scale factor = √(36/49) = 6/7
Take the square root: 6 sevenths.
Perimeters scale by 6 sevenths too: 42 over P is 6 over 7, so P is 49 inches.
The side: 30 over s is 6 over 7, so s is 35 inches.

stem: Determine whether the triangles are similar. If they are, write a similarity statement.
title: Similar by AA? Yes
steps: find the missing angles (Triangle Sum Theorem)
Find the third angle of each triangle: the angles add to 180.
Triangle H J K has 40, 50, and 90 degrees. Triangle A N S has 40, 90, and 50.
two pairs of angles match → similar (AA)
Two pairs of congruent angles are enough: the triangles are similar by A A.
Match vertices by equal angles: H with A, J with S, K with N. So H J K is similar to A S N.

stem: Determine whether the triangles are similar. If they are, write a similarity statement.
title: Similar by AA? No
steps: find the missing angles
Find each triangle's third angle.
Triangle C D E has 31, 62, and 87 degrees. Triangle J L P has 26, 87, and 67.
only one angle matches (87°) → not similar
Only the 87 degree angles match. You need two matching pairs, so the triangles are not similar.

stem: In △ABC, m∠A = 69° and m∠B = 73°. In △DEF, m∠D = (x + 7)° and m∠E = (y + 12)°. Find the values of x and y that make △ABC ~ △DEF.
title: Angles that make triangles similar
steps: △ABC ~ △DEF → ∠D ≅ ∠A, ∠E ≅ ∠B
The similarity statement pairs D with A and E with B, so those angles must be congruent.
Angle D equals angle A: x plus 7 is 69, so x is 62.
Angle E equals angle B: y plus 12 is 73, so y is 61.

stem: You measure the width of a lake using a surveying technique. Segments VW and YZ are parallel, and VY and WZ intersect at X, with W and X on opposite shores of the lake. VW = 120 m, YZ = 12 m, and XZ = 10 m. Find the width WX of the lake.
title: Similar triangles in real life: across a lake
steps: ∥ segments + vertical angles at X → similar triangles (AA)
The angles at X are vertical angles, and V W parallel to Y Z gives congruent alternate interior angles. So the triangles are similar by A A.
WX/XZ = VW/YZ
Set up matching sides: the lake width W X over X Z equals V W over Y Z.
x over 10 equals 10, so x is 100 meters.

stem: A flagpole casts a shadow that is 30 feet long. At the same time, a person standing nearby who is 5 feet tall casts a shadow that is 48 inches long. How tall is the flagpole?
title: Similar triangles in real life: shadows
steps: the sun's rays → similar triangles
The sun hits both at the same angle, so each object and its shadow make similar triangles.
same units: 48 in. = 4 ft
First make the units match: 48 inches is 4 feet.
height/shadow: x/30 = 5/4
Height over shadow is the same for both: x over 30 equals 5 over 4.
Multiply by 30: the flagpole is 37.5 feet tall.

stem: A 6-foot-tall person stands so that the tip of their shadow lands exactly at the tip of a tree’s shadow. The person is 4 feet from the tip of the shadows, and the tree is 32 feet behind the person. How tall is the tree?
title: Challenge: overlapping shadows
steps: both stand straight up, same sun angle → similar by AA
The person and the tree both stand straight up and share the sun's angle, so the two triangles are similar.
tree's shadow: 4 + 32 = 36 ft
The tree's shadow goes from the tree to the tip: 32 plus 4 is 36 feet.
Height over shadow: h over 36 equals 6 over 4.
So the tree is 54 feet tall.

stem: Determine whether the triangles are similar. If they are, find the scale factor of △STU to △GJZ.   △STU: ST = 15, US = 18, TU = 17;  △GJZ: GJ = 37.5, ZG = 45, JZ = 42.5
title: SSS Similarity: similar
steps: shortest to shortest, longest to longest, middle to middle
Match the sides by size: shortest with shortest, longest with longest, and the middle ones together.
Divide each pair: 37.5 over 15, 42.5 over 17, and 45 over 18 all equal 2.5.
all equal → similar (SSS), scale factor 5/2
All three ratios are equal, so the triangles are similar by S S S, with scale factor 5 halves.

stem: Determine whether the triangles are similar. If they are, find the scale factor of △MPW to △ABC.   △MPW: MP = 11, PW = 18, WM = 20;  △ABC: AB = 16.5, BC = 28, CA = 30
title: SSS Similarity: not similar
steps: Match the sides by size and divide: 1.5, about 1.56, and 1.5.
not all equal → not similar
The ratios aren't all the same, so the triangles are not similar.

stem: Determine whether the triangles are similar. If they are, find the scale factor of △GKW to △MNP.   △GKW: GK = 10, GW = 12, m∠G = 76°;  △MNP: MN = 25, MP = 30, m∠M = 76°
title: SAS Similarity: similar
steps: included angles: ∠G = ∠M = 76° → congruent
First check the angles between the given sides. Both are 76 degrees, so they're congruent.
Then check the sides that form those angles: both ratios are 5 halves.
similar (SAS), scale factor 5/2
A congruent included angle and proportional sides: similar by S A S, with scale factor 5 halves.

stem: Determine whether the triangles are similar. If they are, find the scale factor of △UVW to △HJY.   △UVW: UV = 10, UW = 8, m∠U = 42°;  △HJY: HJ = 7.5, HY = 6, m∠H = 48°
title: SAS Similarity: the angles don't match
steps: included angles: 42° and 48° → not congruent
The included angles are 42 and 48 degrees. They're not congruent.
not similar
Even though the side ratios are equal, the angles don't match, so the triangles are not similar by S A S.

stem: Determine whether the triangles are similar. If they are, find the scale factor of △DEF to △CPY.   △DEF: DE = 8, DF = 12, m∠D = 83°;  △CPY: CP = 32, CY = 49, m∠C = 83°
title: SAS Similarity: the sides don't match
steps: included angles: 83° and 83° → congruent
The included angles are both 83 degrees.
But the side ratios are 4 and about 4.08. They're not equal.
not similar
So the triangles are not similar.

stem: Find the value of x that makes △DEF ~ △XYZ.   DE = 10, EF = 14;  XY = x + 6, YZ = 21
title: Find x so the triangles are similar
steps: scale factor from a known pair: YZ/EF = 21/14 = 3/2
Use the pair of sides you know to get the scale factor: 21 over 14 is 3 halves.
X Y over D E must also be 3 halves.
Multiply by 10: x plus 6 is 15, so x is 9.

stem: △XYZ has side lengths 7, 9, 12. The longest side of a triangle similar to △XYZ is 30 units long. Find the other side lengths of the triangle.
title: Similar triangles: the other sides
steps: scale factor: 30/12 = 5/2
The longest side, 12, becomes 30. The scale factor is 30 over 12: 5 halves.
Multiply the other sides by 5 halves: 17.5 and 22.5.

stem: In △BCD, BC = 8, BD = 6, and CD = 4. In △GLQ, GL = 4x − 12, GQ = 3x − 9, and ∠G ≅ ∠B. Find the value of x that makes △BCD ~ △GLQ, and then find LQ.
title: Challenge: SAS similarity with algebra
steps: ∠G ≅ ∠B → the sides around them are proportional
The congruent angles are at G and B, so the sides that form them must be proportional.
G L over B C equals G Q over B D.
Cross multiply and solve. The equation works out to x equals 6, where both sides make a real triangle.
GL = 12 → scale factor 12/8 = 3/2
Then G L is 12, so the scale factor is 12 over 8: 3 halves.
L Q matches C D, 4: times 3 halves is 6.

stem: P̅Q̅ ∥ M̅N̅. Find the length of L̅Q̅.
title: Triangle Proportionality Theorem
steps: P̅Q̅ ∥ M̅N̅ → it splits the sides proportionally
A segment parallel to one side of a triangle divides the other two sides proportionally.
LP/PM = LQ/QN
On one side, L P over P M. On the other side, L Q over Q N. They're equal.
L P is 5, P M is 10, L Q is x, and Q N is 26.
Multiply by 26: x is 13.

stem: Determine whether U̅W̅ ∥ E̅L̅.
title: Is the segment parallel? Yes
steps: Compare how the segment splits each side: 15 to 7 on both sides.
equal ratios → parallel
The ratios are equal, so the segment divides the sides proportionally. By the converse of the Triangle Proportionality Theorem, it's parallel to the third side.

stem: Determine whether J̅K̅ ∥ G̅H̅.
title: Is the segment parallel? No
steps: Compare the splits: 6 to 8, which is 3 fourths, and 18 to 23.
3/4 ≠ 18/23 → not parallel
18 over 23 isn't 3 fourths, so the ratios aren't equal. The segment is not parallel.

stem: Three parallel lines intersect two transversals. Find the value of x.
title: Three Parallel Lines Theorem
steps: three parallel lines split transversals proportionally
When three parallel lines cross two transversals, they cut the transversals into proportional pieces.
The pieces on one transversal are 18 and 4. The matching pieces on the other are 9 and x.
9 is half of 18, so x is half of 4: 2.

stem: G̅W̅ bisects ∠NGQ. Find the value of x.
title: Triangle Angle Bisector Theorem
steps: angle bisector → splits the opposite side in the ratio of the other two sides
An angle bisector divides the opposite side into pieces proportional to the two sides next to the angle.
NW/WQ = GN/GQ
The piece next to N over the piece next to Q equals side G N over side G Q.
N W is 5, W Q is x, G N is 8, and G Q is 12.
Cross multiply: 8 x is 60, so x is 7.5.

stem: In △FGH, F̅D̅ bisects ∠F, with D on G̅H̅. FG = 18, FH = 12, and GH = 10. Find GD and DH.
title: Challenge: angle bisector splits the opposite side
steps: GD/DH = FG/FH = 18/12
The bisector from F splits G H in the ratio of the sides next to F: 18 to 12.
GD = 18k, DH = 12k, and 18k + 12k = 10
Call the pieces 18 k and 12 k. Together they make G H, which is 10.
So 30 k is 10, and k is one third.
GD = 6, DH = 4
G D is 18 times one third, 6. D H is 12 times one third, 4.

stem: Find the value of x. Then tell whether the side lengths form a Pythagorean triple.
title: Pythagorean Theorem: find the hypotenuse
steps: a² + b² = c²
Pythagorean Theorem: the legs squared add up to the hypotenuse squared.
x is across from the right angle → hypotenuse
x is across from the right angle, so it's the hypotenuse.
x squared is 64 plus 225, which is 289. The square root is 17.
8, 15, 17: all whole numbers → a Pythagorean triple
All three sides are whole numbers, so they form a Pythagorean triple.

stem: Find the value of x. Then tell whether the side lengths form a Pythagorean triple.
title: Pythagorean Theorem: find a leg
steps: x is a leg; the hypotenuse is 8
Here x is a leg, and the hypotenuse is 8.
Subtract: x squared is 64 minus 16, which is 48.
Simplify the root: 48 is 16 times 3, so x is 4 root 3.
not a whole number → not a Pythagorean triple
x isn't a whole number, so the sides are not a Pythagorean triple.

stem: Tell whether the triangle is a right triangle.
title: Is it a right triangle? Yes
steps: longest side² vs. sum of the other two²
Square the longest side, and compare with the sum of the squares of the other two.
17 squared is 289. 8 squared plus 15 squared is also 289.
equal → right triangle
They're equal, so it's a right triangle, by the Converse of the Pythagorean Theorem.

stem: Tell whether the triangle is a right triangle.
title: Is it a right triangle? No
steps: The longest side squared is 4900. The other two squared add to 4624.
not equal → not a right triangle
They're not equal, so it's not a right triangle.

stem: Determine whether the segment lengths form a triangle. If so, is the triangle acute, right, or obtuse?   3, 8, √73
title: Acute, right, or obtuse? Right
steps: check it's a triangle: 3 + 8 > √73 ≈ 8.5 ✓
First make sure it's a triangle: the two shorter sides add to 11, more than root 73, about 8.5.
Square the longest side: 73. Add the squares of the others: 73.
equal → right
Equal means right.

stem: Determine whether the segment lengths form a triangle. If so, is the triangle acute, right, or obtuse?   21, 28, 23
title: Acute, right, or obtuse? Acute
steps: The longest side is 28: its square is 784. The others squared add to 970.
The longest side squared is smaller, so the triangle is acute.

stem: Determine whether the segment lengths form a triangle. If so, is the triangle acute, right, or obtuse?   10, 16, 8
title: Acute, right, or obtuse? Obtuse
steps: The longest side, 16, squared is 256. The others squared add to 164.
256 > 164 → obtuse
The longest side squared is bigger, so the triangle is obtuse.

stem: Determine whether the segment lengths form a triangle. If so, is the triangle acute, right, or obtuse?   11, 5, 6
title: Acute, right, or obtuse? Not a triangle
steps: 5 + 6 = 11, not more than 11
The two shorter sides add to 11, which isn't more than the longest side, 11.
not a triangle (Triangle Inequality)
So the pieces can't make a triangle.

stem: Television sizes are measured by the length of their diagonal. You want a television that is at least 55 inches. A television is 52 inches wide and 27 inches tall. Should you buy it?
title: Pythagorean Theorem in real life: a TV
steps: diagonal² = 52² + 27²
The width and height are the legs, and the diagonal is the hypotenuse.
52 squared plus 27 squared is 3433. The square root is about 58.6 inches.
That's at least 55 inches, so yes, buy it.

stem: A ladder runs straight from one platform to another. The upper platform is 11.2 feet above the lower one, and the platforms are 5.7 feet apart horizontally. Find the length of the ladder. Round to the nearest tenth.
title: Pythagorean Theorem in real life: a ladder
steps: legs: 11.2 ft up, 5.7 ft across
The height difference and the horizontal distance are the legs. The ladder is the hypotenuse.
Square and add: 157.93.
The square root is about 12.6 feet.

stem: A 29-foot ladder leans against a wall with its base 20 feet from the wall. How high up the wall does it reach? If the base slides 3 more feet away from the wall, how far does the top slide down? Round to the nearest tenth.
title: Challenge: a sliding ladder
steps: The ladder is the hypotenuse, 29. The base is 20 from the wall. The height is root of 841 minus 400: 21 feet.
new base: 20 + 3 = 23 ft
The base slides 3 more feet: 23 feet from the wall.
new height = √(29² − 23²) = √312 ≈ 17.7 ft
The new height is root of 841 minus 529, which is root 312, about 17.7 feet.
The top slides down about 21 minus 17.7: 3.3 feet.

stem: Find the value of x. Write your answer in simplest form.
title: 30°-60°-90° triangles
steps: 30°-60°-90°: short leg s, long leg s√3, hypotenuse 2s
In a 30 60 90 triangle, call the short leg s. It's across from the 30 degree angle. The long leg is s root 3, and the hypotenuse is 2 s.
the 7√2 side is across from 30° → s = 7√2
The side marked 7 root 2 is across from the 30 degree angle, so it's the short leg.
x is the hypotenuse: 2s = 14√2
x is across from the right angle, the hypotenuse: 2 times 7 root 2 is 14 root 2.
going backward: s = hypotenuse ÷ 2, or s = long leg ÷ √3
If you're given a different side, work back to s first: halve the hypotenuse, or divide the long leg by root 3.

stem: Find the value of x. Write your answer in simplest form.
title: 45°-45°-90° triangles
steps: 45°-45°-90°: legs equal, hypotenuse = leg · √2
In a 45 45 90 triangle the two legs are equal, and the hypotenuse is a leg times root 2.
8√6 is the hypotenuse; x is a leg
Here 8 root 6 is the hypotenuse and x is a leg.
So 8 root 6 equals x root 2. Divide by root 2: root 6 over root 2 is root 3. x is 8 root 3.

stem: The side length of an equilateral triangle is 26 centimeters. Find the length of an altitude. Write your answer in simplest form.
title: The altitude of an equilateral triangle
steps: the altitude splits it into two 30°-60°-90° triangles
The altitude cuts the equilateral triangle into two 30 60 90 triangles.
hypotenuse 26, short leg 26 ÷ 2 = 13
Each has hypotenuse 26, the side of the triangle, and short leg 13, half the base.
altitude = long leg = 13√3 cm
The altitude is the long leg: 13 root 3 centimeters.

stem: The perimeter of a square is 20 inches. Find the length of a diagonal. Write your answer in simplest form.
title: The diagonal of a square
steps: side = 20 ÷ 4 = 5 in.
A square has 4 equal sides: 20 divided by 4 is 5 inches.
a diagonal makes two 45°-45°-90° triangles
A diagonal splits the square into two 45 45 90 triangles. The diagonal is the hypotenuse.
diagonal = 5√2 in.
So the diagonal is 5 root 2 inches.

stem: Each half of a drawbridge is about 96 feet long. How high does the drawbridge rise when it makes an angle of 60° with the road? Round to the nearest tenth if needed.
title: Special right triangles in real life: a drawbridge
steps: the raised half is the hypotenuse: 96 ft
The raised half of the bridge is the hypotenuse of a 30 60 90 triangle: 96 feet.
short leg = 96 ÷ 2 = 48
The short leg is half the hypotenuse: 48.
height is across from 60° → long leg = 48√3 ≈ 83.1 ft
The height is across from the 60 degree angle, so it's the long leg: 48 root 3, about 83.1 feet.

stem: A regular hexagon has sides 16 inches long. Find the distance between two opposite (parallel) sides, and the length of the longest diagonal. Give exact answers.
title: Challenge: special right triangles in a regular hexagon
steps: 6 equilateral triangles with side 16
A regular hexagon splits into 6 equilateral triangles, each with side 16.
longest diagonal: 2 · 16 = 32
The longest diagonal goes through the center, across two of those triangles: 32.
each altitude: short leg 8 → 8√3
The altitude of one triangle is the long leg of a 30 60 90 triangle with short leg 8: 8 root 3.
opposite sides: 2 · 8√3 = 16√3
The distance between opposite sides is two altitudes: 16 root 3.

stem: Find the geometric mean of the two numbers.   33 and 42
title: Geometric mean of two numbers
steps: geometric mean of a and b = √(ab)
The geometric mean of two numbers is the square root of their product.
33 times 42 is 1386.
1386 is 9 times 154, and the square root of 9 is 3. So it's 3 root 154.

stem: Find the value of x. Write your answer in simplest form.
title: Altitude to the hypotenuse: find the altitude
steps: altitude² = (one segment)(other segment)
The altitude to the hypotenuse is the geometric mean of the two pieces of the hypotenuse.
The pieces are 5 and 5, so x is root 25, which is 5.

stem: Find the value of x. Write your answer in simplest form.
title: Altitude to the hypotenuse: find a leg
steps: leg² = (whole hypotenuse)(the piece next to that leg)
A leg is the geometric mean of the whole hypotenuse and the piece of the hypotenuse touching that leg.
hypotenuse = 4 + 9 = 13;  piece next to x = 4
The whole hypotenuse is 4 plus 9, which is 13. The piece next to x is 4.
x is root 52, which simplifies to 2 root 13.

stem: Find the value of x. Write your answer in simplest form.
title: Altitude to the hypotenuse: find a segment
steps: altitude² = (segment)(segment)
The altitude squared equals the product of the two pieces of the hypotenuse.
The altitude is 5 root 19, and one piece is 25.
5 root 19 squared is 25 times 19, which is 475. Divide by 25: x is 19.

stem: In right △ABC, the altitude from the right angle C divides the hypotenuse into segments of length 64 and 225. Find the length of the altitude and the lengths of both legs.
title: Challenge: altitude and both legs from the hypotenuse segments
steps: The altitude is the geometric mean of the pieces: root of 64 times 225, which is 120.
hypotenuse = 64 + 225 = 289
The whole hypotenuse is 289.
Each leg is the geometric mean of the hypotenuse and its touching piece: 17 times 8 is 136, and 17 times 15 is 255.

stem: Find tan L. Write your answer as a fraction and as a decimal rounded to four places.
title: The tangent of an angle
steps: tan = opposite/adjacent
Tangent is the opposite side over the adjacent side.
from L: opposite = 15 (QH), adjacent = 8 (LH)
Stand at angle L. The side across from it is Q H, 15. The leg next to it, not the hypotenuse, is L H, 8.
So tangent L is 15 over 8, which is 1.875.

stem: Find the value of x. Round to the nearest tenth.
title: Find a side with tangent: x opposite
steps: tan 43° = opposite/adjacent = x/24
x is across from the 43 degree angle and 24 is next to it. Tangent uses those two.
Multiply both sides by 24: x is 24 times tangent 43, about 22.4.

stem: Find the value of x. Round to the nearest tenth.
pick: x is next to the angle
title: Find a side with tangent: x adjacent
steps: 11 is across from the 28 degree angle and x is next to it.
Multiply both sides by x, then divide by tangent 28: x is about 20.7. When x is on the bottom, you divide.

stem: You stand 250 feet from the base of a building. The angle of elevation from the ground to the top of the building is 73°. Find the height h of the building. Round to the nearest foot.
title: Tangent in real life: angle of elevation
steps: the height is opposite 73°; 250 ft is adjacent
Draw a right triangle: the height of the building is across from the 73 degree angle, and your distance, 250 feet, is next to it.
So tangent 73 equals h over 250.
Multiply by 250: about 818 feet.

stem: Two people stand 500 feet apart on level ground with a building between them. The angle of elevation to the top of the building is 53° for the first person and 48° for the second. How tall is the building, and how far is the first person from its base? Round to the nearest tenth.
title: Challenge: a building between two observers
steps: x = h/tan 53°;  500 − x = h/tan 48°
Let h be the height and x the first person's distance. Tangent gives x equals h over tangent 53, and the other distance, 500 minus x, equals h over tangent 48.
Add the two distances: they make 500.
Solve for h: about 302.3 feet.
The first person is about 227.8 feet from the base.

stem: Find sin J. Write your answer as a fraction and as a decimal rounded to four places.
title: Sine of an angle
steps: sin = opposite/hypotenuse
Sine is the opposite side over the hypotenuse. SOH.
from J: opposite = 10, hypotenuse = 26
Stand at angle J. The side across from it is 10, and the hypotenuse, across from the right angle, is 26.
10 over 26 simplifies to 5 thirteenths, about 0.3846.

stem: Find cos L. Write your answer as a fraction and as a decimal rounded to four places.
title: Cosine of an angle
steps: cos = adjacent/hypotenuse
Cosine is the adjacent side over the hypotenuse. CAH.
from L: adjacent = 8, hypotenuse = 17
Stand at angle L. The leg next to it is 8, and the hypotenuse is 17.
So cosine L is 8 over 17, about 0.4706.

stem: Write the expression in terms of sine.   cos 69°
title: Complementary angles: write cosine as sine
steps: sin A = cos(90° − A)
The sine of an angle equals the cosine of its complement, and the other way around.
The complement of 69 is 21.
= sin 21°
So cosine 69 equals sine 21.

stem: Write the expression in terms of cosine.   sin 16°
title: Complementary angles: write sine as cosine
steps: sin A = cos(90° − A)
The sine of an angle equals the cosine of its complement.
The complement of 16 is 74, so sine 16 equals cosine 74.

stem: Find the value of each variable using sine and cosine. Round to the nearest tenth.
title: Find legs with sine and cosine
steps: hypotenuse 10, angle 28°
The hypotenuse is 10 and the angle is 28 degrees.
x is opposite: sin 28° = x/10 → x = 10 sin 28° ≈ 4.7
x is across from the angle, so use sine: x is 10 sine 28, about 4.7.
y is adjacent: cos 28° = y/10 → y = 10 cos 28° ≈ 8.8
y is next to the angle, so use cosine: y is 10 cosine 28, about 8.8.

stem: You fly a kite on a 250-foot string that makes a 63° angle with the horizontal. You hold the string 4.5 feet above the ground. How high is the kite, and how far away is it horizontally? Round to the nearest tenth.
title: Challenge: a kite's height and distance
steps: the string is the hypotenuse: 250 ft
The string is the hypotenuse, 250 feet, at 63 degrees from the horizontal.
vertical: 250 sin 63° ≈ 222.8 ft
The vertical leg is opposite the angle: 250 sine 63, about 222.8 feet.
Add the 4.5 feet where you hold it: about 227.3 feet high.
horizontal: 250 cos 63° ≈ 113.5 ft
The horizontal leg is adjacent: 250 cosine 63, about 113.5 feet away.

stem: Determine which of the two acute angles has the given trigonometric ratio.   The sine of the angle is 8/17.
title: Which angle has the ratio?
steps: sine = opposite/hypotenuse = 8/17
The sine is opposite over hypotenuse. The hypotenuse is 17, so we need the angle whose opposite side is 8.
the side 8 is across from ∠Q
The side of length 8 is across from angle Q.
∠Q
So sine Q is 8 seventeenths. Check: for angle L, the opposite side would be 15.

stem: Let ∠D be an acute angle. Use technology to approximate m∠D to the nearest tenth of a degree.   tan D = 3.34
title: Inverse trig: find the angle
steps: tan D = 3.34 → m∠D = tan⁻¹(3.34)
To find an angle from a ratio, use the inverse: tan inverse.
calculator (degree mode): ≈ 73.3°
In degree mode, tan inverse of 3.34 is about 73.3 degrees. Use sin inverse or cos inverse the same way for sine and cosine.

stem: Solve the right triangle. Round decimal answers to the nearest tenth.
title: Solve a right triangle: two legs
steps: Solving means finding every missing side and angle. First the hypotenuse: root of 25 plus 36, about 7.8.
At L, the opposite leg is 6 and the adjacent leg is 5. Tan inverse of 6 fifths is about 50.2 degrees.
The acute angles add to 90, so angle Q is about 39.8 degrees.

stem: Solve the right triangle. Round decimal answers to the nearest tenth.
title: Solve a right triangle: a leg and the hypotenuse
steps: The missing leg: root of 289 minus 81, about 14.4.
At N, the 9 is adjacent and 17 is the hypotenuse: cos inverse of 9 over 17, about 58 degrees.
Angle P is 90 minus 58: about 32 degrees.

stem: Solve the right triangle. Round decimal answers to the nearest tenth.
title: Solve a right triangle: a side and an angle
steps: The other acute angle is 90 minus 68: 22 degrees.
The hypotenuse is 19. E F is next to the 68 degree angle, so use cosine: about 7.1.
E G is across from it, so use sine: about 17.6.

stem: To unload clay easily, the body of a dump truck must be elevated to at least 50°. The body of a dump truck that is 18 feet long has been raised 10 feet. Will the clay pour out easily?
title: Right triangles in real life: find an angle
steps: truck body = hypotenuse 18;  rise = opposite 10
The truck body is the hypotenuse, 18 feet, and the rise is the side opposite the angle, 10 feet.
Sine is opposite over hypotenuse. Sin inverse of 10 over 18 is about 33.7 degrees.
That's less than 50, so the clay won't pour out easily.

stem: You are standing on a footbridge that is 10 feet above a lake. You see a duck in the water 5 feet from the point on the water directly below you. What is the angle of depression from you to the duck? Round to the nearest tenth of a degree.
title: Angle of depression
steps: depression from you = elevation from the duck
The angle of depression from you down to the duck equals the angle of elevation from the duck up to you.
tan θ = 10/5
From the duck, your height, 10, is opposite, and the 5 feet is adjacent.
Tan inverse of 2 is about 63.4 degrees.

stem: An isosceles triangle has legs 25 cm long and a base 41 cm long. Find the measures of its base angles and its vertex angle. Round to the nearest tenth.
title: Challenge: all three angles of an isosceles triangle
steps: altitude bisects the base: half-base 20.5
The altitude from the vertex cuts the base in half, making two right triangles with hypotenuse 25 and a leg of 20.5.
cos(base angle) = 20.5/25 → ≈ 34.9°
At a base angle, 20.5 is adjacent and 25 is the hypotenuse: cos inverse gives about 34.9 degrees.
The vertex angle is 180 minus two base angles: about 110.2 degrees.

stem: Use technology to find the trigonometric ratio. Round to four decimal places.   tan 164°
title: Trig ratios of obtuse angles
steps: degree mode
Make sure your calculator is in degree mode.
Type tangent 164: about negative 0.2867. For obtuse angles, cosine and tangent are negative, and sine is positive.

stem: Find the area of the triangle. Round your answer to one decimal place.   B = 74°,   a = 38,   c = 13
pick: Two sides and the angle between
title: Area of a triangle: two sides and the included angle
steps: Area = (1/2)ac sin B
When you know two sides and the angle between them, the area is one half times the two sides times the sine of that angle.
The sides a and c are 38 and 13, and the angle between them is B, 74 degrees.
That's about 237.4 square units.

stem: Find the area of the triangle. Round your answer to one decimal place.   A = 75°,   B = 21°,   a = 21
title: Area of a triangle: two angles and a side
steps: First find the third angle: 84 degrees.
b = a sin B / sin A = 21 sin 21° / sin 75° ≈ 7.79
You need two sides. Use the Law of Sines to find b: about 7.79.
Now use one half a b sine C, with C between sides a and b: about 81.4 square units.

stem: Use the Law of Sines to solve the triangle. Round your answers to two decimal places.   A = 9°,   C = 48°,   b = 17
title: Law of Sines: two angles and a side
steps: Find the third angle first: 123 degrees.
a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C
Law of Sines: each side over the sine of its opposite angle is the same.
b is 17 and B is 123. So a is 17 times sine 9 over sine 123, about 3.17.
c is 17 times sine 48 over sine 123, about 15.06.

stem:
Use the Law of Sines to solve the triangle, if possible. If two triangles are possible, find both. Round your answers to two decimal places.   A = 72°,   a = 15,   b = 28
How many triangles are possible, and what is B?
title: Law of Sines, ambiguous case: no triangle
steps: sin B = b sin A / a = 28 sin 72° / 15 ≈ 1.7753
Use the Law of Sines to find sine B: about 1.78.
sine can't be more than 1 → no triangle
A sine can never be more than 1, so no triangle fits these measurements.

stem:
Use the Law of Sines to solve the triangle, if possible. If two triangles are possible, find both. Round your answers to two decimal places.   A = 109°,   a = 93.1,   b = 59
How many triangles are possible, and what is B?
title: Law of Sines, ambiguous case: one triangle
steps: Find sine B: about 0.5992.
Two angles have that sine: 36.81 and its supplement, 143.19.
But A is already 109, so 143.19 is too big. Only 36.81 works: one triangle.
Then C is 180 minus 109 minus 36.81, about 34.19, and c is about 55.33.

stem:
Use the Law of Sines to solve the triangle, if possible. If two triangles are possible, find both. Round your answers to two decimal places.   A = 76°,   a = 11.9,   b = 12
How many triangles are possible, and what is B?
title: Law of Sines, ambiguous case: two triangles
steps: Find sine B: about 0.9784.
The two angles with that sine are 78.08 and 101.92.
both fit with A = 76° → two triangles
Both work with A, 76, since each total is less than 180. So there are two triangles.
Finish each one: find C from 180, then c from the Law of Sines.

stem: Use the Law of Cosines to solve the triangle. Round your answers to two decimal places.   a = 50.2,   b = 54,   c = 27
title: Law of Cosines: three sides
steps: find the largest angle first (across from the longest side)
Start with the largest angle, across from the longest side, so you know if it's obtuse.
The longest side is b, 54. Cosine B is a squared plus c squared minus b squared, over 2 a c: about 0.1229, so B is about 82.94 degrees.
Then angle A the same way: about 67.31 degrees.
The last angle is what's left: about 29.75 degrees.

stem: Use the Law of Cosines to solve the triangle. Round your answers to two decimal places.   C = 115°,   a = 4,   b = 20
title: Law of Cosines: two sides and the included angle
steps: c² = a² + b² − 2ab cos C
With two sides and the angle between them, use the Law of Cosines for the third side.
4 squared plus 20 squared minus 2 times 4 times 20 times cosine 115. Cosine 115 is negative, so this adds: about 483.62. c is about 21.99.
Find the angle across from the shorter given side next. It must be acute. Law of Sines gives about 9.49 degrees.
The last angle is about 55.51 degrees.

stem: A triangle has sides 17, 18, and 15. Find the measure of its largest angle and its area. Round to the nearest tenth.
title: Challenge: the largest angle, then the area
steps: largest angle: across from 18
The largest angle is across from the longest side, 18.
Law of Cosines: 324 equals 225 plus 289 minus 510 cosine C. So cosine C is 190 over 510, which is 19 over 51.
Cos inverse gives about 68.1 degrees.
The area is one half times 15 times 17 times sine C: about 118.3.

stem: Use the diagram. Name a tangent.
title: Parts of a circle
steps: ⊙D: named by its center, D
A circle is named by its center. This is circle D.
radius D̅E̅;  diameter E̅H̅ (a chord through the center)
A radius goes from the center to the circle, like D E. A diameter is a chord through the center, like E H.
chord P̅L̅: joins two points on the circle
A chord joins two points on the circle, like P L. P L doesn't go through the center, so it's not a diameter.
secant line QT: crosses the circle at two points
A secant is a line that crosses the circle at two points, like line Q T.
tangent line UX: touches at exactly one point, U
A tangent is a line that touches the circle at exactly one point, like line U X. U is the point of tangency.
a tangent: line UX
So the tangent is line U X.

stem: How many common tangents do the circles have?
title: Common tangents
steps: separate circles: 4;  touching outside: 3;  crossing: 2
A common tangent touches both circles. Two separate circles have 4. Two circles touching from outside have 3. Two circles that cross have 2.
touching inside: 1;  one inside the other: 0
One circle inside the other and touching at one point: 1. One completely inside the other without touching: 0.
inside and touching at one point → 1
Here the small circle is inside the big one and touches it at one point, so there's just 1 common tangent, at that point.

stem: Tell whether L̅Q̅ is tangent to ⊙H. Explain your reasoning.
title: Is the segment tangent? Yes
steps: tangent ⊥ radius → check for a right triangle
A tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of tangency. So check whether triangle H Q L is a right triangle.
The hypotenuse goes from the center to L: the radius 8 plus 9, which is 17.
8 squared plus 15 squared is 289, and 17 squared is 289.
equal → right angle → tangent
They're equal, so it's a right triangle, and L Q is tangent.

stem: Tell whether G̅H̅ is tangent to ⊙F. Explain your reasoning.
title: Is the segment tangent? No
steps: The side from the center to G is the radius 5 plus 10: 15.
5 squared plus 12 squared is 169, but 15 squared is 225.
not equal → not a right angle → not tangent
They're not equal, so there's no right angle at H, and G H is not tangent.

stem: Point Q is a point of tangency. Find the radius r of ⊙H.
title: Find the radius with a tangent
steps: tangent ⊥ radius → right △HQL
The tangent is perpendicular to the radius at Q, so triangle H Q L is a right triangle.
legs r and 15; hypotenuse r + 9
The legs are r and 15. The hypotenuse goes from H to L: r plus 9.
Pythagorean Theorem.
Expand the right side: r squared plus 18 r plus 81.
The r squared terms cancel. 225 minus 81 is 144, so 18 r is 144, and r is 8.

stem: Points P and Q are points of tangency. Find the value of x.
title: Tangent segments from one point
steps: tangent segments from one point are congruent
Two tangent segments from the same outside point are congruent.
Set them equal. Subtract 3 x and 12: x is 8.

stem: Points Q and U are points of tangency. Find the value(s) of x.
title: Tangent segments from one point: x squared
steps: The tangent segments from L are congruent. Set them equal.
Subtract 4 x from both sides; they cancel. Then subtract 4: 4 x squared is 144.
Divide by 4: x squared is 36. Both 6 and negative 6 work, so x is plus or minus 6.

stem: A circle is inscribed in △LXY, so each side is tangent to the circle. LX = 21, XY = 20, and YL = 19. Find the lengths of the tangent segments from L and from X (from each vertex to the nearest points of tangency).
title: Challenge: tangent segments of a circumscribed triangle
steps: from L: a, from X: b, from Y: c
Tangent segments from the same vertex are congruent. Call them a from L, b from X, and c from Y.
Each side is made of two tangent segments.
Add all three equations: 2 times the total is 60, so the total is 30.
Subtract: a is 30 minus b plus c, which is 10. b is 30 minus c plus a, which is 11.

stem: Name the minor arc and find its measure. Then name the major arc and find its measure.
title: Minor and major arcs
steps: minor arc LQ = its central angle = 45°
A minor arc is the short way around between two points. It's named with its two endpoints, and its measure equals its central angle: 45 degrees.
major arc LUQ = 360° − 45° = 315°
The major arc is the long way around. It's named with three letters, and its measure is 360 minus the minor arc: 315 degrees.

stem: L̅Q̅ is a diameter of ⊙H. Identify arc TQ as a major arc, minor arc, or semicircle. Then find its measure.
title: Major arc, minor arc, or semicircle?
steps: L̅Q̅ is a diameter → each half is 180°
L Q is a diameter, so it splits the circle into two semicircles of 180 degrees.
Arc L T is 50, so arc T Q, the rest of that half, is 130 degrees.
less than 180° → minor arc
Less than 180 is a minor arc. More than 180 is a major arc, and exactly 180, with endpoints on a diameter, is a semicircle.
minor arc; 130°
So arc T Q is a minor arc measuring 130 degrees.

stem: Find the measure of arc NQU in ⊙B.
title: Arc Addition
steps: arc NQU = arc NQ + arc QU
Arc Addition Postulate: the measure of an arc made of two adjacent arcs is the sum of their measures.
Each arc equals its central angle: 125 plus 95 is 220 degrees.

stem: A survey asked students their favorite type of music. A circle graph shows the results: Rock: 6%, Hip-Hop: 24%, Country: 22%, Pop: 21%, Classical: 27%. Find the measure of the arc for Pop and Classical together.
title: Arcs in a circle graph
steps: The whole circle is 360 degrees, which is 100 percent. So each percent is 3.6 degrees.
Pop + Classical = 21% + 27% = 48%
Pop and Classical together are 48 percent.
48 percent of 360 is 172.8 degrees.

stem: Tell whether the red arcs are congruent. Explain why or why not.
title: Are the arcs congruent? Yes
steps: congruent arcs: same measure AND same or congruent circles
Arcs are congruent only when they have the same measure and are in the same circle or congruent circles.
same circle, both 45° → Yes
These are in the same circle and both measure 45 degrees, so yes.

stem: Tell whether the red arcs are congruent. Explain why or why not.
title: Are the arcs congruent? No (different measures)
steps: 100° and 115° → different measures
The arcs measure 100 and 115 degrees.
No
Different measures, so they are not congruent, even though the circles are the same size.

stem: Tell whether the red arcs are congruent. Explain why or why not.
title: Are the arcs congruent? No (different circles)
steps: same measure, but radii 14 and 19
The arcs have the same measure, but the circles have radii 14 and 19.
circles not congruent → No
The circles aren't congruent, so the arcs have different lengths. They are not congruent.

stem: G̅K̅ is a diameter of ⊙F. Find the value of x. Then find the measure of the red arc HJK.
title: Arcs with algebra: a semicircle
steps: the arcs make a semicircle → add to 180°
G K is a diameter, so the arcs on one side make a semicircle: they add to 180.
Add the expressions and combine like terms.
Add 29 and divide by 19: x is 11.
The red arc is made of two of the arcs: 88 plus 26 is 114 degrees.

stem: Find the value of x. Then find the measure of the red arc EFG.
title: Arcs with algebra: the whole circle
steps: the arcs make the whole circle → add to 360°
The arcs go all the way around, so they add to 360.
Add the expressions and combine like terms.
Subtract 8 and divide by 22: x is 16.
The red arc is two of the arcs: 80 plus 95 is 175 degrees.

stem: In ⊙P, three central angles that don’t overlap fill the whole circle: m∠APB = (5x − 19)°, m∠BPC = (4x + 5)°, and m∠CPA = (5x + 24)°. Find x and the measure of major arc ACB (the arc from A to B through C).
title: Challenge: central angles fill the circle
steps: The central angles around the center add to 360.
Combine and solve: x is 25.
m∠APB = 5(25) − 19 = 106° → minor arc AB = 106°
Angle A P B is 106 degrees, so minor arc A B is 106.
major arc ACB = 360° − 106° = 254°
The major arc A C B is the rest: 254 degrees.

stem: G̅H̅ ≅ J̅K̅. Find the measure of the red arc JK.
title: Congruent chords have congruent arcs
steps: G̅H̅ ≅ J̅K̅
The chords G H and J K are congruent.
congruent chords → congruent arcs
Congruent Corresponding Chords Theorem: in the same circle, congruent chords have congruent minor arcs.
arc JK = arc GH = 100°
So arc J K is 100 degrees, the same as arc G H.

stem: Arc MN ≅ arc PQ. Find the length of the red chord P̅Q̅.
title: Congruent arcs have congruent chords
steps: arc MN ≅ arc PQ (both 80°)
The two minor arcs are congruent.
congruent arcs → congruent chords
So their chords are congruent too.
PQ = MN = 9
Chord P Q is 9, the same as M N.

stem: Diameter T̅U̅ is perpendicular to chord L̅Q̅. Arc LT measures 36°. Find the measure of the red arc LTQ.
title: A perpendicular diameter bisects the arc
steps: diameter ⊥ chord → bisects the chord and its arc
A diameter perpendicular to a chord cuts the chord and its arc exactly in half.
arc TQ = arc LT = 36°
So arc T Q is the same as arc L T: 36 degrees.
The whole arc L T Q is 72 degrees.

stem: In ⊙G, the chords H̅J̅ and K̅L̅ are the same distance from the center. Find the value of x.
title: Chords the same distance from the center
steps: equidistant from the center → congruent chords
Chords that are the same distance from the center are congruent.
Set the chord lengths equal.
Subtract 6 x and 10: 3 x is 18, so x is 6.

stem: Diameter R̅S̅ is perpendicular to chord P̅Q̅ at T. Find the value of x.
title: A perpendicular diameter bisects the chord
steps: diameter ⊥ chord → bisects the chord: PT = TQ
A diameter perpendicular to a chord cuts it in half, so P T equals T Q.
Set them equal. Subtract 6 x and add 11: x is 9.

stem: Diameter N̅Q̅ is perpendicular to chord D̅E̅. Find the value of x.
title: A perpendicular diameter bisects the arc (with x)
steps: diameter ⊥ chord → bisects the arc
A diameter perpendicular to a chord cuts the chord's arc in half, so the two arcs are equal.
Set the arcs equal. Subtract 6 x and add 4: 2 x is 18, so x is 9.

stem: Determine whether H̅L̅ is a diameter of the circle. Explain your reasoning.
title: Is the chord a diameter? Yes
steps: a chord that is the ⊥ bisector of another chord is a diameter
Perpendicular Chord Bisector Converse: if one chord is the perpendicular bisector of another chord, it's a diameter.
right angle, and QU = UT = 3 → H̅L̅ bisects Q̅T̅ at a right angle
H L meets Q T at a right angle and splits it into 3 and 3.
Yes
So H L is a diameter.

stem: Determine whether E̅F̅ is a diameter of the circle. Explain your reasoning.
title: Is the chord a diameter? No
steps: GJ = 6, JH = 12 → not bisected
E F crosses G H, but the pieces are 6 and 12. It doesn't cut G H in half.
No
So E F is not the perpendicular bisector, and we can't say it's a diameter.

stem: Chord L̅Q̅ is 16 units long and is 15 units from the center of ⊙H. Find the radius of ⊙H.
title: Radius from a chord
steps: the ⊥ from the center bisects the chord: half = 16 ÷ 2 = 8
The perpendicular from the center to a chord cuts it in half: 8 on each side.
right triangle: legs 8 and 15, hypotenuse r
That makes a right triangle with legs 8 and 15. The hypotenuse is a radius.
r squared is 289, so r is 17.

stem: Two parallel chords are on the same side of the center of a circle. One chord is 30 cm long and the other is 14 cm long. The chords are 4 cm apart. Find the radius of the circle and the distance from the center to the longer chord.
title: Challenge: radius from two parallel chords
steps: halves: 15 and 7;  distances d and d + 4
A perpendicular from the center bisects each chord: half chords of 15 and 7. Let d be the distance to the longer chord; the shorter one is d plus 4 away.
r² = 15² + d² = 7² + (d + 4)²
Both right triangles have hypotenuse r.
Expand and cancel d squared: 160 equals 8 d, so d is 20.
The radius is root of 225 plus 400: 25 centimeters.

stem: Find m∠L.
title: Inscribed angle: find the angle
steps: inscribed angle = (1/2)(intercepted arc)
An inscribed angle has its vertex on the circle. It's half the arc it cuts off.
Angle L intercepts a 60 degree arc, so it's 30 degrees.

stem: Find the measure of arc MP.
title: Inscribed angle: find the arc
steps: arc = 2 × inscribed angle
The intercepted arc is twice the inscribed angle.
The angle is 50 degrees, so arc M P is 100 degrees.

stem: E̅G̅ is a diameter. Find m∠EFG.
title: An angle inscribed in a semicircle
steps: E̅G̅ is a diameter → arc EG = 180°
E G is a diameter, so the arc it cuts off is a semicircle, 180 degrees.
inscribed angle = (1/2)(180°) = 90°
Half of 180 is 90. An angle inscribed in a semicircle is always a right angle.

stem: Quadrilateral BHNR is inscribed in the circle. Find the values of x and y.
title: Inscribed quadrilaterals
steps: opposite angles of an inscribed quadrilateral are supplementary
