When a quadrilateral is inscribed in a circle, its opposite angles add to 180.
The 5 x angle is across from 100 degrees: 5 x is 80, so x is 16.
The 3 y angle is across from 90 degrees: 3 y is 90, so y is 30.

stem: Determine whether every kite can be inscribed inside a circle. Explain your reasoning.
title: Can every one be inscribed in a circle?
steps: a quadrilateral can be inscribed ⇔ opposite angles are supplementary
A quadrilateral fits in a circle exactly when its opposite angles add to 180. Every triangle can be inscribed.
always: rectangles, squares, isosceles trapezoids
Rectangles and squares have all right angles, so they always work. Isosceles trapezoids do too, because their base angles match.
not always: rhombuses, parallelograms, kites
Most rhombuses, parallelograms, and kites have opposite angles that don't add to 180.
kite → No
So not every kite can be inscribed. Only kites with two opposite right angles can.

stem: A right triangle with legs 6 and 8 is inscribed in a circle. Find the radius of the circle.
title: Right triangle in a circle: from the legs
steps: the hypotenuse is a diameter
The right angle is inscribed in a semicircle, so the hypotenuse is a diameter.
hypotenuse = √(6² + 8²) = 10
The hypotenuse is root of 36 plus 64: 10.
radius = 10 ÷ 2 = 5
The radius is half the diameter: 5.

stem: A rectangle that is 24 cm by 70 cm is inscribed in a circle. Find the diameter of the circle.
title: Rectangle in a circle
steps: each diagonal is a diameter
Each angle of a rectangle is a right angle, so each diagonal is a diameter.
diagonal = √(24² + 70²) = √5476 = 74 cm
The diagonal is root of 576 plus 4900, which is 74 centimeters.

stem: A right triangle is inscribed in a circle with radius 8 inches. Find the length of the hypotenuse.
kind: inscribed in a circle with radius
title: Right triangle in a circle: from the radius
steps: the hypotenuse is a diameter
The hypotenuse of an inscribed right triangle is a diameter.
hypotenuse = 2 · 8 = 16 in.
The radius is 8, so the hypotenuse is 16 inches.

stem: Quadrilateral CDEF is inscribed in a circle. m∠C = (4x + 4y)°, m∠E = 40°, m∠D = (x + 3y)°, and m∠F = 109°. Find x and y.
title: Challenge: inscribed quadrilateral with two variables
steps: Opposite angles are supplementary. C and E: 4 x plus 4 y plus 40 is 180.
D and F: x plus 3 y plus 109 is 180.
Divide the first by 4: x plus y is 35. Substitute x equals 35 minus y: 2 y is 36, so y is 18.
Then x is 17.

stem: Line t is tangent to the circle at G. Find m∠1.
title: Tangent and chord: find the angle
steps: tangent–chord angle = (1/2)(intercepted arc)
An angle formed by a tangent and a chord is half the arc it cuts off.
The arc is 130 degrees, so angle 1 is 65 degrees.

stem: Line t is tangent to the circle at L. Find the measure of arc LQ.
title: Tangent and chord: find the arc
steps: arc = 2 × the tangent–chord angle
The arc is twice the angle formed by the tangent and the chord.
The angle is 35 degrees, so the arc is 70 degrees.

stem: Find the value of x.
title: Chords crossing inside: find the angle
steps: angle inside = (1/2)(sum of the two intercepted arcs)
When two chords cross inside a circle, each angle is half the sum of the arc it cuts off and the arc its vertical angle cuts off.
The arcs are 50 and 75: half of 125 is 62.5.

stem: Find the measure of arc QU.
title: Chords crossing inside: find an arc
steps: Use the same rule, with the arc unknown.
115 = 60 + arc QU → arc QU = 55°
Multiply both sides by 2: 115. Subtract 60: arc Q U is 55 degrees.

stem: Find the value of x.
title: Angle outside a circle: two secants
steps: angle outside = (1/2)(far arc − near arc)
When two lines meet outside a circle, the angle is half the difference of the far arc and the near arc.
The far arc is 160 and the near arc is 75: half of 85 is 42.5.

stem: Find the value of x.
title: Angle outside a circle: a tangent and a secant
steps: angle outside = (1/2)(far arc − near arc)
A tangent and a secant meeting outside the circle work the same way: half the difference of the arcs.
Half of 140 minus 50 is 45.

stem: K̅F̅ and K̅G̅ are tangent to the circle. Find the value of x.
title: Angle outside a circle: two tangents
steps: Two tangents cut the circle into two arcs. The small arc is 360 minus 265: 95 degrees.
The angle is half the difference: half of 170 is 85.

stem: Find the measure of the red arc.
title: Angle outside a circle: find an arc
steps: Use the outside-angle rule with the far arc unknown.
Multiply by 2: 65. Add 20: the arc is 85 degrees.

stem: From a hot air balloon 3 miles above the ground, you can see the part of Earth between the two points where your lines of sight are tangent to Earth. Earth's radius is about 4000 miles. Find the measure of the arc of Earth you can see. Round to the nearest hundredth of a degree.
title: Tangents in real life: the view from a balloon
steps: line of sight is tangent → ⊥ to the radius
Each line of sight touches Earth at one point, so it's tangent and makes a right angle with Earth's radius.
right triangle: adjacent 4000, hypotenuse 4000 + 3 = 4003
In the right triangle, the radius 4000 is next to the central angle, and the hypotenuse goes from Earth's center to the balloon: 4003.
Cos inverse of 4000 over 4003 is about 2.218 degrees.
The visible arc is two of those angles: about 4.44 degrees.

stem: Two secants meet at a point outside a circle and form a 62° angle. The arcs they intercept measure (6x + 39)° (the far arc) and (3x − 10)° (the near arc). Find x and the measures of both arcs.
title: Challenge: angle outside a circle with algebraic arcs
steps: The angle outside is half the difference of the far and near arcs.
Multiply by 2 and simplify inside: 124 equals 3 x plus 49, so x is 25.
The far arc is 189 degrees and the near arc is 65 degrees.

stem:
Line BZ is tangent to ⊙O at B, and A̅C̅ is a diameter.
m(arc BC) = 80°, m(arc CD) = 45°, m(arc DE) = 25°.
Find m∠1.
title: Angles in circles: angle 1
steps: First find each arc: AB = 180° − 80° = 100° (A̅C̅ is a diameter)
In this figure, A C is a diameter, so arcs on each side of it add to 180. Arc A B is 180 minus 80: 100 degrees.
∠1 is a central angle → equals its arc
Angle 1 has its vertex at the center, so it equals its arc.
m∠1 = arc AB = 100°
So angle 1 is 100 degrees.

stem:
Line BZ is tangent to ⊙O at B, and A̅C̅ is a diameter.
m(arc BC) = 90°, m(arc CD) = 25°, m(arc DE) = 35°.
Find m∠2.
title: Angles in circles: angle 2
steps: ∠2 intercepts arc ABC, a semicircle
Angle 2 is inscribed, and its arc goes from A through B to C. A C is a diameter, so that arc is a semicircle.
inscribed in a semicircle → 90°
An angle inscribed in a semicircle is a right angle: 90 degrees.

stem:
Line BZ is tangent to ⊙O at B, and A̅C̅ is a diameter.
m(arc BC) = 100°, m(arc CD) = 45°, m(arc DE) = 20°.
Find m∠3.
title: Angles in circles: angle 3
steps: ∠3 is inscribed; it intercepts arc CE = 45° + 20°
Angle 3 is an inscribed angle. Its arc goes from C to E: 45 plus 20, which is 65 degrees.
An inscribed angle is half its arc: 32.5 degrees.

stem:
Line BZ is tangent to ⊙O at B, and A̅C̅ is a diameter.
m(arc BC) = 80°, m(arc CD) = 25°, m(arc DE) = 15°.
Find m∠4.
title: Angles in circles: angle 4
steps: Find arc A E first. A C is a diameter, so arcs C D, D E, and E A add to 180: arc A E is 140 degrees.
∠4 is inscribed and intercepts arc AE
Angle 4 is inscribed, and it cuts off arc A E.
Half of 140 is 70 degrees.

stem:
Line BZ is tangent to ⊙O at B, and A̅C̅ is a diameter.
m(arc BC) = 100°, m(arc CD) = 25°, m(arc DE) = 15°.
Find m∠5.
title: Angles in circles: angle 5
steps: ∠5: chords crossing inside → half the sum
Angle 5 is where two chords cross inside the circle. It's half the sum of its arc and its vertical angle's arc.
Those arcs are B C, 100, and D E, 15. Half of 115 is 57.5 degrees.

stem:
Line BZ is tangent to ⊙O at B, and A̅C̅ is a diameter.
m(arc BC) = 90°, m(arc CD) = 40°, m(arc DE) = 25°.
Find m∠6.
title: Angles in circles: angle 6
steps: Angle 6 makes a linear pair with angle 5, so find angle 5 first: half of 90 plus 25, which is 57.5.
A linear pair adds to 180, so angle 6 is 122.5 degrees.

stem:
Line BZ is tangent to ⊙O at B, and A̅C̅ is a diameter.
m(arc BC) = 85°, m(arc CD) = 25°, m(arc DE) = 25°.
Find m∠7.
title: Angles in circles: angle 7
steps: ∠7: two secants meet outside → half the difference
Angle 7 is outside the circle, where two secants meet. It's half the difference of the far arc and the near arc.
arc AB = 180° − 85° = 95° (far);  arc DE = 25° (near)
The far arc is A B: 180 minus 85, which is 95. The near arc is D E: 25.
Half of 70 is 35 degrees.

stem:
Line BZ is tangent to ⊙O at B, and A̅C̅ is a diameter.
m(arc BC) = 80°, m(arc CD) = 25°, m(arc DE) = 30°.
Find m∠8.
title: Angles in circles: angle 8
steps: ∠8: chords BD and AC cross inside
Angle 8 is where chords B D and A C cross inside the circle.
arcs AB and CD: AB = 180° − 80° = 100°, CD = 25°
It and its vertical angle cut off arcs A B and C D. Arc A B is 180 minus 80: 100. Arc C D is 25.
Half the sum: 62.5 degrees.

stem:
Line BZ is tangent to ⊙O at B, and A̅C̅ is a diameter.
m(arc BC) = 95°, m(arc CD) = 40°, m(arc DE) = 30°.
Find m∠9.
title: Angles in circles: angle 9
steps: ∠9: tangent BZ meets radius OB at B
Angle 9 is between the tangent line and the radius at the point of tangency.
tangent ⊥ radius → m∠9 = 90°
A tangent is always perpendicular to the radius there, so angle 9 is 90 degrees.

stem:
Line BZ is tangent to ⊙O at B, and A̅C̅ is a diameter.
m(arc BC) = 90°, m(arc CD) = 25°, m(arc DE) = 35°.
Find m∠10.
title: Angles in circles: angle 10
steps: ∠10: tangent and chord BD
Angle 10 is formed by the tangent at B and the chord B D.
intercepted arc BCD = 90° + 25° = 115°
Its arc goes from B through C to D: 90 plus 25, which is 115.
A tangent-chord angle is half its arc: 57.5 degrees.

stem: Find the value of x.
title: Segments of chords
steps: part × part = part × part
Segments of Chords Theorem: when two chords cross, the two parts of one chord multiply to the same number as the two parts of the other.
One chord is split into 4 and 4. The other is split into 4 and x.
16 equals 4 x, so x is 4.

stem: Find the value of x.
title: Segments of secants
steps: outside part × whole secant = outside part × whole secant
Segments of Secants Theorem: for each secant from the outside point, multiply the outside part by the whole secant. The products are equal.
The top secant has outside part 4 and whole length 4 plus 3, which is 7. The bottom has outside part x and whole length x plus 12.
Expand and move everything to one side.
Factor: x is 2 or negative 14. A length is positive, so x is 2.

stem: Find the value of x.
title: A secant and a tangent
steps: tangent² = outside part × whole secant
When a tangent and a secant come from the same point, the tangent squared equals the outside part of the secant times the whole secant.
The tangent is 15. The secant's outside part is 9, and the whole secant is 9 plus x.
Distribute, subtract 81, and divide by 9: x is 16.

stem: From point P outside a circle, one secant has external segment x and internal segment 18. Another secant from P has external segment 4 and whole length 36. Find x, and the length of a tangent segment from P to the circle.
title: Challenge: two secants, then a tangent
steps: For every secant from P, the outside part times the whole is the same. The second secant gives 4 times 36: 144.
The first secant has outside part x and whole x plus 18.
Factor: x is 6, since a length can't be negative.
tangent² = 144 → tangent = 12
A tangent from P squared is that same number, 144. So the tangent is 12.

stem: The center of a circle is (1, −1), and a point on the circle is (−2, 0). Write the standard equation of the circle.
title: Equation of a circle: center and a point
steps: (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r²
The standard equation of a circle uses its center, h, k, and its radius, r.
The radius is the distance from the center to the point. You need r squared, so skip the square root: 9 plus 1 is 10.
With center 1, negative 1: x minus 1 squared plus y plus 1 squared equals 10. Minus a negative becomes plus.

stem: The endpoints of a diameter of a circle are (0, 10) and (12, −4). Write the standard equation of the circle.
title: Equation of a circle: from a diameter
steps: The center is the midpoint of the diameter: 6, 3.
r squared is the squared distance from the center to an endpoint: 85.
So the equation is x minus 6 squared plus y minus 3 squared equals 85.

stem: Write the standard equation of the circle with center (−4, −7) and radius 4.
title: Equation of a circle: center and radius
steps: The center is negative 4, negative 7, and r squared is 16.
x minus negative 4 is x plus 4, and y minus negative 7 is y plus 7.

stem: Write the standard equation of the circle.
kind: ## Write the standard equation of the circle\.$
title: Equation of a circle: from a graph
steps: center (−3, −1)
Read the center from the graph: negative 3, negative 1.
radius 5 (count to the circle)
Count from the center to the circle in a straight line: 5 units.
So the equation is x plus 3 squared plus y plus 1 squared equals 25.

stem: Find the center and radius of the circle.   (x − 7)² + (y − 8)² = 121
title: Center and radius from an equation
steps: compare with (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r²
Match the equation to the standard form.
h is 7 and k is 8. Watch the signs: x minus 7 means h is positive 7.
center (7, 8), radius √121 = 11
The radius is the square root of 121: 11.

stem: Find the center and radius, then graph the circle: place the center, then one point on the circle.   (x − 3)² + (y − 4)² = 25
title: Graph a circle from its equation
steps: center (3, 4), r² = 25 → r = 5
Compare with the standard form: center 3, 4 and radius 5.
plot the center; then a point 5 away, like (8, 4)
Place the center, then a point 5 units away, such as 5 to the right: 8, 4.

stem: Find the center and radius, then graph the circle with a diameter from (3, 5) to (7, 5): place the center, then one point on the circle.
title: Graph a circle from a diameter
steps: center = midpoint of (3, 5) and (7, 5) = (5, 5)
The center is the midpoint of the diameter: 5, 5.
radius = half of 4 = 2
The diameter is 4 long, so the radius is 2.
plot (5, 5), then (7, 5)
Place the center, then a point 2 away, like 7, 5.

stem: Prove or disprove: The point (6, 4) lies on the circle centered at the origin and containing the point (−9, −1).
title: Is the point on the circle? (radius from a point)
steps: radius = distance from (0, 0) to (−9, −1) = √82
The radius is the distance from the origin to the given point: root of 81 plus 1, root 82.
The distance to the test point is root 52.
They're not equal, so the point is not on the circle.

stem: Prove or disprove: The point (−4, −7) lies on the circle centered at the origin with radius √65.
title: Is the point on the circle? (radius given)
steps: Find the distance from the center to the point: root 65.
equals the radius √65 → Yes
That equals the radius, so the point is on the circle.

stem: A city's commuter system has three zones. Zone 1 serves people living within 4 miles of the city's center. Zone 2 serves those between 4 and 8 miles from the center. Zone 3 serves those more than 8 miles from the center. On a coordinate plane in miles with the city's center at the origin, which zone serves a home at (3, 6)?
title: Circles in real life: commuter zones
steps: distance = √(3² + 6²) = √45 ≈ 6.7 mi
Find how far the home is from the center: root of 9 plus 36, about 6.7 miles.
That's between 4 and 8 miles, so it's in Zone 2.

stem: Point (6, −4) is on the circle (x − 2)² + (y + 1)² = 25. Write an equation of the line tangent to the circle at that point. Give its slope and y-intercept.
title: Challenge: tangent line to a circle
steps: center (2, −1); radius slope to (6, −4): −3/4
The center is 2, negative 1. The radius to 6, negative 4 has slope negative 3 over 4.
tangent ⊥ radius → slope 4/3
A tangent is perpendicular to the radius, so its slope is the opposite reciprocal: 4 thirds.
Point-slope form through 6, negative 4, then simplify: y intercept negative 12.

stem: Find the circumference of a circle with a diameter of 18 meters. Round to the nearest hundredth.
title: Find the circumference
steps: C = πd = 2πr
Circumference is pi times the diameter, or 2 pi times the radius.
The diameter is 18, so C is 18 pi.
18 pi is about 56.55 meters.

stem: Find the diameter of a circle with a circumference of 51 centimeters. Round to the nearest hundredth.
title: Find the diameter from the circumference
steps: C = πd → d = C/π
Solve C equals pi d for d: divide by pi.
51 divided by pi is about 16.23 centimeters.

stem: Find the radius of a circle with a circumference of 44π centimeters.
title: Find the radius from the circumference
steps: C = 2πr → 44π = 2πr
Use C equals 2 pi r.
Divide both sides by 2 pi: the pis cancel, and r is 22 centimeters.

stem: Find the length of the red arc LQ. Round to the nearest hundredth.
title: Arc length
steps: arc length = (arc measure/360°) · 2πr
An arc is a fraction of the whole circle: its measure over 360. Its length is that fraction of the circumference.
The arc is 70 degrees and the radius is 17.
That's about 20.77 meters.

stem: The red arc is 30.63 in. long. Find the measure of arc NP. Round to the nearest degree.
title: Arc length: find the arc measure
steps: Put the arc length and radius into the formula, with the measure m unknown.
Solve for m: multiply by 360 and divide by 2 pi times 13. About 135 degrees.

stem: The red arc is 89.54 cm long. Find the radius of ⊙E. Round to the nearest hundredth.
title: Arc length: find the radius
steps: Put in the arc length and measure, with r unknown.
Solve for r: about 18 centimeters.

stem: The red arc is 9.64 ft long. Find the circumference of ⊙A. Round to the nearest hundredth.
title: Arc length: find the circumference
steps: the arc is 65/360 of the circle
A 65 degree arc is 65 three-hundred-sixtieths of the circle.
So the whole circumference is 9.64 times 360 over 65: about 53.39 feet.

stem: You ride your bicycle 110 meters. The front wheel has a radius of 28 centimeters. How many complete revolutions does the front wheel make?
title: Wheels: how many revolutions?
steps: one revolution = C = 2π(28) ≈ 175.93 cm ≈ 1.76 m
One turn of the wheel covers its circumference: about 175.93 centimeters, or 1.76 meters.
Divide the distance by one turn: about 62.5.
62 complete revolutions
So the wheel makes 62 complete turns.

stem: A measuring wheel is used to find the length of a path. The diameter of the wheel is 10 inches. The wheel makes 34 complete revolutions along the path. How many feet long is the path? Round to the nearest hundredth.
title: Wheels: how far?
steps: one revolution = πd = π(10) ≈ 31.42 in.
One turn covers the circumference: about 31.42 inches.
34 turns cover about 1068.14 inches.
Divide by 12 to get feet: about 89.01 feet.

stem: Find the perimeter of the shaded region. Semicircles are cut out of both ends. Round to the nearest hundredth.
title: Perimeter with semicircles
steps: straight sides: 2 · 21 = 42
The perimeter is the distance around the outside. The two straight sides are 21 each: 42.
two semicircles of diameter 11 = one circle: π · 11 ≈ 34.56
The two half circles together make one whole circle with diameter 11: about 34.56.
Add them: about 76.56. Don't count the cut-off straight edges, since they're not on the outside.

stem: Convert 30° to radians. Write your answer in terms of π.
title: Degrees to radians
steps: To change degrees to radians, multiply by pi over 180.
30 over 180 simplifies to one sixth: pi over 6 radians.

stem: Convert 9π/8 radians to degrees.
title: Radians to degrees
steps: To change radians to degrees, multiply by 180 over pi.
The pis cancel: 9 times 180 over 8 is 202.5 degrees.

stem: Find the circumference of the circle represented by the equation. Write the circumference in terms of π.   (x + 3)² + (y + 4)² = 16
title: Circumference from an equation
steps: The equation shows r squared on the right: 16. So r is 4.
The circumference is 8 pi.

stem: A semicircle has endpoints (4, 2) and (5, −6). Find the arc length of the semicircle. Round to the nearest hundredth.
title: Arc length of a semicircle from its endpoints
steps: The endpoints are the ends of a diameter. Distance Formula: root 65.
half the circumference: (1/2)π√65 ≈ 12.66
A semicircle is half of pi d: about 12.66.

stem: In a circle, a 210° arc has length 49π/2 centimeters. Find the radius and the circumference of the circle (in terms of π).
title: Challenge: radius from an arc length
steps: Put the arc length and measure into the formula. 210 over 360 times 2 pi is 7 pi over 6.
Divide: the pis cancel, and r is 21 centimeters.
The circumference is 42 pi centimeters.

stem: Find the area of a circle with a radius of 4 feet. Round to the nearest hundredth.
kind: area of a circle with a radius
title: Area of a circle from the radius
steps: A = πr²
The area of a circle is pi times the radius squared.
A = π(r)² → square the radius, then multiply by π
Square the radius first, then multiply by pi. Round at the end.

stem: Find the area of a circle with a diameter of 28 inches. Round to the nearest hundredth.
kind: area of a circle with a diameter
title: Area of a circle from the diameter
steps: The formula uses the radius, so halve the diameter: 14.
14 squared is 196. Times pi is about 615.75 square inches.

stem: Find the radius of a circle with an area of 14 square inches. Round to the nearest hundredth.
title: Radius from the area
steps: A = πr² → r = √(A/π)
Solve the area formula for r: divide by pi, then take the square root.
14 divided by pi is about 4.46. The square root is about 2.11 inches.

stem: Find the diameter of a circle with an area of 280 square centimeters. Round to the nearest hundredth.
title: Diameter from the area
steps: First find the radius: the square root of the area over pi, about 9.44.
The diameter is twice that: about 18.88 centimeters.

stem: Find the area of the smaller sector formed by ∠LHQ. Round to the nearest hundredth.
title: Area of a sector
steps: sector area = (arc measure/360°) · πr²
A sector is a slice of the circle. Its area is the fraction arc over 360, times the whole area.
The arc is 50 degrees and the radius is 8.
That's about 27.93 square centimeters.

stem: Find the area of the larger sector formed by ∠NMP. Round to the nearest hundredth.
title: Area of the larger sector
steps: larger sector arc = 360° − 85° = 275°
The larger sector goes the long way around: 360 minus 85 is 275 degrees.
Its area is 275 over 360 times pi times 16 squared: about 614.36 square meters.

stem: The area of the shaded sector is 59.86 m². Find the area of ⊙M. Round to the nearest hundredth.
title: From a sector to the whole circle
steps: the sector is 140/360 of the circle
A 140 degree sector is 140 over 360 of the circle.
So the sector's area is that fraction of the whole area.
Multiply by 360 over 140: about 153.93 square meters.

stem: Find the area of the shaded region. The circles have the same center. Round to the nearest hundredth.
title: Shaded region: a ring
steps: shaded = big circle − small circle
The shaded ring is the big circle with the small circle taken out.
Big: 100 pi. Small: 9 pi. Subtract: 91 pi.
About 285.88 square centimeters.

stem: Find the area of the shaded region (half of the ring). The circles have the same center. Round to the nearest hundredth.
title: Shaded region: half a ring
steps: First the whole ring: big circle minus small circle, 240 pi.
half: 120π ≈ 376.99 in.²
Only half is shaded: 120 pi, about 376.99 square inches.

stem: A circle fits exactly inside a square with side length 44 ft. Find the area of the shaded region. Round to the nearest hundredth.
title: Shaded region: a circle in a square
steps: square: 44² = 1936
The square's area is 44 squared: 1936.
circle: diameter 44 → r = 22 → π(22)² = 484π
The circle fits exactly inside, so its diameter is 44 and its radius is 22. Its area is 484 pi.
The shaded corners are the square minus the circle: about 415.47 square feet.

stem: A sector of a circle with radius 13 inches has an area of 507π/5 square inches. Find the central angle of the sector and the length of its arc (in terms of π).
title: Challenge: central angle from a sector's area
steps: Put the area and radius into the sector formula.
Divide both sides by 169 pi and multiply by 360: theta is 216 degrees.
The arc length is 216 over 360 of the circumference, 26 pi: 78 pi over 5 inches.

stem: Find the area of the rhombus.
title: Area of a rhombus
steps: A = ½d₁d₂
The area of a rhombus is half the product of its diagonals.
The diagonals are 22 and 16.
A = ½ · 22 · 16 = 176 square units
Half of 22 times 16 is 176 square units.

stem: Find the area of the kite.
title: Area of a kite
steps: A = ½d₁d₂
A kite works the same way: half the product of its diagonals.
A = ½ · 7 · 8 = 28 square units
The diagonals are 7 and 8, so the area is half of 56: 28 square units.

stem: Find the measure of a central angle of a regular polygon with 24 sides.
title: Central angle of a regular polygon
steps: central angle = 360° ÷ n
The central angles of a regular polygon split the full 360 degrees into equal parts, one for each side.
With 24 sides, each central angle is 15 degrees.

stem: Find m∠DTE in regular octagon BDEFHKQR with center T.
title: Angles in a regular polygon: a central angle
steps: central angle = 360° ÷ 8 = 45°
In a regular octagon, each central angle is 360 divided by 8: 45 degrees.
∠DTE is a central angle → 45°
Angle D T E has its vertex at the center T and its sides go to two neighboring vertices. So it is a central angle: 45 degrees.

stem: Find m∠VXR in regular hexagon RSTUVW with center X.
title: Angles in a regular polygon: two central angles
steps: central angle = 360° ÷ 6 = 60°
In a regular hexagon, each central angle is 60 degrees.
∠VXR spans two sides → 2 · 60° = 120°
Angle V X R reaches across two sides, so it is made of two central angles: 120 degrees.

stem: Find m∠DWX in regular octagon ADFHJKLQ with center W.
title: Angles in a regular polygon: half a central angle
steps: central angle = 360° ÷ 8 = 45°
In a regular octagon, each central angle is 45 degrees.
the apothem W̅X̅ bisects ∠DWF
The apothem goes from the center to the midpoint of a side, and it cuts the central angle in half.
So angle D W X is half of 45: 22.5 degrees.

stem: Find m∠HCG in regular pentagon BCDEF with center G.
title: Angles in a regular polygon: the right triangle
steps: central angle = 360° ÷ 5 = 72°, half is 36°
In a regular pentagon, each central angle is 72 degrees. The apothem splits it into two 36 degree angles.
△CGH has a right angle at H
The apothem meets the side at a right angle, so triangle C G H has a right angle at H.
The angles of a triangle add to 180: 180 minus 90 minus 36 is 54 degrees.

stem: Find the area of a regular octagon with an apothem of 7 units. Round to the nearest tenth.
title: Area of a regular polygon from the apothem
steps: A = ½aP
The area of a regular polygon is one half times the apothem times the perimeter. You know the apothem, so you need the perimeter.
Each central angle is 45 degrees. The apothem splits it, making a right triangle with a 22.5 degree angle at the center.
In that right triangle the apothem is the adjacent side and the radius is the hypotenuse. So r is 7 divided by cosine of 22.5: about 7.58.
Half a side is r times sine of 22.5, so a full side is about 5.80. Eight sides make about 46.39.
A ≈ ½ · 7 · 46.39 ≈ 162.4 square units
Area is one half times 7 times 46.39: about 162.4 square units.

stem: Find the area of a regular octagon with a radius of 10 units. Round to the nearest tenth.
title: Area of a regular polygon from the radius
steps: A = ½aP
The area is one half times the apothem times the perimeter. You know the radius, so you need both.
Each central angle is 45 degrees. The apothem splits it into 22.5 degrees, making a right triangle with the radius as the hypotenuse.
The apothem is the adjacent side: 10 times cosine of 22.5, about 9.24.
Half a side is 10 times sine of 22.5, so a side is about 7.65. Eight sides make about 61.23.
A ≈ ½ · 9.24 · 61.23 ≈ 282.8 square units
Area is one half times 9.24 times 61.23: about 282.8 square units.

stem: An equilateral triangle is inscribed in a circle with radius 9. Find the area of the shaded region (inside the circle but outside the polygon). Round to the nearest tenth.
title: Shaded region: triangle in a circle
steps: shaded = circle − triangle
The shaded part is the circle with the triangle taken out.
circle: π(9)² ≈ 254.47
The circle's area is pi times 9 squared: about 254.47.

Draw radii to the 3 vertices to cut the triangle into 3 pieces. Each has two sides of 9 with a 120 degree angle between them, so each is one half times 9 times 9 times sine 120. Together about 105.22.
Subtract: about 149.2 square units.

stem: A square is inscribed in a circle with radius 6. Find the area of the shaded region (inside the circle but outside the polygon). Round to the nearest tenth.
title: Shaded region: square in a circle
steps: circle: π(6)² ≈ 113.10
The circle's area is pi times 6 squared: about 113.10.
square: 4 · ½ · 6 · 6 · sin 90° = 72
Radii cut the square into 4 triangles, each with two sides of 6 and a right angle between them. Each is 18, so the square is 72.
Subtract: about 41.1 square units.

stem: A regular hexagon is inscribed in a circle with radius 13. Find the area of the shaded region (inside the circle but outside the polygon). Round to the nearest tenth.
title: Shaded region: hexagon in a circle
steps: circle: π(13)² ≈ 530.93
The circle's area is pi times 13 squared: about 530.93.
Radii cut the hexagon into 6 triangles, each with two sides of 13 and a 60 degree angle. Together about 439.07.
Subtract: about 91.9 square units.

stem: A regular hexagon has sides 14 meters long. Find its apothem and its area. Give exact answers.
title: Challenge: exact apothem and area of a hexagon
steps: central angle 60° → two 30°-60°-90° triangles, short leg 7
The central angle is 60 degrees. The apothem splits that triangle into two 30 60 90 triangles. The short leg is half a side: 7.
apothem = 7√3
The apothem is the long leg: the short leg times root 3, so 7 root 3.
The perimeter is 6 times 14: 84.
Area is one half times 7 root 3 times 84: 294 root 3 square meters.

stem: A rectangular state is about 220 miles long and 150 miles wide and has a population of about 1,649,000 people. Find the population density in people per square mile. Round to the nearest tenth.
title: Population density of a rectangular region
steps: density = people ÷ area
Population density is the number of people per square mile: people divided by area.
The state is a rectangle, so its area is 220 times 150: 33,000 square miles.
Divide the population by the area: about 50 people per square mile.

stem: About 277,000 people live in a circular region with a 4-mile radius. Find the population density in people per square mile. Round to the nearest whole number.
title: Population density of a circular region
steps: area = π(4)² ≈ 50.27 mi²
The region is a circle with radius 4, so its area is pi times 4 squared: about 50.27 square miles.
density = 277,000 ÷ 50.27 ≈ 5511 people per mi²
Density is people divided by area: about 5511 people per square mile.

stem: A circular region with a 7-mile radius has a population density of 3,477 people per square mile. Find the number of people who live in the region. Round to the nearest whole number.
title: Number of people from the density
steps: people = density · area
If density is people per square mile, then people equals density times area.
area = π(7)² ≈ 153.94 mi²
The area of the circle is pi times 7 squared: about 153.94 square miles.
Multiply: about 535,243 people.

stem: About 749,000 people live in a circular region with a population density of about 4,211 people per square mile. Find the radius of the region. Round to the nearest tenth.
title: Radius from the population density
steps: area = people ÷ density = 749,000 ÷ 4,211 ≈ 177.87 mi²
First find the area: people divided by density, about 177.87 square miles.
The area of a circle is pi r squared. Divide by pi and take the square root: about 7.5 miles.

stem: A farmer wants to plant corn so that there are 30,000 plants per acre in a field shaped like a trapezoid with bases 800 feet and 950 feet and height 900 feet. How many seeds does the farmer need? (1 acre = 43,560 ft²) Round to the nearest whole number.
title: Density with a unit conversion: seeds per acre
steps: The field is a trapezoid: one half times the sum of the bases times the height, 787,500 square feet.
The density is per acre, so convert: divide by 43,560 square feet per acre, about 18.079 acres.
Seeds equal density times area: about 542,355.

stem: One measure of rug quality is knot density. A rug that is 3 feet by 3 feet is made of 103,680 knots. Find the knot density in knots per square inch.
title: Density with a unit conversion: knots per square inch
steps: The density is per square inch, so convert feet to inches first. 3 feet is 36 inches, so the area is 1296 square inches.
103,680 ÷ 1296 = 80 knots per in.²
Divide the knots by the area: 80 knots per square inch.

stem: A rectangular field has a perimeter of 340 yards. What dimensions give the greatest possible area, and what is that area?
title: Greatest area for a fixed perimeter
steps: Half the perimeter is length plus width: 170.
area ℓ(170 − ℓ) is greatest when ℓ = w
For a fixed perimeter, the rectangle with the greatest area is a square.
85 yd by 85 yd → A = 85² = 7225 yd²
So each side is 170 divided by 2: 85 yards. The area is 85 squared, 7225 square yards.

stem: A rectangular exhibit must cover 2,209 square feet. What dimensions use the least amount of fencing?
title: Least perimeter for a fixed area
steps: for a fixed area, a square has the least perimeter
The least fencing means the smallest perimeter. For a fixed area, that's a square.
side = √2209 = 47 → 47 ft by 47 ft
The side of the square is the square root of the area: root 2209 is 47. So use 47 feet by 47 feet.

stem: You have 392 feet of fence to make a rectangular pen along a straight river. The river side needs no fence. What dimensions give the largest area, and what is that area? (Try several widths and look for the pattern.)
title: Challenge: largest pen along a river
steps: let w = each side away from the river; river side = 392 − 2w
Let w be each side that goes away from the river. Two of those use 2 w of fence, and the rest, 392 minus 2 w, goes along the river.
The area is w times 392 minus 2 w.
Try some widths. The area goes up, then back down, with the biggest at 98, a quarter of the fence.
98 ft by 196 ft → 19208 ft²
So the pen is 98 by 196 feet, with area 19,208 square feet.

stem: Tell whether the solid is a polyhedron. If it is, name the polyhedron.
title: Is it a polyhedron? A solid with a curved surface
steps: polyhedron: every face is a flat polygon
A polyhedron is a solid whose faces are all flat polygons.
curved surface → not a polyhedron
This solid has a curved surface, so it is not a polyhedron. Cylinders, cones, and spheres are never polyhedra.
two circular bases + a curved side → cylinder
It has two circle bases joined by a curved side, so it's a cylinder.

stem: Tell whether the solid is a polyhedron. If it is, name the polyhedron.
title: Is it a polyhedron? Naming a prism
steps: all faces are flat polygons → polyhedron
Every face is a flat polygon, so it is a polyhedron.
two congruent parallel bases → prism
It has two congruent bases that are parallel, joined by rectangles. That makes it a prism.
the bases are hexagons → hexagonal prism
Name a prism by the shape of its base. The bases have 6 sides, so it's a hexagonal prism.

stem: Tell whether the solid is a polyhedron. If it is, name the polyhedron.
title: Is it a polyhedron? Naming a pyramid
steps: all faces are flat polygons → polyhedron
Every face is a flat polygon, so it is a polyhedron.
one base; triangles meet at a point → pyramid
It has one base, and its other faces are triangles that meet at one vertex. That makes it a pyramid.
the base is a triangle → triangular pyramid
Name a pyramid by the shape of its base. The base is a triangle, so it's a triangular pyramid.

stem: Name the figure: a prism with 6 faces.
title: Name a prism from its faces
steps: n-sided prism: n + 2 faces
A prism with an n sided base has n side faces plus 2 bases: n plus 2 faces.
So n plus 2 is 6, and n is 4.
4-sided base → rectangular prism
A 4 sided base makes it a rectangular prism.

stem: Name the figure: a prism with 18 edges.
title: Name a prism from its edges
steps: n-sided prism: 3n edges
A prism with an n sided base has n edges on each base plus n side edges: 3 n edges.
3n = 18 → n = 6 → hexagonal prism
3 n is 18, so n is 6. A 6 sided base makes it a hexagonal prism.

stem: Name the figure: a prism with 8 vertices.
title: Name a prism from its vertices
steps: n-sided prism: 2n vertices
A prism has n vertices on each of its 2 bases: 2 n vertices.
2n = 8 → n = 4 → rectangular prism
2 n is 8, so n is 4: a rectangular prism.

stem: Name the figure: a pyramid with 5 faces.
title: Name a pyramid from its faces
steps: n-sided pyramid: n + 1 faces
A pyramid with an n sided base has n triangle faces plus 1 base: n plus 1 faces.
n + 1 = 5 → n = 4 → rectangular pyramid
n plus 1 is 5, so n is 4: a rectangular pyramid.

stem: Name the figure: a pyramid with 14 edges.
title: Name a pyramid from its edges
steps: n-sided pyramid: 2n edges
A pyramid has n edges around the base and n edges up to the top: 2 n edges.
2n = 14 → n = 7 → heptagonal pyramid
2 n is 14, so n is 7. A 7 sided base makes it a heptagonal pyramid.

stem: Name the figure: a pyramid with 8 vertices.
title: Name a pyramid from its vertices
steps: n-sided pyramid: n + 1 vertices
A pyramid has n vertices around the base plus 1 at the top: n plus 1 vertices.
n + 1 = 8 → n = 7 → heptagonal pyramid
n plus 1 is 8, so n is 7: a heptagonal pyramid.

stem: A polyhedron has 7 faces and 10 vertices. How many edges does it have? (Use Euler's Formula, F + V = E + 2.)
title: Euler's Formula: find the edges
steps: F + V = E + 2
Euler's Formula: faces plus vertices equals edges plus 2.
7 plus 10 is 17, which equals E plus 2. So E is 15.

stem: A polyhedron has 6 faces and 10 edges. How many vertices does it have? (Use Euler's Formula, F + V = E + 2.)
title: Euler's Formula: find the vertices
steps: F + V = E + 2
Euler's Formula: faces plus vertices equals edges plus 2.
6 plus V equals 12, so V is 6.

stem: A polyhedron has 12 edges and 6 vertices. How many faces does it have? (Use Euler's Formula, F + V = E + 2.)
title: Euler's Formula: find the faces
steps: F + V = E + 2
Euler's Formula: faces plus vertices equals edges plus 2.
F plus 6 equals 14, so F is 8.

stem: Describe the shape formed by the intersection of the plane and the solid: a plane cuts a hexagonal prism parallel to its bases.
title: Cross section: a prism cut parallel to its bases
steps: a cut parallel to the bases matches the bases
When a plane cuts a prism parallel to its bases, the cross section is the same shape as the bases.
hexagonal prism → hexagon
The bases of a hexagonal prism are hexagons, so the cross section is a hexagon.

stem: Describe the shape formed by the intersection of the plane and the solid: a plane cuts a cube parallel to a face.
title: Cross section: a cube cut parallel to a face
steps: cut parallel to a face → same shape as the face
A cut parallel to a face has the same shape as that face.
cube faces are squares → square
Every face of a cube is a square, so the cross section is a square.

stem: Describe the shape formed by the intersection of the plane and the solid: a plane cuts a rectangular prism perpendicular to its base.
title: Cross section: a rectangular prism cut perpendicular to its base
steps: perpendicular cut → goes straight down through the prism
A cut perpendicular to the base slices straight down from top to bottom.
straight sides and parallel edges → rectangle
It crosses two parallel faces and the top and bottom, so the cross section is a rectangle.

stem: Describe the shape formed by the intersection of the plane and the solid: a plane cuts a cylinder parallel to its bases.
title: Cross section: a cylinder cut parallel to its bases
steps: cut parallel to the bases → same shape as a base
A cut parallel to the bases has the shape of a base.
cylinder bases are circles → circle
A cylinder's bases are circles, so the cross section is a circle.

stem: Describe the shape formed by the intersection of the plane and the solid: a plane cuts a cylinder perpendicular to its bases, through the center.
title: Cross section: a cylinder cut perpendicular to its bases
steps: perpendicular cut through the center → straight down
The cut goes straight down through the cylinder, from one base to the other.
two straight sides + two diameters → rectangle
The sides of the cut are straight lines down the curved side, and the top and bottom are diameters of the bases. That makes a rectangle.

stem: Describe the shape formed by the intersection of the plane and the solid: a plane cuts a cone parallel to its base.
title: Cross section: a cone cut parallel to its base
steps: cut parallel to the base → same shape as the base, smaller
A cut parallel to the base of a cone is a smaller copy of the base.
the base is a circle → circle
The base is a circle, so the cross section is a circle.

stem: Describe the shape formed by the intersection of the plane and the solid: a plane cuts a cone perpendicular to its base, through the vertex.
title: Cross section: a cone cut through its vertex
steps: perpendicular through the vertex → two slanted sides meet at the top
The cut goes down through the vertex, so its two sides slant up and meet at the top.
bottom edge: a diameter of the base → triangle
The bottom is a straight segment across the base. Three straight sides make a triangle.

stem: Describe the shape formed by the intersection of the plane and the solid: a plane cuts a sphere through its center.
title: Cross section: a sphere
steps: every cut of a sphere is a circle
Any plane that cuts a sphere makes a circle.
through the center → circle (the largest one)
Through the center, it's the biggest possible circle: a great circle.

stem: Describe the shape formed by the intersection of the plane and the solid: a plane cuts a square pyramid parallel to its base.
title: Cross section: a square pyramid cut parallel to its base
steps: cut parallel to the base → smaller copy of the base
A cut parallel to the base of a pyramid is a smaller copy of the base.
square base → square
The base is a square, so the cross section is a square.

stem: Describe the shape formed by the intersection of the plane and the solid: a plane cuts a square pyramid perpendicular to its base, through the vertex.
kind: square pyramid perpendicular to its base, through
title: Cross section: a square pyramid cut through its vertex
steps: perpendicular through the vertex → two sides meet at the top
The cut passes through the top vertex, so its two sides meet there.
bottom edge across the base → triangle
The bottom is a segment across the square base. Three sides make a triangle.

stem: Describe the shape formed by the intersection of the plane and the solid: a plane cuts a square pyramid perpendicular to its base, not through the vertex.
title: Cross section: a square pyramid cut beside its vertex
steps: perpendicular, but missing the vertex → the top is cut off
The cut goes straight down but misses the top vertex, so it doesn't come to a point.
a short top edge, a longer bottom edge, parallel → trapezoid
It has a short top edge and a longer bottom edge, and they're parallel. That makes a trapezoid.

stem: A polyhedron has 8 faces and 14 edges. All of its faces are triangles except one base. How many vertices does it have, and what is the solid?
title: Challenge: Euler's Formula, then a pyramid
steps: Use Euler's Formula: 8 plus V equals 16, so V is 8.
triangles + one base → pyramid
All faces are triangles except one base, so it's a pyramid.
n + 1 = 8 → n = 7 → heptagonal pyramid
A pyramid has n plus 1 faces. n plus 1 is 8, so n is 7: a heptagonal pyramid.

stem: A polyhedron has 5 faces and 9 edges. All of its faces are rectangles except two congruent bases. How many vertices does it have, and what is the solid?
title: Challenge: Euler's Formula, then a prism
steps: Use Euler's Formula: 5 plus V equals 11, so V is 6.
rectangles + two congruent bases → prism
All faces are rectangles except two congruent bases, so it's a prism.
n + 2 = 5 → n = 3 → triangular prism
A prism has n plus 2 faces. n plus 2 is 5, so n is 3: a triangular prism.

stem: Find the surface area of the right triangular prism.
title: Surface area of a triangular prism
steps: S = 2B + Ph
The surface area of a prism is the two bases, 2 B, plus the side faces, which unroll into a rectangle: perimeter of the base times the height.
The bases are right triangles with legs 9 and 12, so each base is one half times 9 times 12: 54.
The perimeter of the triangle is 36, and the prism's height is 3.
2 times 54 is 108, and 36 times 3 is 108. Together, 216 square yards.

stem: Find the surface area of the right prism.
title: Surface area of a rectangular prism
steps: S = 2B + Ph
The surface area of a prism is 2 bases plus the perimeter of the base times the height.
The base is 4 by 4, so B is 16 and the perimeter is 16.
The height is 9. 32 plus 144 is 176 square inches.

stem: Find the surface area of the right cylinder. Round to the nearest hundredth.
title: Surface area of a cylinder
steps: S = 2πr² + 2πrh
A cylinder's surface area is its two circle bases, 2 pi r squared, plus the side, which unrolls into a rectangle: circumference times height, 2 pi r h.
The diameter is 26, so the radius is 13.
Two bases: 338 pi. The side: 468 pi. Together, 806 pi.
That's about 2532.12 square yards.

stem: A right rectangular prism has a surface area of 636 cm². Its base is 12 cm by 10 cm. Find the height h.
title: Find the height of a prism from its surface area
steps: S = 2B + Ph
Start with the surface area formula and fill in what you know.
The base is 12 by 10: B is 120 and the perimeter is 44.
636 equals 240 plus 44 h. Subtract 240: 396 equals 44 h.
h = 9 cm
Divide by 44: h is 9 centimeters.

stem: A right cylinder has a surface area of 352π yd² and a radius of 8 yd. Find the height h.
title: Find the height of a cylinder from its surface area
steps: S = 2πr² + 2πrh
Start with the cylinder formula and put in the radius, 8.
The bases are 128 pi, and the side is 16 pi h.
Subtract 128 pi, then divide by 16 pi: h is 14 yards.

stem: The cones are similar. Solid A has a radius of 9 yd and a surface area of 26 yd². Solid B has a radius of 27 yd. Find the surface area of solid B.
title: Similar solids: surface area of a cone
steps: The scale factor is the ratio of matching lengths: 27 over 9, which is 3.
surface areas: ratio k²
Surface area is measured in square units, so it scales by k squared.
26 times 9 is 234 square yards.

stem: The cylinders are similar. Solid A has a radius of 3 in. and a surface area of 270 in.². Solid B has a radius of 12 in. Find the surface area of solid B.
title: Similar solids: surface area of a cylinder
steps: The scale factor is 12 over 3: 4.
Surface area scales by k squared, 16: 270 times 16 is 4320 square inches.

stem: The pyramids are similar. Solid A has a height of 6 cm and a surface area of 209 cm². Solid B has a height of 24 cm. Find the surface area of solid B.
title: Similar solids: surface area of a pyramid
steps: The heights match up, so the scale factor is 24 over 6: 4.
Surface area scales by k squared, 16: 3344 square centimeters.

stem: The prisms are similar. Solid A has a height of 12 cm and a surface area of 225 cm². Solid B has a height of 36 cm. Find the surface area of solid B.
title: Similar solids: surface area of a prism
steps: The scale factor is 36 over 12: 3.
Surface area scales by k squared, 9: 2025 square centimeters. If B were smaller, k would be less than 1 and the area would shrink.

stem: A right cylinder has height 13 feet and a surface area of 396π square feet. Find the radius, then the volume (in terms of π).
title: Challenge: cylinder radius from its surface area
steps: 396π = 2πr² + 2πr(13) = 2πr² + 26πr
Put the surface area and height into the formula.
Divide everything by 2 pi and move 198 over: a quadratic.
Factor: r is 9, since a radius can't be negative.
The volume is pi r squared h: 81 times 13 is 1053, so 1053 pi cubic feet.

stem: Find the surface area of the regular square pyramid.
kind: Find the surface area of the regular square pyramid
title: Surface area of a pyramid from its slant height
steps: S = B + ½Pℓ
A pyramid's surface area is its base plus its triangle faces. The faces add up to one half times the base perimeter times the slant height, l.
The base is a 4 by 4 square: B is 16 and the perimeter is 16.
The slant height is 10. One half of 16 times 10 is 80. Add the base: 96 square inches.

stem: A regular square pyramid has a height of 15 yd and a base edge length of 16 yd. Find its surface area.
title: Surface area of a pyramid from its height
steps: ℓ² = h² + (½ base edge)²
You're given the height, not the slant height. The height, half the base edge, and the slant height form a right triangle, with the slant height as the hypotenuse.
Half of 16 is 8. Root of 225 plus 64 is root 289: 17.
The base is 256 and the perimeter is 64.
One half of 64 times 17 is 544. Add the base: 800 square yards.

stem: Find the surface area of the right cone. Round to the nearest hundredth.
kind: Find the surface area of the right cone
title: Surface area of a cone from its slant height
steps: S = πr² + πrℓ
A cone's surface area is its circle base, pi r squared, plus its curved side, pi r l, where l is the slant height.
The radius is 3 and the slant height is 12: 9 pi plus 36 pi is 45 pi.
About 141.37 square inches.

stem: A right cone has a radius of 9 yd and a height of 12 yd. Find its surface area. Round to the nearest hundredth.
kind: has a radius of .* and a height
title: Surface area of a cone from its height
steps: ℓ = √(r² + h²)
You need the slant height. The radius, height, and slant height form a right triangle.
Root of 81 plus 144 is root 225: 15.
The base is 81 pi and the side is 135 pi. Together 216 pi.
About 678.58 square yards.

stem: Solids A and B are similar pyramids. The surface area of pyramid A is 414 in.², and the scale factor from A to B is k = 2/3. Find the surface area of pyramid B.
title: Similar pyramids: surface area
steps: surface areas: ratio k²
Surface areas of similar solids are in the ratio k squared.
The scale factor is 2 thirds, so k squared is 4 ninths.
414 times 4 ninths is 184 square inches.

stem: Solids A and B are similar cones. The surface area of cone A is 486π yd², and the scale factor from A to B is k = 4/3. Find the surface area of cone B.
title: Similar cones: surface area
steps: Surface area scales by k squared. 4 thirds squared is 16 ninths.
486 divided by 9 is 54, times 16 is 864. Keep the pi: 864 pi square yards.

stem: A right cone has radius 16 cm and height 12 cm. Find its slant height and its surface area (in terms of π).
title: Challenge: slant height, then surface area of a cone
steps: The radius, height, and slant height form a right triangle: root of 256 plus 144 is 20.
The base is 256 pi and the side is 320 pi.
= 576π cm²
Total: 576 pi square centimeters.

stem: Find the volume of the right triangular prism.
title: Volume of a triangular prism
steps: V = Bh
The volume of a prism is the area of its base, B, times its height.
The base is a right triangle with legs 9 and 12: one half times 9 times 12 is 54.
The prism is 2 long, so the volume is 108 cubic yards.

stem: Find the volume of the prism.
title: Volume of a rectangular prism
steps: V = Bh
The volume of a prism is the base area times the height.
The base is 3 by 4: 12.
Times the height, 9: 108 cubic inches.

stem: Find the volume of the cylinder. Round to the nearest hundredth.
title: Volume of a cylinder
steps: V = πr²h
A cylinder is like a prism with a circle base: base area pi r squared, times the height.
The diameter is 26, so the radius is 13.
169 times 18 is 3042. So the volume is 3042 pi, about 9556.72 cubic yards.

stem: The volume of the rectangular prism is 1080 cm³. Find the height h.
title: Find the height of a prism from its volume
steps: V = Bh
Put the volume and the base into V equals B h.
The base is 12 by 10, so B is 120.
Divide by 120: h is 9 centimeters.

stem: The volume of a cylinder is 768π cm³. Its radius is 8 cm. Find the height.
title: Find the height of a cylinder from its volume
steps: V = πr²h
Put the volume and the radius into V equals pi r squared h.
8 squared is 64, so 768 pi equals 64 pi h.
Divide by 64 pi: h is 12 centimeters.

stem: The volume of a cylinder is 324π cm³. Its height is 9 cm. Find the radius.
title: Find the radius of a cylinder from its volume
steps: V = πr²h
Put the volume and the height into V equals pi r squared h.
Divide both sides by 9 pi: r squared is 36.
Take the square root: r is 6 centimeters.

stem: The prisms are similar. Solid A has a height of 10 m and a volume of 293 m³. Solid B has a height of 20 m. Find the volume of solid B.
title: Similar solids: volume of a prism
steps: The scale factor is the ratio of the heights: 20 over 10, which is 2.
volumes: ratio k³
Volume is measured in cubic units, so it scales by k cubed.
2 cubed is 8, and 293 times 8 is 2344 cubic meters.

stem: The cylinders are similar. Solid A has a radius of 4 m and a volume of 1632 m³. Solid B has a radius of 2 m. Find the volume of solid B.
title: Similar solids: volume of a cylinder
steps: The scale factor is 2 over 4: 0.5. Solid B is smaller, so k is less than 1.
Volume scales by k cubed: 0.5 cubed is 0.125. 1632 times 0.125 is 204 cubic meters.

stem: A rectangular container 17 in. by 18 in. is filled with water to a depth of 8 in. The water is poured into an empty cylinder with radius 10 in. How much water is there, and how deep is it in the cylinder? Round the depth to the nearest tenth.
title: Challenge: pour from a box into a cylinder
steps: The water in the box is a rectangular prism: 17 times 18 times 8 is 2448 cubic inches.
in the cylinder: π(10)²h = 2448
Poured into the cylinder, the volume stays the same. Now it's pi times 10 squared times the depth h.
Divide by 100 pi: about 7.8 inches deep.

stem: Find the volume of the square pyramid.
title: Volume of a square pyramid
steps: V = ⅓Bh
A pyramid's volume is one third of the base area times the height: one third of a prism with the same base and height.
The base is an 11 by 11 square: 121.
121 times 18 is 2178. One third of that is 726 cubic yards.

stem: Find the volume of the pyramid with a rectangular base.
title: Volume of a pyramid with a rectangular base
steps: V = ⅓Bh
One third of the base area times the height.
The base is 3 by 6: 18.
18 times 14 is 252, and a third of that is 84 cubic inches.

stem: Find the volume of the cone. Round to the nearest hundredth.
title: Volume of a cone
steps: V = ⅓πr²h
A cone's volume is one third of a cylinder's: one third pi r squared h.
The diameter is 26, so the radius is 13.
169 times 18 is 3042. A third of that is 1014, so 1014 pi.
About 3185.57 cubic yards.

stem: A cone has a volume of 648π yd³ and a height of 24 yd. Find the radius.
title: Find the radius of a cone from its volume
steps: V = ⅓πr²h
Put the volume and the height into the cone formula.
648π = ⅓πr²(24) = 8πr²
One third of 24 is 8, so 648 pi equals 8 pi r squared.
r² = 81 → r = 9 yd
Divide by 8 pi: r squared is 81, so r is 9 yards.

stem: A cone has a volume of 288π m³ and a radius of 6 m. Find the height.
title: Find the height of a cone from its volume
steps: V = ⅓πr²h
Put the volume and the radius into the cone formula.
288π = ⅓π(6)²h = 12πh
6 squared is 36, and a third of 36 is 12. So 288 pi equals 12 pi h.
h = 24 m
Divide by 12 pi: h is 24 meters.

stem: A pyramid with a square base has a volume of 864 cm³ and a height of 18 cm. Find the side length of the base.
title: Find the base side of a pyramid from its volume
steps: V = ⅓Bh, B = s²
The base is a square with side s, so B is s squared.
One third of 18 is 6, so 864 equals 6 s squared.
Divide by 6: s squared is 144, so s is 12 centimeters.

stem: The cones are similar. Find the volume of cone B.
title: Similar cones: find the volume
steps: The scale factor from A to B is 10 over 20: one half.
volumes: ratio k³ = 1/8
Volumes scale by k cubed: one half cubed is one eighth.
3888 divided by 8 is 486. So cone B has volume 486 pi cubic yards.

stem: The pyramids are similar. Find the volume of pyramid B.
title: Similar pyramids: find the volume
steps: The scale factor is 6 over 24: one fourth. Cubed, that's 1 over 64.
7560 divided by 64 is about 118.13 cubic centimeters.

stem: The cones are similar. Find the height x of cone B.
title: Similar cones: find a height from the volumes
steps: Go backward: the ratio of the volumes is k cubed. 22464 over 2808 is 8.
The cube root of 8 is 2, so that's the scale factor.
Multiply the height of A by 2: 24 yards.

stem: The pyramids are similar. Find the height x of pyramid B.
title: Similar pyramids: find a height from the volumes
steps: The ratio of the volumes is k cubed: 69120 over 8640 is 8.
The cube root of 8 is 2. So pyramid B's height is 4 times 2: 8 inches.

stem: A cone has radius 10 cm and height 16 cm. A plane parallel to the base cuts it halfway up, and the top (a smaller cone) is removed. Find the volume of the part that is left (in terms of π).
title: Challenge: a cone with its top cut off
steps: The whole cone is one third pi times 100 times 16: 1600 pi over 3.
top: radius 5, height 8 → ⅓π(5)²(8) = 200π/3
Cut halfway up, the top is a similar cone with half the radius and height. Its volume is 200 pi over 3, one eighth of the whole.
Subtract: 1400 pi over 3 cubic centimeters are left.

stem: Find the surface area of the sphere. Round to the nearest hundredth.
title: Surface area of a sphere from the radius
steps: S = 4πr²
The surface area of a sphere is 4 pi r squared: exactly 4 of its great circles.
The radius is 4. 4 squared is 16, times 4 is 64 pi.
About 201.06 square inches.

stem: Find the surface area of the sphere. Round to the nearest hundredth.
title: Surface area of a sphere from the diameter
steps: The segment goes all the way across, so it's a diameter. Halve it: the radius is 9.
4 pi r squared: 4 times 81 is 324 pi.
About 1017.88 square centimeters.

stem: Find the surface area of the sphere. The circumference of a great circle is 30π yd. Round to the nearest hundredth.
title: Surface area of a sphere from a great circle
steps: A great circle goes around the widest part of the sphere, so it has the sphere's radius. 2 pi r is 30 pi, so r is 15.
4 pi times 225 is 900 pi, about 2827.43 square yards.

stem: Find the radius of a sphere with a surface area of 144π square meters.
title: Radius of a sphere from its surface area
steps: S = 4πr² → 144π = 4πr²
Put the surface area into the formula.
r² = 36 → r = 6 m
Divide both sides by 4 pi: r squared is 36, so r is 6 meters.

stem: Find the diameter of a sphere with a surface area of 1444π square meters.
title: Diameter of a sphere from its surface area
steps: Divide by 4 pi: r squared is 361, so the radius is 19.
The diameter is twice the radius: 38 meters.

stem: Find the volume of the sphere. Round to the nearest hundredth.
title: Volume of a sphere from the radius
steps: V = ⁴⁄₃πr³
The volume of a sphere is four thirds pi r cubed.
The radius is 4, and 4 cubed is 64. Four thirds of 64 is about 85.33.
So about 85.33 pi, or 268.08 cubic inches.

stem: Find the volume of the sphere. Round to the nearest hundredth.
title: Volume of a sphere from the diameter
steps: The segment goes all the way across, so it's a diameter. The radius is 9.
9 cubed is 729, and four thirds of 729 is 972.
972 pi is about 3053.63 cubic centimeters.

stem: Find the volume of the sphere. The circumference of a great circle is 30π yd. Round to the nearest hundredth.
title: Volume of a sphere from a great circle
steps: The great circle has the sphere's radius: 2 pi r is 30 pi, so r is 15.
15 cubed is 3375. Four thirds of that is 4500.
4500 pi is about 14137.17 cubic yards.

stem: Find the volume of a sphere with a surface area of 400π yd². Round to the nearest hundredth.
title: Volume of a sphere from its surface area
steps: First find the radius from the surface area: divide by 4 pi, r squared is 100, so r is 10.
Then the volume: four thirds pi times 1000.
About 4188.79 cubic yards.

stem: Find the volume of the hemisphere. Round to the nearest hundredth.
title: Volume of a hemisphere from the radius
steps: V = ½ · ⁴⁄₃πr³ = ⅔πr³
A hemisphere is half a sphere, so its volume is half of four thirds pi r cubed: two thirds pi r cubed.
The radius is 5. 5 cubed is 125, and two thirds of that is about 83.33.
About 261.80 cubic meters.

stem: Find the volume of the hemisphere. Round to the nearest hundredth.
title: Volume of a hemisphere from the diameter
steps: The segment goes across the flat face, so it's a diameter. The radius is 5.
Half of a sphere: two thirds pi r cubed, about 261.80 cubic inches.

stem: Find the surface area of the hemisphere. Round to the nearest hundredth.
title: Surface area of a hemisphere from the radius
steps: S = ½ · 4πr² + πr² = 3πr²
A hemisphere has a curved half, 2 pi r squared, plus a flat circle on the bottom, pi r squared. Together, 3 pi r squared.
The radius is 13. 3 times 169 is 507 pi, about 1592.79 square yards.

stem: Find the surface area of the hemisphere. Round to the nearest hundredth.
title: Surface area of a hemisphere from the diameter
steps: The segment is a diameter, so the radius is 5.
Curved half plus the flat circle: 3 pi r squared, 75 pi, about 235.62 square feet.

stem: A sphere fits exactly inside a cube with edges 16 inches long (it touches all six faces). Find the volume of the sphere (in terms of π) and the volume of the empty space inside the cube (to the nearest tenth).
title: Challenge: a sphere inside a cube
steps: The sphere touches all six faces, so its diameter equals the edge: 16. The radius is 8.
sphere: ⁴⁄₃π(8)³ = 2048π/3 in.³
8 cubed is 512, and four thirds of that is 2048 over 3. So the sphere's volume is 2048 pi over 3.
cube: 16³ = 4096 in.³
The cube is 16 cubed: 4096.
Subtract: about 1951.3 cubic inches of empty space.

stem: An object has a mass of 283 grams and a volume of 178 cubic centimeters. Find its density. Round to the nearest hundredth.
title: Density from mass and volume
steps: density = mass ÷ volume
Density is how much mass is packed into each unit of volume: mass divided by volume.
283 grams divided by 178 cubic centimeters is about 1.59 grams per cubic centimeter.
not volume ÷ mass
Keep the order: grams on top, because the units are grams per cubic centimeter.

stem: A block of silver is a rectangular prism 7 cm by 10 cm by 1 cm. The density of silver is about 10.5 grams per cubic centimeter. Find the mass of the block. Round to the nearest hundredth.
title: Mass of a block from its density
steps: First the volume of the block: 7 times 10 times 1 is 70 cubic centimeters.
mass = density · volume
Density is mass over volume, so mass is density times volume.
10.5 times 70 is 735 grams.

stem: An oak wood coin is a cylinder with a diameter of 5 cm and a thickness of 1.5 cm. The density of oak wood is 0.75 grams per cubic centimeter. Find the mass of the coin. Round to the nearest hundredth.
title: Mass of a coin from its density
steps: The coin is a cylinder. Its diameter is 5, so the radius is 2.5.
Volume is pi r squared h, with the thickness as the height: about 29.45 cubic centimeters.
Mass is density times volume: about 22.09 grams.

stem: A ball has a circumference of 16 centimeters and a density of 0.6 gram per cubic centimeter. Find its mass. Round to the nearest hundredth.
title: Mass of a ball from its circumference
steps: Circumference is 2 pi r, so divide 16 by 2 pi to get the radius: about 2.55.
V = ⁴⁄₃πr³ ≈ 69.17 cm³
The ball is a sphere: four thirds pi r cubed, about 69.17 cubic centimeters.
Mass is density times volume: about 41.50 grams.

stem: A steel pipe is 40 cm long. Its outer radius is 3 cm and its walls are 1 cm thick. Steel has a density of 7.8 g/cm³. Find the volume of the steel and the mass of the pipe. Round to the nearest tenth.
title: Challenge: mass of a hollow pipe
steps: inner radius = 3 − 1 = 2 cm
The wall is 1 centimeter thick, so the hole has radius 3 minus 1: 2.
The metal is the outer cylinder minus the hole: 360 pi minus 160 pi, which is 200 pi, about 628.3 cubic centimeters.
Mass is density times volume: about 4900.9 grams.

stem: Identify and describe the solid produced by rotating the figure around the given axis.
title: Solid of revolution: a right triangle
steps: the leg on the axis stays put → height (7)
Picture spinning the triangle around the axis. The leg on the axis doesn't move, so it becomes the height: 7.
the other leg sweeps a circle → radius (9)
The other leg sweeps out a circle on the bottom, so it is the radius: 9.
the hypotenuse sweeps the slanted side → cone
The hypotenuse sweeps out a slanted surface that meets at a point. The solid is a cone with radius 9 and height 7.

stem: Identify and describe the solid produced by rotating the figure around the given axis.
title: Solid of revolution: a rectangle
steps: the side on the axis stays put → height (2)
Spin the rectangle around the axis. The side on the axis stays fixed: that's the height, 2.
the opposite side sweeps the curved surface
The opposite side sweeps around in a circle, making a curved wall.
the perpendicular side → radius (4) → cylinder
The sides perpendicular to the axis sweep out the circle bases, so they are the radius: 4. The solid is a cylinder with radius 4 and height 2.

stem: Identify and describe the solid produced by rotating the figure around the given axis.
title: Solid of revolution: a semicircle
steps: rotate a semicircle around its diameter
Spin the half circle around its straight edge, the diameter.
→ a sphere with the same radius (8)
It sweeps out a whole ball: a sphere with the same radius, 8.

stem: Find the volume of the solid produced by rotating the figure around the given axis. Round to the nearest hundredth.
title: Volume of a solid of revolution: a cone
steps: triangle → cone, r = 9, h = 7
Spinning the right triangle makes a cone. The leg on the axis is the height, 7, and the other leg is the radius, 9.
One third pi times 81 times 7 is 189 pi.
≈ 593.76 cubic units
About 593.76 cubic units.

stem: Find the volume of the solid produced by rotating the figure around the given axis. Round to the nearest hundredth.
title: Volume of a solid of revolution: a cylinder
steps: rectangle → cylinder, r = 4, h = 2
Spinning the rectangle makes a cylinder. The side on the axis is the height, 2, and the side perpendicular to it is the radius, 4.
V = π(4)²(2) = 32π ≈ 100.53 cubic units
Pi r squared h: 32 pi, about 100.53 cubic units.

stem: Find the volume of the solid produced by rotating the figure around the given axis. Round to the nearest hundredth.
title: Volume of a solid of revolution: a sphere
steps: semicircle → sphere, r = 8
Spinning a semicircle around its diameter makes a sphere with radius 8.
V = ⁴⁄₃π(8)³ ≈ 682.67π ≈ 2144.66 cubic units
Four thirds pi times 512 is about 682.67 pi, or 2144.66 cubic units.

stem: The region enclosed by x = 0, y = 0, y = −2x + 4 is rotated around the x-axis. Find the volume of the solid. Round to the nearest hundredth.
title: Rotate a triangle around the x-axis
steps: y = −2x + 4 meets the axes at (2, 0) and (0, 4)
Sketch the region. The line crosses the x-axis at 2 and the y-axis at 4, so the region is a right triangle with vertices 0 0, 2 0, and 0 4.
around the x-axis: the leg on the x-axis is the height (2)
Spinning around the x-axis, the leg along the x-axis stays put: the height is 2.
the leg on the y-axis sweeps a circle → radius 4 → cone
The vertical leg sweeps out the base, so the radius is 4. The solid is a cone.
V = ⅓π(4)²(2) ≈ 33.51 cubic units
One third pi times 16 times 2: about 33.51 cubic units.

stem: The region enclosed by x = 0, y = 0, y = −1/2x + 2 is rotated around the y-axis. Find the volume of the solid. Round to the nearest hundredth.
title: Rotate a triangle around the y-axis
steps: y = −½x + 2 meets the axes at (4, 0) and (0, 2)
Sketch the region: a right triangle with vertices 0 0, 4 0, and 0 2.
around the y-axis: height 2, radius 4 → cone
Spinning around the y-axis, the leg on the y-axis is the height, 2, and the leg on the x-axis sweeps the base, radius 4. It's a cone.
V = ⅓π(4)²(2) ≈ 33.51 cubic units
One third pi times 16 times 2: about 33.51 cubic units.

stem: The region enclosed by x = 2, y = 0, y = 1/2x is rotated around the x-axis. Find the volume of the solid. Round to the nearest hundredth.
title: Rotate y = mx around the x-axis
steps: Sketch the region: the line y equals one half x from the origin up to x equals 2, where y is 1. It's a right triangle with vertices 0 0, 2 0, and 2 1.
around the x-axis: height 2, radius 1 → cone
The point of the triangle is at the origin. Spinning around the x-axis, the bottom leg is the height, 2, and the vertical side at x equals 2 sweeps the base, radius 1. It's a cone.
V = ⅓π(1)²(2) ≈ 2.09 cubic units
One third pi times 1 times 2: about 2.09 cubic units.

stem: The region enclosed by x = 6, y = 0, y = 1/2x is rotated around the y-axis. Find the volume of the solid. Round to the nearest hundredth.
title: Rotate y = mx around the y-axis
steps: Sketch the region: a right triangle with vertices 0 0, 6 0, and 6 3. Its vertical side is at x equals 6, away from the y-axis.
cylinder (r = 6, h = 3) with a cone removed
Spinning around the y-axis, the vertical side sweeps out a cylinder wall with radius 6 and height 3. The slanted side carves a cone out of the middle, with the same radius and height.
V = πr²h − ⅓πr²h = ⅔πr²h
Cylinder minus cone: pi r squared h minus one third of it leaves two thirds.
⅔π(6)²(3) ≈ 226.19 cubic units
Two thirds pi times 36 times 3: about 226.19 cubic units.

stem: The region bounded by y = (3/2)x, the x-axis, and x = 8 is rotated around the x-axis. Describe the solid and find its volume (in terms of π).
title: Challenge: rotate a triangle bounded by lines
steps: The line y equals 3 halves x reaches 12 when x is 8. So the region is a right triangle with vertices 0 0, 8 0, and 8 12.
around the x-axis → cone, h = 8, r = 12
Spinning around the x-axis makes a cone. Its height runs along the x-axis, 8, and the vertical side, 12, is the radius.
One third pi times 144 times 8 is 384 pi.
